Question: How much parsley can I feed my rabbit a day? Does the amount matter?
Answer: I would not feed parsley daily. Maybe a few times a week in moderation, or every other week. Parsley is high in oxalic acid (as are spinach and mustard greens), which is toxic in higher amounts, so while a small amount of parsley a few times a week is very healthy, with lots of vitamins and nutrients, you should be cautious in feeding too much or too often. I usually don't give my rabbit (or my guinea pig) more than a few sprigs of parsley at a time, and it's also not a bad idea to only feed it at intervals, e.g. if you feed parsley one week, skip it the next week. (EDIT: there are other herbs that are also very healthy and are safe to feed every day, such as cilantro/coriander, dill, and basil.) But yes, the amount matters. Parsley can even be toxic to humans in larger quantities, and rabbits are a lot smaller and a lot more delicate than we are.

Question: What Hollywood actor experienced the most tragedy?
Answer: Gotta be Kelsey Grammer. In 1968, when he was 13, his estranged father, Frank, was shot to death in a home invasion. In 1975, a 20-year-old Grammer had to identify the remains of his 18-year-old sister Karen, who had been abducted, raped, and murdered by spree killer Freddie Glenn in Colorado Springs, Colorado. He then had to give his mother the news of Karen's murder. In 1980, his two teenage half-brothers, Stephen and Billy, were killed in a scuba diving accident in the U.S. Virgin Islands. With all this personal tragedy, it shouldn't be surprising that Grammer developed substance abuse problems. He used cocaine and alcohol as self-medication for years; during production of both Cheers and Frasier he was arrested multiple times for possession and DUI, and his costars on both shows held interventions for him at different times. Grammer finally checked himself into rehab in 1996, and has been clean and sober ever since.

Question: As a white person, when did you start to realize not all white people are your allies and not all black people your enemies?
Answer: I never realized it, because there was never a time in my life that I felt either that white people were my allies or black people were my enemies. I grew up in a small town 50 miles north of New York City that was overwhelmingly white and middle class. However, my parents, bless their souls, were two of the least racist people you could meet, and were both NYC natives. From the time I was very little we were a host family for kids in the Fresh Air Fund, a nonprofit in NYC that sends disadvantaged city kids to the Hudson Valley for a few weeks in summer to spend some time in the country. All of the kids who stayed with us were black, and we played with them like all our other friends. A couple of them even came back several years in a row. I was bullied all throughout school — mostly just for being “weird”, although I also changed schools often and had the misfortune of always being the “new kid”. From preschool up through 4th grade, all of the kids who bullied me were white kids. Every one of them. So I learned as early as preschool that not all white people were my allies. I had a few Asian classmates in kindergarten, but other than our Fresh Air Fund kids, I didn't really know any black people until I was in the 5th grade, when we moved to the Bronx after my parents' divorce. In the 5th grade, I had an experience I'll never forget, where I, the weird new kid, was being bullied and taunted in the schoolyard by a bunch of girls (of various races). The person who came to my rescue was Tanisha, another classmate — a very tall, skinny black girl with pretty braids, who put an arm around my shoulders and led me away from that group of jeering girls, talking calmly to me, and stayed with me until I calmed down. I had one other defender at PS 83, a Puerto Rican girl named Iris, who would leap in and verbally assault anyone she saw picking on me. Both Iris and Tanisha were well-liked and fairly popular, and I wasn't really friends with either outside of school; neither of them had to step up and defend me, but both of them did. And while there were a few black and brown girls among my bullies, I didn't see them any differently than the white girls who bullied me — the mean girls were the mean girls, and mean girls come in every shade. I never attributed their treatment of me to their race. Sometimes kids are little assholes, and that's universal. The idea that there are people who see other people as either allies or enemies based simply on skin color is just wild to me. Over the course of my life, I'd say about 95% of the people who have mistreated me have been fellow white people. Whether someone is a good or bad person has nothing to do with skin tone. People are individuals.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What great filmmaker never won an Oscar?
Answer: My favorite: Robert Altman. Altman was nominated for seven Oscars in total — five as Best Director (for MASH, Nashville, The Player, Short Cuts, and Gosford Park) and two for Best Picture (Nashville and Gosford Park), but he never won a competitive Oscar. He was an iconoclastic filmmaker always regarded as a “maverick”; he didn't care much for big Hollywood or the studios’ insistence on meddling with his films to make them more marketable to a mass audience, and he passed up a lot of money in order to stay true to his own artistic vision. British film writer Ian Freer went so far as to call Altman “the scourge of the film establishment”. He was awarded the Academy Honorary Award — the Oscars’ version of a Lifetime Achievement Award — in 2006 at age 81, and joked in his acceptance speech that he felt the decision was “premature”. He died nine months after receiving the honor. Altman himself didn't seem too perturbed about his lack of a competitive Oscar win, having said not long before his death: I don't think there's a filmmaker alive, or who ever lived, who's had a better shake than I've had. I've never been without a project and it's always been a project of my own choosing. So I don't know how much better it could be. I have not become a mogul, I don't build castles and I don't have a vast personal fortune, but I have been able to do what I've wanted to do and I've done it a lot.

Question: Is it ok to put bubble wrap in a rabbits play pen to play with? 🐇 🐰
Answer: Absolutely not. Bubble wrap is made of plastic, rabbits chew, and if your rabbits ingest it they can get an intestinal blockage and die. The loud pops made by breaking the bubbles are also not appealing to rabbits, who aren't fond of sudden loud noises. There's nothing whatsoever about bubble wrap that makes it a good or safe rabbit toy. Plain packing paper, on the other hand — the bunched up kind that often comes in Amazon boxes — can be very entertaining for rabbits to tear and chew, and unlike bubble wrap, it's safe for them to ingest. Eddie loves to destroy packing paper.

Question: Are rabbits high-maintenance pets? Are they harder to keep than birds?
Answer: These are two different questions. First, yes, rabbits are much higher maintenance than most people think if you're taking proper care of them, which is one of the main reasons they're so often surrendered or abandoned within a few months of being adopted or purchased. Studies estimate that they are more expensive to care for than cats, and they are absolutely higher maintenance than cats are. They need a very specific diet to be healthy, and while small amounts of commercial rabbit pellets can be part of that diet, they aren't necessary, and a rabbit needs unlimited grass hay as well as a daily serving of fresh greens and herbs for optimum health. That gets expensive. Veterinary care for rabbits is also expensive, and not all vets treat them. In the U.S., rabbits are considered exotic pets, and they need a veterinarian who is familiar with their unique anatomy, which is very different than that of a dog or cat. Spay and neuter for rabbits can be as much as twice the cost as for dogs and cats, and surgery in general is also more expensive. My vet charges $500 for a neuter and $650 for a spay (spaying is a longer and more invasive procedure). Rabbits are also intelligent animals who need plenty of attention and enrichment, and they're active little guys too, so they need space to run and play. The kind of cages sold at pet stores are wholly inadequate for rabbits, and they need at least a large puppy exercise pen as a living space. With a little effort, they can also be free roamed, as they can easily be litter trained; you just need to protect things like electrical cords and baseboards, as rabbits have an inherent need to chew. Having said all of this, rabbits make fabulous pets for the right owner — and the right owner is going to be an adult, not a child, preferably who lives a relatively quiet life. Question two — all birds are not equal. The level of maintenance and responsibility goes up with the size and longevity of the bird. Caring for a budgie or cockatiel is not the same as caring for a macaw or African grey. Smaller parrots, finches, canaries, etc. are lower maintenance than rabbits. Larger parrots are much higher maintenance.

Question: What is the longest and happiest Hollywood marriage?
Answer: Alan and Arlene Alda celebrated their 66th wedding anniversary this past March. They married in 1957, when Alan was 21 and Arlene was 24, and they are still going strong at 87 and 90, respectively. They have three daughters and 8 grandchildren. According to Alan, they met at a party, where the dessert, a rum cake, fell on the floor. He and Arlene, alone among the party guests, grabbed spoons and ate the cake right from the floor, and he says that's when he knew she was the one. I've actually seen comments online denigrating Arlene - who is a photographer and an author of children's books - as unattractive, and speculating as to why Alan, a very successful actor and always a handsome man, would be with her when he could have had a younger, “hotter” woman. The only answer is, true love. Well, and maybe rum cake.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is a Hollywood mystery never to be solved?
Answer: The murder of Bob Crane. Crane was the star of the very popular series Hogan's Heroes, which ran on CBS from 1965 to 1971. Onscreen, Crane was the beloved Colonel Robert Hogan. Off screen, he was reportedly not nearly so lovable. He also had a voracious sexual appetite, and was known to videotape his sexual encounters with multitudes of women - some of whom were unaware that they were being filmed. In June of 1978, Crane, then 49, was found bludgeoned to death, with an electrical cord tied around his neck, in his apartment in Scottsdale, Arizona. His friend, video equipment salesman John Henry Carpenter, would be charged with and tried for Crane's murder. Crane's son Robert testified that not long before his murder, his father had expressed a desire to end his friendship with Carpenter, whom he called a “hanger-on” who just liked the women that Crane's celebrity brought into his circle. But without a murder weapon or DNA evidence, Carpenter was acquitted, and he continued to maintain his innocence until his death in 1998. Robert Crane also posited that Crane's widow (and Hogan's Heroes costar), second wife Sigrid Valdis (real name Patricia Olson), may have had something to do with his father's death, as Crane's will left Olson his entire fortune, and excluded his first wife Anne Terzian and their five children. Olson, who was never charged or even investigated as a suspect, died in 2007. Based on the evidence, most people today believe that John Henry Carpenter did, in fact, kill Bob Crane. But with Carpenter long dead (and having officially been acquitted of the crime), and Crane's reputation as a highly unlikable man off-camera, we will never know. The identity of his murderer will always remain a mystery.

Question: Has the average life expectancy of a pet dropped?
Answer: No. In the Western world, at least, the average life expectancy of almost every species of pet has gotten higher and higher, as we've learned more about proper care and diet. Dogs live on average more than twice as long as they did a hundred years ago. The average housecat's life expectancy is almost three times what it was 40 years ago, while the average lifespan of a pet rabbit has doubled in the last 30 years. Advances in veterinary medicine and surgery, better knowledge of proper diet, and perhaps most importantly, improved living environments, have all worked to extend the lifespans of our pets. One of the biggest reasons the lifespan of the average cat has grown by so much is that cats are much more likely to be kept indoors now, safe from traffic, predators, etc., than they used to be. It's the same with rabbits; the average indoor rabbit lives 8–12 years, while rabbits housed outdoors average about 4–5, and at least in the U.S., it is now much more common for pet rabbits to be housed indoors than in an outdoor hutch, as they once were. So, no. Our pets are living longer lives these days, not shorter ones.

Question: "plus sized" people = morbidly obese people. Why do people need to sugarcoat everything?
Answer: Um, plus-sized clothing in the U.S. starts at size 16, or 2XL. A woman who is a size 16 is absolutely overweight (unless maybe they're like 6′4″), but “overweight” and “morbidly obese” are not the same thing. At my heaviest in 2009 I was a size 14, pushing a 16, so teetering on the edge of plus size. My BMI was a hair over 30, putting me in the “Obese Class I” category. What used to be called morbid obesity is now called “Obese Class II”, meaning a BMI over 35. (A BMI over 40 is now Obese Class III, what used to be “super morbid obesity”.) Obesity has become a problem in the Western world, but most people classified as obese are not morbidly obese. Many are closer to where I was 14 years ago: just barely into the Class I category. And forget plus-sized models; with the exception of extreme outliers like Tess Holliday (who is actually morbidly obese), the average “plus-sized model” isn't even plus-sized when it comes to clothing. American plus-sized models are usually between a size 10 and a size 14 (as compared to standard sized models, who almost never wear larger than a size 4). They're only plus-sized in relation to the typical fashion model. Ashley Graham is probably the most famous American plus-sized model who is actually plus-sized, and she is just barely plus-sized: she's 5′9″ and wears a size 16. I also would definitely not call her “morbidly obese “. Look, obesity is an issue, and I personally have a big problem with the attempts I'm seeing now to normalize it. But simply being plus-sized is not the same as being morbidly obese.

Question: What is your favorite scene where a good actor plays a bad actor?
Answer: Pretty much every onstage or audition scene in Waiting for Guffman. Christopher Guest's mockumentary centers on the fictional town of Blaine, Missouri, and the musical, “Red, White and Blaine", being put on by its community theater group in recognition of the town's 150th anniversary. The play is directed by eccentric Corky St. Clair, played by Guest, and its cast are an assortment of small town locals — dentist Allan Pearl (Eugene Levy), travel agents Ron and Sheila Albertson (Fred Willard and Catherine O'Hara), Dairy Queen waitress Libby Mae Brown (Parker Posey), mechanic Johnny Savage (Matt Keeslar). Among this cast, the only person who appears to have any actual acting talent is Clifford Wooley (Lewis Arquette), who is the play's narrator. The cast all also sing quite badly, including O'Hara, who is actually a fine singer. The film does this on purpose, of course. Corky is convinced they can take “Red, White and Blaine” to Broadway, but outside of Clifford and musical director Lloyd Miller (Bob Balaban), nobody involved has even a little bit of talent — and Lloyd, the high school music teacher who is actually not only competent, but really good, is consistently dismissed and derided by the others whenever he tries to make any suggestions. Waiting for Guffman is a film that features an entire cast of good actors who all have to play bad actors, and they all excel at it. Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is 127 lbs (5'8) too much to ride an average horse?
Answer: Not remotely. The general rule is that a rider plus tack should weigh less than 20% of the horse's body weight, ideally no more than 15%. At 127 pounds you could safely ride any (healthy) horse over around 700 pounds, which is most horses. The average standard horse (meaning neither a draft breed nor a pony, so breeds like the Thoroughbred, Quarter Horse, Morgan, Arabian, Appaloosa, etc.) weighs between 900 and 1,200 pounds. Pretty sure the Arabian is the lightest of those, but even they are usually over 800 pounds. It's really not until you get close to the 200 pound range that you have to worry about whether you're too big for a specific horse, assuming that horse is full sized and healthy. Also, for the record, your height doesn't matter, as long as you're not so tall that you're out of proportion to the horse you're riding. Being too heavy to ride a horse isn't about being fat or thin, it's strictly about how much you weigh. You could be overweight at 5′2″ and 160 pounds and ride a 950 pound horse. You could be a weightlifter in prime shape at 6′1″, 220 pounds and be too heavy to ride that same horse. Height only matters relative to the height of the horse, not its weight.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Are large dog crates large enough to house pet rabbits?
Answer: No. First of all, a dog crate is basically just a cage, and rabbits don't belong in cages. Secondly, a large dog crate typically measures 2.5′x3.5′, or 8.75 square feet, and even an extra large dog crate — which usually measures 2.5′x4′, or 10 square feet — is not large enough to give a rabbit adequate living space. Rabbits should have at least 16 square feet of living space, and more is better. (Also note that even rabbits in adequately sized enclosures still need time out of those enclosures, at least several hours every day, to exercise and play.) Rather than a crate, of any size, I would recommend a 4′x4′ puppy exercise pen, at least 30″ tall. Assuming you're litter training your rabbit (and there's no reason not to), a throw rug or plush blanket works well for flooring. The pen and flooring combined will cost the same or less than a large crate anyway, and will give your rabbit(s) a lot more space. The lack of a ceiling also makes the setup feel more open, and allows you to interact with your rabbit even when he or she is in the pen. Pens are also much more lightweight and far less cumbersome than crates, which is very helpful if you need to travel with your rabbit. Please don't keep rabbits in cages. They don't deserve to live their lives in cages any more than dogs or cats do.

Question: While discussing racism in the USA, why do I get the impression that black people get more attention than native Americans? Native Americans are almost never included in diverse cast of fiction and movies, unlike black people.
Answer: Black Americans make up 13% of the U.S. population. Native Americans make up less than 1%, and that <1% includes mixed race and multiracial people, e.g. people with as little as 1/8 or less Native ancestry, whom you would never suspect had any Native ancestry by looking at them. Indigenous Americans are also mostly concentrated in specific areas of the country, mainly on reservations. Here in New York state, only 1.1% of people have any Native ancestry, and less than one half of one percent are full Native. Most of those people live on reservations upstate and in Western New York. Meanwhile, 15% of New Yorkers are black or African-American. Relative to its overall population, Alaska has the most indigenous Americans among its population of any U.S. state, at about 19%; it's followed by New Mexico, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Montana, and North Dakota. Most of these states are home to large reservations, some, like Oklahoma and New Mexico, several of them. Growing up in New York state, I never met anyone indigenous until I started going to powwows as a teenager (and even there, most of the Natives were dancers and vendors who traveled around to different powwows across the country), and never met anyone Native in day to day life until I moved to Colorado, where I had a job working with two cousins who were full blood Navajos from Arizona. Native Americans are probably the the most poorly treated ethnic demographic in the United States; they have the highest rates of poverty, alcoholism, and infant mortality, and the lowest rate of education. The Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota is the single poorest place in the U.S. — much of it looks like the third world. But unfortunately, Natives do not make up a large enough segment of the population to really stand out. Having random Native people in most movies wouldn't make sense, because it doesn't reflect reality. Off the top of my head, I can only think of three movies not specifically about Native Americans that featured indigenous actors in prominent roles: Heat (Wes Studi), The Score (Gary Farmer), and Doctor Sleep (Zahn McClarnon). That's because there just aren't many Natives, and there are even fewer Native actors.

Question: What is the most haunting "last moments alive" picture you've ever seen?
Answer: The last photo of Jolee Callan. Jolee's ex-boyfriend Loren Bunner took this photo of her on a hike in Cheaha State Park in Alabama, August 30, 2015. He even posted it on Instagram. Moments later, he shot her twice, and threw her body 40 feet from the edge of the cliff she had been standing on. Jolee, who was 18, had broken up with Bunner, 20, not long before, but had tried to stay friends with him, even though he continually tried to get her to take him back. Before the hike, she texted a friend to tell them where she was going, and joked, “if anything happens to me, you know who I was with”. Bunner called the police himself, and confessed to what he had done, the same day. He tried to claim that he and Jolee had made a suicide pact, but that after shooting Jolee, he had been unable to go through with taking his own life. A jury didn't buy it, however, and Bunner was sentenced to 52 years in prison for Jolee's murder.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What actor or actress was known as a "triple threat" in their prime career period?
Answer: Forget triple threat — Gene Kelly was a quintuple threat, a dancer, actor, singer, director, and choreographer, who starred in and co-directed some of the most beloved movie musicals of the 1940s and 50s. Unlike the refined and debonair Fred Astaire, Kelly's style of dance was more athletic and “blue collar”, his body more compact and muscular than that of the lithe, willowy Astaire. Kelly, who was born into a middle-class, Irish-American family in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, first began taking dance lessons at age 8, but due to ridicule by other boys, who called him a “sissy" for dancing, he quit and focused on baseball, and it wasn't until he was in high school that he picked up dancing again. He worked as a dance instructor, and in his late 20s, branched into musical theater, making his Broadway debut in 1939, aged 27. Three years later, he made his film debut opposite Judy Garland in For Me and My Gal, for which he also did his own choreography, something that would become standard for him. His directorial debut came in 1949, when he co-directed On the Town with friend and longtime collaborator Stanley Donen; he also starred in and co-choreographed the film. He would do the same three years later on perhaps his most iconic and beloved film, Singin' in the Rain. Working in musicals means not only dancing and acting, but also singing, and in addition to his otherworldly dancing skills and charismatic screen presence, Kelly was graced with a lovely singing voice. He was also a very handsome man, with a natural twinkle in his eye and an infectious grin. Gene Kelly is a true legend — a guy who seemed to be able to do just about anything. Fun fact: Kelly was sick with the flu and running a fever of 104°F during filming of the iconic title scene in Singin' in the Rain. But you'd never know it, because he still managed to make it look effortless.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why is it so hard to lose weight?
Answer: For most people (meaning those without underlying medical conditions), it's not that hard to lose weight, at least biologically. Losing weight is a very simple thing: burn more calories than you consume. If you burn 500 more calories every day than you expend, you'll lose a pound a week. The main reason it's hard to lose weight, at least for those of us in much of the Western world, is that the kind of foods that usually cause the most weight gain tend to be both ubiquitous and addictive. Fast food, chips, cookies, donuts, frozen dinners (even those that claim to be healthy) and other processed foods, they're all loaded with sugar and refined carbs, neither of which is conducive to weight loss — sugar, not fat, is primarily what makes us fat, along with simple carbs. They're also specifically designed to be addictive by the companies that manufacture them, and because they're so low in any real nutritional value, they leave you feeling hungry again for more of them in short order. Whole foods that are high in protein and complex carbs, with a generous dose of fat, are much more satiating even when you consume less of them. 250 calories worth of grilled chicken breast and green beans is not the same to your body as a 250-calorie brownie or 250 calories worth of Doritos. The brownie and Doritos are pure simple carbs and sugar. They'll taste great, but they spike your blood sugar and then make you crash, so in an hour you're not only tired, you're hungry again. The chicken and green beans, on the other hand, which are all protein and complex carbs, will leave you satiated for much longer. If you really want to lose weight, cut out processed food and refined carbohydrates, and monitor your caloric intake. That means all of your calories, including those from beverages, sauces, dressings, etc. Calculate your BMR (basal metabolic rate), which is the amount of calories your body burns in a day just on its necessary biological functions. (There are any number of websites with BMR calculators.) If you want to eat carbs, choose healthy carbs from whole sources — vegetables, whole grain bread (without added sugar), fruit, nuts, beans, nut butters, brown rice, etc. Read nutrition labels; you'd be surprised at how many foods have added sugar. Find healthy alternatives to favorite foods — if you're craving French fries, slice up a whole potato, blanch it, toss it with a little olive oil, and air fry it. Voila — yummy fries, with far less fat and calories than fast food fries and with the healthy starch still intact. After you've been eating healthy, high-protein, low-sugar food for a few weeks, you'll probably find you have more energy, and once you start seeing results in your weight loss, you'll be motivated to continue. However, this needs to be a permanent change. The reason a lot of people gain weight back after losing it is that once they lose the weight, they a) quit monitoring their caloric intake, and b) go back to eating the crap foods that made them fat in the first place. A burger and fries from McDonald's, a jelly donut, or a handful of Cheetos every so often won't hurt you, but those foods, especially in excess, cannot be a regular part of your diet. Your eating habits overall need to change or you will not have long term success. And honestly, the less of those processed foods you eat, the less you will end up wanting. I'll just also say, a lot of people have a huge aversion to ever feeling hungry, so anytime they start feeling hunger pangs, they eat something. Hunger pangs are not starvation, and if you never allow yourself to be hungry, you will not lose weight. Your body needs to burn some of its fat reserves; that's what losing weight is. If you're continually feeding it, it will simply run on the calories you're consuming and not burn the reserves. Hunger pangs are unpleasant, but they also pass, usually within about ten minutes. The bottom line is that for most people, what makes weight loss hard is consuming the wrong foods, not calculating how much they're eating, and not having the willpower to stick out some hunger pangs and allow their bodies to burn their fat reserves.

Question: What if my pet is a caged animal? Can a landlord restrict it?
Answer: In the U.S., at least in everyplace I've lived, a landlord can restrict any kind of pets they want. Some landlords will actually allow dogs and/or cats but not allow rabbits; that's how I ended up with my first rabbit — he belonged to my coworker's daughter, and they found out right before moving into a new apartment complex that although it allowed dogs and cats, it didn't allow rabbits. So they asked me to take him rather than bringing him back to the Humane Society. Some people still view rabbits as livestock or outdoor animals, and that can affect their decision to allow or not allow them. I had that same rabbit when I moved from Boulder, Colorado (where my apartment complex had no restrictions on caged animals, just a no dogs policy) to Denver, and I had to pay a non-refundable $300 pet fee to have him. In my current apartment, I had to pay a pet deposit equal to one month's rent for my rabbit and guinea pig. (My rabbit lives in a large pen during the day and overnight, but free roams in my living room every evening.) The bottom line is, you need to ask the landlord, even if it says cats or dogs are allowed. The first thing I asked my current landlord when I called about the apartment was whether rabbits and guinea pigs were allowed, because the listing just said cats. Most landlords probably won't have a problem with a hamster or a couple of gerbils, or even a pair of guinea pigs, but you never know, and some landlords will strictly forbid rabbits even if they allow dogs and cats. And please, do not try to keep any pets if your lease forbids them, no matter how small or quiet they are. If you get caught you could face eviction or, at the very least, having to surrender your pet(s).

Question: Do you think pet breeds that inherently bring health issues should be banned?
Answer: I think that breeds that are extremely prone to health problems due to unnatural physical characteristics we breed them for should be bred differently, for their own well-being. Pugs didn't used to have faces so short they couldn't breathe properly; their breeding has gotten more and more extreme in the last hundred years or so. So start breeding pugs for longer faces again to make things easier on the dogs. Same with English and French bulldogs, Boston terriers, Pekingese, etc. This also applies to cat breeds like Persians and Exotic shorthairs, and rabbits like the Netherland dwarf and Lionhead. Those short faces leave the animals vulnerable to a plethora of health problems that cats and rabbits with normal faces are not prone to. So breed for longer faces. The one case in which I think a breed or breeds should actually be eradicated is that of lop-eared rabbits. It's not possible to breed a rabbit with lop ears that isn't highly prone to ear disease, deafness, ear infections, etc., because lop ears are 100% unnatural for rabbits and don't allow them to be normal rabbits. Their skulls are abnormally shaped as well, to accommodate the unnatural position of their ears, so they're also prone to dental problems (and lop breeds that are also short faced, such as the Holland lop, are doubly prone to dental disease). Everyone loves lops with their floppy ears, because they look like stuffed animals, but that cuteness often has terrible consequences for the rabbits themselves, and I personally don't think it's ethical to breed lop rabbits at all. Question: What are some creative ways to incorporate more physical activity into a sedentary lifestyle?
Answer: Why do you need to be creative? Just go for a walk when you have a little free time. In the park, up the road, around your block; hell, in the U.S., people will even go walk in the shopping mall in poor weather. Several laps around a decent sized mall will get you a mile or more of walking. If it's multiple levels, go up and down the stairs on each lap. Get a standing desk. Standing is better than sitting. Some people will also get a treadmill to use at the desk, so they can even walk while they're working. Park farther away when you run errands or go shopping. Everyone seems to try to park as close to the entrance as possible, but the farther away you park, the more exercise you get. If you park on the street, park your car a block or two away from your building. If you need to visit multiple stores in one plaza or shopping center, don't drive from one spot to the other. Get the extra steps in. If you order food, order pickup instead of delivery. Go get it yourself. Take the stairs instead of the elevator or escalator. Put on some good music and dance around your living room for ten minutes. If you're not physically disabled, a sedentary lifestyle is usually a matter of choice and laziness. Everyone can get some exercise if they actually want to do it. It's just a matter of going out and doing it. You don't need to spend 12 hours a week in the gym, or lift weights, or take spin classes. Just walk. It takes the average person 20 to 25 minutes to walk a mile, walking is a low-impact exercise that almost anyone can do, and I refuse to believe that anyone is so busy that they can't find 20 minutes to just take a walk.

Question: Why are fat actors mostly relegated to comedic roles? I can't think of one playing straight action or dramatic roles.
Answer: Broderick Crawford won an Oscar for All the King's Men in 1950 as a fat actor (especially for the time period, in which far fewer people were overweight), and also starred in the very popular dramatic TV series Highway Patrol in the 1950s. John Goodman is no longer fat, but was for most of his career, and has played both comedic and dramatic roles with equal adeptness. Kathy Bates has been some degree of overweight for most of her career and is an Oscar winner, while two-time Oscar winner Dianne Wiest gained considerable weight in her 40s without losing out on dramatic roles, and Gabourey Sidibe received an Oscar nomination for her role in the decidedly non-comedic Precious. For that same film, Mo'Nique, generally known as a comedic actor, won the Best Supporting Actress Oscar for a dramatic performance. (EDIT: I neglected to mention Gary Farmer, a Canadian First Nations actor who has been significantly overweight for his entire career and is a fabulous dramatic actor.) Honestly, I think a lot of overweight actors end up being comedic actors because overweight people in general often use humor to deal with some of the stigma their weight brings. I'm pretty sure Rebel Wilson, who is also no longer fat, has said that this was the case for her. My brother has struggled with his weight a lot, although he slimmed down considerably a few years ago and has kept the weight off, and he frequently used humor in talking about his weight. He even cracked jokes about his weight directly after colon cancer surgery when the doctor said his weight had made the surgery more complicated than normal. (This is what led him to change his diet and lifestyle to lose the excess weight.) Fat people are stereotyped as funny because many fat people use humor to deflect from their fatness, and therefore are funny.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How do I bathe your pet rabbit?
Answer: Um, you will not do anything to my rabbit, thank you very much. And rabbits that are cared for properly and kept in a clean environment do not need to be bathed. Ever. Rabbits are exceptionally clean animals — cleaner than cats, and far cleaner than dogs — who are meticulous about their own hygiene and spend a fair amount of their waking time grooming themselves (and each other). Rabbits themselves have no smell or odor to them; if you stick your nose into a rabbit's fur and inhale, you will smell absolutely nothing. (This trait is inherited from their wild ancestors, whom it helped to avoid detection by predators.) If a rabbit smells bad, you're not keeping their enclosure and/or litterbox clean. Bathing is incredibly stressful for rabbits, and that stress can make them go into shock or even kill them. In addition to this, rabbits have extremely dense fur that takes a very long time to dry, so they are highly susceptible to hypothermia if they get wet, which can also kill them. The only time you might need to interfere with a rabbit's personal hygiene routine is in the case of sick, elderly, or special needs rabbits who cannot clean their own bottoms properly, and in that case, you should just use a warm, damp cloth to clean the area. Never submerge a rabbit in water or use any kind of shampoo on them. It's not only unnecessary, it's hazardous to their health, and they are very good at keeping themselves clean.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is a completely unnecessary movie remake?
Answer: Most of them. One of the most egregious was probably Steven Zaillian's 2005 remake of All the King's Men. The 1949 original, directed by Robert Rossen and starring Broderick Crawford as corrupt Southern politician Willie Stark (based on ill-fated Louisiana governor Huey Long) was a spectacular film, and took home the Best Picture Oscar, as well as Best Actor for Crawford and Best Supporting Actress for Mercedes McCambridge. Zaillian's remake featured stellar production values, and assembled a cast packed with talent — Sean Penn as Stark, supported by Kate Winslet, Jude Law, Patricia Clarkson, James Gandolfini, Mark Ruffalo, Anthony Hopkins, Kathy Baker, and Jackie Earle Haley — and the film still managed to suck donkey balls. It's plodding, it's pretentious, it's narratively incohesive, and Penn — who I think is a fantastic actor when he's at his best — spends its entire two-hour runtime chewing the scenery in a completely over-the-top performance. I watched it strictly because I had been a fan of Haley's when he was a teen actor in the 70s and this was his first role in over a decade, and while Haley's performance (in a small but key role) was one of the film's brightest spots, it still wasn't worth the time I lost sitting through it, which would have been better spent watching paint dry. Not even a cast that talented could overcome the script and direction. I was not an outlier in my thinking — the film was a box office bomb, grossing less than $10 million against its budget of $55 million, and sits at an 11% “fresh” critic rating on Rotten Tomatoes. (For comparison, the original sits at 97%.) (Honorable mention: the 2008 remake of the 1951 sci-fi classic The Day the Earth Stood Still, and the 2010s remakes of 80s classics Footloose, Poltergeist, and Ghostbusters — none of these films ever needed to exist.)

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Are White people more beautiful than Black people? Why or why not?
Answer: Neither white people nor black people are a monolith. We come in all shapes, sizes, and shades. In other words, people are individuals, and it's individuals that we find beautiful or not beautiful. Beauty is also subjective, so I might find someone beautiful, regardless of race, that you don't, and vice versa. Speaking strictly from a standpoint of aesthetics, there are white people I find beautiful and white people I find not so beautiful. There are also black people I find beautiful and others I find less beautiful. The same can be said for Asians, Latinos, Native Americans, etc. Beauty is subjective, and most often it has nothing whatsoever to do with race or skin color. We fancy what we fancy, our eyes are drawn to what they're drawn to. And perhaps most importantly, whether an individual is physically beautiful or not does not affect their worth or value as a human being, whatever their race. We need to stop putting people in boxes based on stupid things like skin color, and making these inane comparisons like “which race is more beautiful”. Such things treat humans as nothing more than the color of their skin, regardless of what that color is, when we are all the same underneath and we are all individuals. Neither black people nor white people are objectively or on the whole “more beautiful”. Neither are Asians or indigenous people, e.g. Maori, aboriginal Australians, or indigenous North and South Americans. Races aren't beautiful. People are.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How long do rabbits live?
Answer: Domestic rabbits? It depends on a few factors, including their breed/size — smaller rabbits, like smaller dogs, tend to live longer than larger ones, mixed breeds often live longer and have fewer health problems than purebreds, and lop-eared breeds are more prone to certain health issues than erect-eared breeds — as well as their general care, diet, and living conditions. The English lop, a large (10–12lb) breed with lop ears, only lives an average of five to seven years, while the tiny, 2lb Netherland dwarf averages 10 to 12. Indoor rabbits live considerably longer on average than outdoor rabbits, and rabbits who are fed a balanced and proper diet live longer than those who are not. In females, spaying usually increases life expectancy significantly, as uterine and ovarian cancer are very common in older, unspayed does. (Unaltered bucks can get testicular or prostate cancer, but it's much less common, and neutering males is usually done more to fix behavioral problems than for health reasons.) In the UK, where it's still more common to house rabbits outdoors than in, the average lifespan of a pet rabbit is just over four years, according to this study: Rabbits housed outdoors are highly susceptible to flystrike, wherein botflies or blowflies lay eggs on the rabbit and the resulting maggots eat the rabbit's flesh, and flystrike is the leading cause of death of pet rabbits in the UK. Keeping pet rabbits inside, as is much more common in the U.S., doesn't completely eliminate the risk of flystrike, but it greatly reduces it, thus rabbits in the U.S. tend to live longer on average than they do in the UK. (EDIT: I should also add that rabbits kept indoors are also much easier to keep tabs on, which means that illness and injuries are usually detected sooner than in outdoor rabbits. Gastrointestinal stasis, which occurs when a rabbit stops eating and the GI tract slows down or stops, can kill a rabbit very quickly, and if your rabbit lives inside with you, you're likely to notice much sooner if he or she stops eating.) Generally speaking, and taking breed and size into consideration, a well-cared-for pet rabbit can be expected to live anywhere from 7 to 12 years, with some making it to 14 or 15. (The record for a domestic rabbit is 18 years.) And when I say “well-cared-for”, that absolutely includes indoor housing: thirty years ago, when it was still more common to keep rabbits in hutches outdoors, the average lifespan of a rabbit in the U.S. was generally estimated at five to seven years — almost half what it is today. So if you want your rabbits to live a long and healthy life, keep them inside with you.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How did Americans get so fat?
Answer: Hold on, kids, it's time for one of those annoying “back in my day" answers from a middle-aged American. I was born in 1973 and grew up in a small, semirural town in the NYC metro area. I didn't meet a single kid who could be classified as obese until the 6th grade. The only significantly overweight person I knew growing up was my oldest brother, who had been overweight since early childhood and struggled with weight all his life. (In his case I do believe genetics played a role, because none of the rest of us kids were overweight, and we all ate the same things. He was also exceptionally tall and had a massive frame.) Even in movies, the “fat kid" was someone like Jerry O'Connell in Stand By Me or Jeff Cohen in The Goonies — kids who by today's standards would barely rate as “chubby" (and neither of whom are overweight as adults). So what changed? My observations: Yes, I know there are other factors. Portion sizes at restaurants are out of control (which is why these days I'm more inclined to order an appetizer than an entree as my meal on those rare occasions that I eat out), HFCS is in everything, fast food is more ubiquitous, etc. But I do think those two things are major factors in why obesity has become a crisis in this country.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Does horse racing provide benefits that outweigh the costs to the horses? Even with reforms, some argue the risks can never be fully eliminated and the sport should be ended.
Answer: There is absolutely zero benefit to the horses, any more than there's a benefit to the cars in a NASCAR race. Racehorses are a commodity, and exist solely to make money for their owners. A glorified version of the New York City carriage horse. In addition to the seven horses that died at Churchill Downs this year during Derby week, three horses died at Aintree in England during the Grand National festival, and 62 horses have died at Aintree since 2000. At Santa Anita racetrack in California, 42 horses died in 2019 alone, and six have died so far this year, while at Saratoga racetrack in upstate New York, over 200 horses have died since 2009. As for the surviving horses, what exactly are they getting out of it? Other than the Man o' Wars and Secretariats who go to retirement and spend their post-racing lives at stud, most end up being sold when they're either not winning or have otherwise outlived their usefulness, and many also wind up with lifelong health issues from racing. The owners of racehorses have no interest in feeding and housing a horse that isn't paying them back for those basic essentials. I've told the story on here of Press Exclusive, a Thoroughbred who lives at a local horse sanctuary. She was a successful racehorse in Canada as a filly and young mare, winning her owner nearly half a million dollars, and at five was repurposed as a broodmare. She had nine foals in 10 years (the sale of her offspring also making her owner money), and once she couldn't get pregnant again, she was sold at auction and sent off to slaughter. She was then trampled and badly injured on the truck and set to be euthanized, but a wonderful woman named Mindy Lovell rescued her, and she ultimately recovered from her horrific injuries and ended up at the sanctuary (where it was discovered that she also had major dental problems due to neglect). Finally, at 17, she was given a good life. (She's now 27 and spends her days in peace and leisure at the sanctuary.) Press's story is not unusual. This is what life often brings for even successful racehorses once they're no longer making money for their owners. The same sanctuary where Press lives is also home to at least a dozen other former racing Thoroughbreds who were discarded once they were no longer profitable. Horse racing does not exist to benefit the horses — it exists to make people money, whether it's the owners, trainers, and jockeys, or the bettors.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Do you consider rodeo events like calf roping & tying and using bucking straps for riding bulls & bucking horses & the use of electric prods to be animal abuse?
Answer: I consider rodeo on the whole to be animal abuse — because it is. Never mind the calves, steers, horses, and bulls that are injured or even die in rodeo events, even barrel racing horses often end up with long-term physical injuries and even emotional trauma from what they're put through. Rodeo is an outdated tradition that needs to go away. This is not limited to rodeo, either; equestrian sports in general are loaded with animal abuse, including the “classy" ones like hunter-jumper and dressage. Multiple professional jumpers have come under fire for using electric spurs on their horses, and abusing horses during training, and don't get me started on the horror that is horse racing. Sport of kings, my ass. How many horses died at Churchill Downs this year? (Newsflash: healthy, well-bred, two-year-old Thoroughbreds don't just drop dead from heart attacks out of nowhere.) (EDIT: for the record, seven horses died at Churchill Downs the week of the 2023 Kentucky Derby, five from injuries sustained while racing or training, two — who, coincidentally, had the same trainer — who simply collapsed and died.) The problem with competitive sports that involve animals is that the animals often aren't seen as living beings, but rather as a means to an end. Winning is the most important thing, so people cheat, and when you're cheating at a sport that relies on the performance of an animal, the animal often becomes a victim. Tasers to make horses and bulls buck in rodeos (and sometimes used on barrel horses as well), electric spurs in jumping, PEDs in racehorses, soring (use of caustic chemicals and other abusive practices) of Tennessee Walking horses to make them step higher — all of these things are extremely common. (Oh, and look up the “gingering” of Saddlebreds, if you dare — it's too horrific for me to describe here.) Mexican charro (rodeo) horses are routinely abused. Because people want to win, whether or not it's at the expense of an animal's physical and emotional health or even its life. Horses that balk at jumps or don't perform will be punished for it. That German brat during the Modern Pentathlon at the Olympics sobbing and whipping the living shit out of her horse because it wasn't doing what she wanted and she lost her lead. Because in things like rodeo and other competitive equestrian sports, winning is what matters; the animal is just supposed to be a mindless machine that does what you want it to do, and if it doesn't, woe unto it. Animal cruelty laws have come a long way in the United States, but for some reason, “livestock” like horses and cattle don't seem to get the same consideration or protection that pets like dogs and cats do. Which is why rodeo and equestrian sports are still a thing in the first place. I'm not saying that all competitive equestrians or rodeo performers are abusive, plenty are not, but humans are competitive by nature, and unfortunately, many are also cruel. Rodeo is abusive by its very nature.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why did "authorities" steal someones rabbit? This story snopes.com/fact-check/sumatran-rabbit-rescued-Facebook shows the government abducting a rare little bunny from its owners. Why stop rare animal breeding? Why go after any pet that isn't cliché?

On top of this, Facebook's policies expressly prohibit the sale of animals on the platform by private users, regardless of whether the animal is endangered. Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Can I adopt another female rabbit if my current one already is 2 years old? Will they be able to bond?
Answer: Rabbits can bond at any age, but I'm curious as to why you're specifically wanting another female. Female rabbits are extremely territorial — more so than males — and female/female bonds are the least likely to be successful. The best bonds between rabbits are usually male/female (always spayed and neutered, obviously), and even two neutered males are more likely to form a successful bond than two spayed females. If you're specifying that you want another female because your current female is unspayed, I would tell you that two unspayed female rabbits are likely to fight, possibly quite violently. Never try to bond rabbits unless both are fixed. Bonding rabbits is tricky no matter what sex they are, and must be done carefully, on neutral ground. And again, whatever their sex, they absolutely must be spayed or neutered. And that means both of them; one being fixed is not going to change the hormonal behavior of the other, and even altered rabbits will very often fight during the bonding process (which you need to be aware will not always be successful — rabbits are individuals and sometimes they just don't get along, so I hope you aren't thinking you can just put them together and everything will work itself out — they can seriously hurt each other). So, age is a lot less relevant than sex, and unaltered rabbits are likely to fight with one another regardless of sex.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why can't we breed a dog to live to 80 years old?
Answer: For the same reason we can't breed humans to live to 500 years old. Everything ages, and every species is limited by its own biology. Dogs actually live a lot longer than they used to. A hundred years ago, more than half of all domestic dogs were dead by age 6. Same with cats, which live on average more than twice as long (15 years) as they did just 40 years ago (7 years), and rabbits, which only 30 years ago averaged five or six years, and now average 8 to 12 (at least in the U.S.). This is because we've learned more about proper care (including medical care) and diet for all three species, and dogs and cats (as well as pet rabbits) are more likely to be housed indoors and away from the hazards of the outdoors (traffic, predators, toxins, etc.) than they used to be. It's not that different than humans, really; in 1900, the average lifespan for an American was around 50 years, and now it's 77 years. We've made advancements in human health care, too. But expecting a dog to live 80 years is just irrational. Dogs are not humans and are not built like we are biologically; expecting a dog to live 80 years is like expecting a mouse to live 20 years. A dog's size is also a factor in its lifespan — the average Papillon lives about 14-16 years, but the average Bernese Mountain dog only lives 6-8. Giant breed dogs have more stress on their organs than smaller ones. According to the American Veterinary Medical Association, the first year in the life of a medium-sized dog — say, a cocker spaniel — is equal to about 15 years for a human. The second year is equal to about 7 human years, and every year thereafter equals five. So by the time your cocker is five years old, he's the equivalent age of a 37-year-old human. An 80-year-old dog would be the equivalent of a 412-year-old human. Does that sound feasible to you? Everyone would love for their pets to be around forever, but biology doesn't care about our wants.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why are bluebirds so commonly associated with happiness in fiction?
Answer: Because in many ancient cultures, blue birds were associated with positive things. In ancient China, a blue bird was the messenger of the goddess Xi Wangmu, the “Queen Mother of the West" and dispenser of prosperity and longevity. This was obviously not one of the three species that we properly call bluebirds, which are small thrushes in the genus Sialia and all native to North America, but a blue bird in general. As far as those three birds, they appeared in the folklore of several Native American tribes, often associated with the sun. The Cochiti Pueblo people said the sun's male child was named Bluebird, while the Navajo considered the mountain bluebird a spirit in animal form, and even today during ceremonies, some sing a “bluebird song" just before dawn to remind everyone it's time to wake up. Mountain bluebird: In the Northeast, the Iroquois saw the Eastern bluebird (our state bird here in New York) as a harbinger of spring, that would fight off Tawiscaron, the evil demigod of winter. They also associated the song of the bluebird with happiness, and would, according to folklore, hang dry gourds to attract the bluebirds, so they could hear them sing. (In northern New York state, bluebirds are only seen during the breeding season in spring and summer; farther south they can be found year-round.) Eastern bluebird: It was from the stories of these cultures that bluebirds came to be widely associated with happiness, peace, harmony, and luck. There is even a national Bluebird of Happiness Day in the U.S. — it's September 24th. I encounter eastern bluebirds pretty commonly where I live in New York state, and to be honest, their bright feathers and beautiful song do always make me happy. They are absolutely lovely little birds.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is the largest breed of horses?
Answer: The Shire, an English draft breed, is usually noted as the world's largest horse breed. They average 17.2 hands (70″) tall at the withers (shoulder), and between 1,800 and 2,400 pounds in weight. The largest horse on record was a Shire gelding named Mammoth, AKA Sampson, who was born in Bedfordshire, England in 1846. He stood at 21.2 hands (86″) and weighed 3,360 pounds. Despite their size, Shires are known as “gentle giants”, with sweet, calm, and docile dispositions. Below is my super sweet pal Wyatt, a 6-year-old Shire gelding who lives at my local horse rescue and sanctuary, having been rescued in very poor condition from an Amish farm when he was three. He's a very big boy already and potentially still growing — Shires and other large draft breeds can keep growing until they are 8 years old.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: If the Migratory Bird Treaty Act makes it illegal to capture, kill, trade, and transport any eagle species within the United States: can one still care for/raise an eagle if someone gifted it to you at your home, unbound, with undisclosed origins?
Answer: No, because you didn't quote the entire thing. 16 U.S. Section 703 specifically states that: it shall be unlawful at any time, by any means or in any manner, to pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, attempt to take, capture, or kill, possess, offer for sale, sell, offer to barter, barter, offer to purchase, purchase, deliver for shipment, ship, export, import, cause to be shipped, exported, or imported, deliver for transportation, transport or cause to be transported, carry or cause to be carried, or receive for shipment, transportation, carriage, or export, any migratory bird, any part, nest, or egg of any such bird, or any product, whether or not manufactured, which consists, or is composed in whole or part, of any such bird or any part, nest, or egg thereof. Note the bolded word “possess". The law is pretty clear if you actually read it. It is absolutely, 100% illegal to own an eagle, or any of the 1,093 species on the list, without a permit. No eagles, no hawks, no owls, falcons, crows, ravens, robins, chickadees, bluebirds, woodpeckers, none of them. Zip, zilch, zero. It's also illegal for anyone to give you any of the birds on the list. (The list includes the bald eagle, golden eagle, white-tailed eagle, and Steller's sea eagle, for the record.) Get a legal, captive-bred budgie, canary, or cockatiel if you want a bird. Eagles are wild birds that need ridiculously specialized care in captivity, and they don't make good pets.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is it better to get a cage or an X-pen for rabbits? For X-pens, can rabbits jump over them/topple them over?
Answer: As I said in my answer to your other question yesterday, an exercise pen is much better for a rabbit than a cage. My 4.5lb rabbit has been living in an ex-pen since I got him almost two years ago. A rabbit cannot “topple over" an exercise pen, and they come in various heights. No rabbit is going to be able to jump a four foot (48”) tall ex-pen, and mine has never even attempted to jump out of his 2.5 foot (30”) tall pen. An ex-pen 36″ tall or taller will hold any rabbit, and many rabbits don't even have any interest in trying to jump out. You can keep asking these questions, but my answer, as someone who is very familiar with rabbits, is always going to be the same. Rabbits don't belong in cages. You don't need to free roam your rabbit, but there are literally no drawbacks to an ex-pen, and your rabbit(s) will be much happier in an ex-pen than in any cage. When I transferred my rabbit from his homemade, 8 square foot starter pen to the 16 square foot pen he's in now, he was absolutely overjoyed to have the extra space. Rabbits need room to run, and a cage does not afford them that.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Which Breakfast Club relationship lasted longer: Andrew & Allison or Bender & Claire?

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is it okay to keep a pet rabbit in a cage for a few hours while you're away at work but let it out when you come home?
Answer: Rabbits don't belong in cages. So if by “cage" you mean one of those tiny prison cells they sell at the pet store, absolutely not. You can buy a 16 square foot, 30” tall puppy exercise pen on Amazon or Chewy for around $50 US, cheaper than any pet store cage. If you have the space, you can link two pens together to create a bigger habitat, but 4′x4′ is the minimum. Rabbits need room to run and jump and play. Would you keep a cat in a cage while you were at work? No, because that would be cruel. And it's no less cruel to do it to a rabbit, especially when there are much better options available. Get an exercise pen, line the floor with a throw rug or plush blanket. Add a litterbox and hay, food and water bowls, a hidey house, maybe a bed, toys, etc. Depending on how long you're gone every day — you say “a few hours", but even the shortest retail shifts are usually at least four to five hours — you may also want to have two rabbits instead of one. Rabbits are social and need company. But the bottom line is, no, it's never okay in my opinion to keep a rabbit in a cage at all (or a hutch, for that matter). It's an outdated practice and totally unnecessary. Rabbits are not hamsters or gerbils. They don't belong in cages.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What happens to horses that are retired from racing?
Answer: That depends on the horse and the owner. Highly successful racehorses will usually either become studs or broodmares once their racing careers are over and will live out their days in retirement. Less successful horses are often not so lucky. My local horse rescue/sanctuary has quite a few retired racehorses, and many of them were saved from slaughter. One of them, Press Exclusive, was actually a very successful racehorse in Canada as a filly — she won her owner almost half a million dollars over the course of her racing career. She was then used as a broodmare, and had nine foals in ten years. Once she couldn't get pregnant anymore, she was going to be sold to slaughter, which is when she was thankfully rescued. She's 26 now and permanently retired. Another of their Thoroughbreds, Tim, is a grandson of Triple Crown winner Seattle Slew, and as a colt, raced under the name Timothy Murphy. After his racing career was over, he was sold to a university to be part of their equine studies program, and when he'd outlived his usefulness there, he too was going to be sold to slaughter until the rescue took him in. Most racehorses don't have a fairy tale ending, unfortunately. However, one of the success stories of the sanctuary is Sergeant York, a Standardbred who was unsuccessful in his harness racing career, and was subsequently purchased by the U.S. Army to be one of their caisson horses. The good Sergeant actually served as the riderless horse at the funeral of former president Ronald Reagan in 2004, and even has his own Wikipedia page. He was retired by the Army last year at age 31 and sent to live out the rest of his days at the sanctuary. Beautiful boy, and he looks fabulous for 32.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: I put blankets and puppy pads in my rabbit’s habitat, but he just digs them and ruins it. How can I stop this? He is neutered.
Answer: Puppy pads are not ideal for rabbit habitats; not only will they shred them up, if they ingest them it can be toxic and/or cause an intestinal blockage. If your rabbit is not litter trained, get on that. Neutered rabbits are usually very easy to litter train with the right setup (a large cat litterbox and either recycled paper or pelleted pine litter, with the rabbit's hay either in or above the litterbox). If your rabbit is properly litter trained, puppy pads are totally unnecessary. You also don't specify the size of the enclosure; it should be 16 square feet at a minimum. If your rabbit is digging a lot, he's probably bored. You can make him a digging box with a large cardboard box and shredded paper, and scatter some treats, pellets, or dried herbs in it to encourage foraging. Get him some enrichment toys and puzzles — even puzzles made for dogs can work very well with rabbits. They're intelligent animals that need stimulation, and, especially if they're single rabbits, they need a lot of attention. If you're not able to spend at least several hours a day interacting with your rabbit, including lots of free roam time in a rabbit-proofed space, you should consider getting another rabbit, preferably a spayed female, as a companion. Many rabbit rescues these days will even do the bonding for you. A single rabbit can live a happy life, but they need a lot of attention from their humans for that to happen, as rabbits are very social animals. So please consider how much time you spend with your rabbit and how many hours a day you are away from home. If you're not home with him for a large portion of the day, please consider getting a second rabbit to keep him company and stave off boredom.

Question: Why did Al Pacino not get the Oscar for the best actor for The Godfather 3?
Answer: Because Jeremy Irons won for Reversal of Fortune, obviously. Question: What are your thoughts on Robert De Niro having a child at the age of 79?
Answer: Did Robert De Niro have a child? Or did his partner have a child? Because the last I checked, Robert De Niro doesn't have the required anatomy to have babies. In other words, the decision to have the child was ultimately its mother's, not De Niro's. Would it have been better if she'd had an abortion? Or is De Niro not allowed to have sex now because he's old? My ultimate opinion is that what I think doesn't matter, and that Robert De Niro's personal life is none of my business. He seems to be happy about having a new baby, and certainly he has the means to support the child financially. I've never heard anything about him being a lousy father to his other six kids, either. Is it a bummer that he's probably not going to be around once the kid is a teenager? Sure, at least for the kid. But that doesn't mean he's going to be a bad father, and anyone of any age can die suddenly, or get terminal cancer, etc., when they have young kids. Robert De Niro's kids are his own business, and just because a child belongs to a celebrity doesn't mean the kid somehow belongs to the public domain. I'm not going to judge him for it, I just like the dude's movies. EDIT: People, the point I'm making by saying that De Niro didn't have a child is that at the end of the day, it was not up to him. Once his partner was pregnant he had no say in whether or not he became a father again. So whether or not he wanted the child, he wasn't the one who decided to have it, because it's the mother who gets to decide whether to have the child, at least in civilized states like New York, which is where he lives.
