Question: Why can we domesticate European rabbits but not cottontail rabbits?
Answer: For the same reason we were able to domesticate horses and donkeys but not zebras — cottontail rabbits don't have temperaments or lifestyles suitable for domestication. Just because they're in the same family and look superficially similar doesn't mean the cottontails and European rabbit are especially similar animals behaviorally. The European rabbit is social, living in large colonies; cottontails are solitary, and only pair up for mating. European rabbits live underground, in large, complex burrow systems called warrens; cottontails live aboveground and only dig shallow nests called forms; they usually rely mainly on brush and shrubs for cover. Cottontails are far more timid, flighty, and easily stressed than European rabbits, in large part because they don't have an entire colony backing them up or warning them of imminent danger, nor do they have underground warrens to retreat to when danger comes. Even rescued baby cottontails are extremely difficult to keep alive to adulthood because they become stressed so easily. The social nature and relative calmness of the European rabbit mean that it's a much better candidate for domestication than the cottontails. Cottontail rabbits are very common around human dwellings, so many people think of them as somehow not really wild, same as species like squirrels and chipmunks, but the reality is that cottontails are as wild as an animal can be — they want absolutely nothing to do with humans. That's why they can't be domesticated.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Were lop-eared rabbits purposefully bred that way, or did they evolve naturally?
Answer: Lop rabbits, like all domestic rabbits, were selectively bred by humans for aesthetic purposes, the same way dogs were. I mean, a pug didn't just evolve from wolves to look like a completely different species, right? And the English lop, with ears as long as two feet, didn't just evolve from the European rabbit to look the way it does. Unfortunately, just like some breeds of dog are prone to certain health problems because of the unnatural physical characteristics they were bred for, so are lop-eared rabbits. Floppy ears are not natural for rabbits, and their skulls are shaped differently than those of erect-eared rabbits. (This goes double for breeds like the Holland lop, which is also extremely brachycephalic, or short-faced). Lop rabbits in general — there are fourteen breeds, the most common being the Holland lop, mini lop, French lop, and English lop — are highly prone to deafness, ear infections, earwax buildup, narrowed ear canals, and severe ear mite infestations. They're also prone to dental problems due to the shape of their skulls, and Holland lops are especially prone to these dental issues thanks to their added brachycephaly, which causes their teeth to become misaligned. (Brachycephalic breeds with erect ears, like the Lionhead and Netherland dwarf, are also prone to the same dental issues.) Lop rabbits also can't move their ears in the way that erect-eared rabbits can, meaning it's harder for them to communicate their feelings — a rabbit's ear position tells you a lot about how they're feeling, but a lop rabbit can't pin its ears or prick them up like an erect-eared rabbit can. A study done in the UK found that lop-eared rabbits are 43 times more likely than erect-eared rabbits to have narrowed ear canals, 15 times more likely to show pain during ear examinations, 23 times more likely to have diseased incisors, and 12 times more likely to have overgrown molars. Roughly half will show dental abnormalities in their lifetimes. Despite all this, the Holland lop is presently the most popular breed of pet rabbit in both the U.S. and UK, and it's mainly because of their appearance — with their floppy ears and squashed faces, they look more like stuffed animals than like living rabbits, so people think they're super cute. Cute they may be, and Holland lops also tend to have nice temperaments, but personally I think breeding lop rabbits is morally wrong, and I don't understand what's so bad about a rabbit looking like a rabbit rather than a plush toy. My Eddie (who is a mixed breed of unknown ancestry, but probably at least part Dutch) has a normal, mesaticephalic face and erect ears. I think he's gorgeous, and he's also far less likely to end up with the kind of health issues that lop and brachy breeds are so prone to.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What was the worst social media stunt you've heard of?
Answer: Oh, it's going on right now. See this idiot here? His name is Cyril Bertheau (social media handle “2raw2ride”), and he's a 24-year-old from Montreal, currently living in Austin, Texas. In March he announced on TikTok that he had quit his “6-figure tech job" (he was the Operations Manager for a transportation company) in order to ride a horse from Austin to Seattle — well over 2,000 miles — in 100 days, via Texas, New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, Idaho, and Washington, riding for ten hours a day, six days a week. His self-imposed “rules" also included no paying for lodging for either himself or his horse. The unfortunate horse tapped for this trip is a 13-year-old Tennessee Walking Horse gelding named Falcon that Bertheau bought off of Craigslist for $3,000 (and whose previous owner he lied to about his plans). He gave the horse only one month to get “conditioned" for the trip, not the year he told the owners he was going to (and even a year isn't long enough for a trip of that length). Poor, sweet Falcon: Bear in mind that even horses specifically trained for endurance racing take years to properly condition, and endurance riders a) are usually going a total of around fifty miles, and b) use ultra light tack to lessen the burden on the horses. But this guy expects to get a horse that's really not even big enough for him ready in a month. His saddle, also purchased off of Craigslist, is not properly fitted to the horse and is also quite heavy, because it was more comfortable for him (screw the horse). He bragged about his Lululemon shirts, custom leather chaps, and Banana Republic jacket, but also brought no grain, hay, or water for Falcon (whom he rechristened “Shiok”, but I will continue to call Falcon), and stated that he expects the horse to live off of “ditch grass”. His saddle, gear, and other tack weigh over 60 pounds, and he's probably at least 160, meaning the horse, who appears to weigh less than 1,000 pounds even in the early photos, is loaded with way too much stuff even for a one hour trail ride. Several equestrians on TikTok and Instagram also noted that he had the horse's bit in upside down and backwards, and that particular sort of bit is very hard on a horse's mouth if you aren't an advanced rider. So Tech Bro — whose plan is apparently to sell his GoPro footage to Netflix for a documentary and become rich and famous — clearly thought he was going to be embraced, and that people would think he was super cool for doing this, but it's backfired on him 100%. He's being crucified now, even by those outside the equestrian community, as an animal abuser, especially since he's been very evasive about Falcon's condition, and has not shown any photos or video of the horse in weeks. However, other people have gotten video and photos of Falcon, who in the past month appears to have lost a significant amount of weight and was shown to have edema on his belly (likely from the saddle girth) as well as lameness in his hind feet and obvious saddle sores and other abrasions. A source at the vet's office that last examined Falcon, just a couple of weeks into the trip, stated that he weighed in at 850 pounds, which is absolutely underweight for a Tennessee Walker, and video also revealed that the horse's backbone is showing and his hindquarters have lost significant muscle mass. The vet also apparently strongly advised him to rest Falcon for two weeks, but Bertheau took the horse and left after only four days. (Bertheau has said he plans on suing the person who spread “misinformation” about Falcon's condition.) He is also, a month into his trip, apparently still in Texas, and since in the U.S., you need a veterinarian's exam and clearance to bring a horse across state lines, that may be at least partly why. Multiple people have offered him large sums of money to buy Falcon before he dies or becomes permanently lame or critically injured. Cyril reportedly rejected an offer of $20,000 for the horse he just paid $3,000 for — because the buyer refused to sign a NDA. Currently he's saying he wants $60,000. Cyril takes great offense to being filmed by people, and has even called the police on some, only to be informed that it's perfectly legal to film someone in public and he can't do a damned thing about it. Apparently he wants to be the only one with footage of his trip, lest he not have “exclusive” content for Netflix, and also to keep his horse's deteriorating condition under wraps. (Also note that he has no deal of any kind with Netflix, and it's highly unlikely that they will want his footage, especially now.) His last Instagram video shows he's clearly losing it, as his trip is not going as planned — if he's not even out of Texas yet, he's certainly not making Seattle in another 60 days — most people, even those who know nothing about horses, don't admire what he's doing, and his horse is getting much more attention than he is. I don't use TikTok, but he's reportedly been flamed really badly on there and is now posting more on Instagram, and in the Instagram video he berates the “snowflakes” who are concerned about his “poor little horsey”. This dude is going down in flames, all because he wanted to go viral and get rich and famous without working for it, and he's endangering the life of an innocent horse in his quest for money and adoration. Please, you guys — if you want to try to get famous pulling some dumb stunt, go for it, but don't drag innocent animals into your foolishness. EDIT: This guy apparently posted a new video showing that he now has a second horse in addition to Falcon, as a pack horse. From the video, the pack horse itself appears to be lame, as does Falcon. So instead of giving up, he's doubling down, and now this idiot is heading into the desert with two horses in poor condition instead of just one. I'd love to find out what idiot sold or gave him a second horse when he can't even take proper care of the first one.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Do you think a southern accent makes someone sound second class or uneducated?
Answer: What Southern accent? There are quite a few of them. A lot of them sound very charming to me, as a New Yorker who doesn't hear them that often, but it depends on how the person speaks overall. Accent alone won't make anyone sound uneducated to me. A lot of people think a New York City accent sounds uneducated, but my mom, born and raised in the Bronx, had a moderate New York accent and never sounded uneducated at all; she was an intellectual and extremely well-spoken, with an excellent vocabulary. Grammar is much more likely to affect how educated someone sounds to me, whatever accent they have. If you have a Southern accent but you speak well, you won't sound uneducated. My cousin lives in Tennessee and has a pronounced accent, but she's highly intelligent, well-educated, and articulate. Doesn't sound uneducated or second class at all. I love her accent. If your grammar and vocabulary are shitty, you're going to sound uneducated if you're from Tennessee, Texas, or Georgia, or if you're from Maine, Minnesota, or Pennsylvania. An accent alone should never make someone think you sound uneducated, it's how you speak that should matter.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Can you turn an animal who eats meat into a vegan?
Answer: No, because veganism is a human concept, and only humans can be vegans. Animals can only be carnivores, herbivores, or omnivores, and no, you can't turn a carnivore or omnivore into an herbivore. I don't have a problem with all vegans, but I can tell you that there's one specific type of vegan that I abso-fucking-lutely hate, and that's the vegan who imposes a vegan lifestyle on non-herbivorous pets. Dogs are scavenging carnivores, meaning they can survive on plant material but will not thrive on it, and their digestive systems are built primarily to digest meat. (Remember that dogs share 99.8% of their DNA with wolves.) Cats, as well as ferrets, are obligate carnivores, meaning they cannot live without meat. They need the taurine in meat or they will die. (All snakes are also obligate carnivores.) The vegan who keeps dogs and cats (or ferrets or snakes) as pets and imposes vegan diets on them is an animal abuser. Full stop, 100%. Even if these animals could survive long-term on vegan diets — and there's very little hard evidence that they can — they don't thrive on them, and perhaps most importantly, they would not choose to eat those diets if they were given a choice in the matter. So, for people who think it's wrong to eat honey or eggs because the bees and chickens didn't consent to giving them to us, or that it's wrong to ride horses because they didn't invite us onto their backs, to then say that it's perfectly ethical to force a vegan diet on a carnivorous animal that would happily eat meat if given the choice, requires a feat of mental gymnastics that would win gold in the hypocrisy Olympics. I'll add that I also think it's wrong to force omnivorous animals to eat vegan diets. Hamsters are omnivores, as are gerbils, rats, and mice. They don't necessarily need animal products to survive, but they enjoy them — give a rat a bit of liver or scrambled egg and you'll see — and they thrive when they have that variety in their diets, because that's what they were built to eat. People always say that if you can't stand to feed animals meat, you should get herbivorous pets, like rabbits or guinea pigs, but personally, I don't endorse this. As a rabbit and guinea pig owner, I adore my pets, but I chose them because I actually wanted rabbits and guinea pigs — they shouldn't be a substitute for another animal, and nobody should choose a pet based solely on its diet. Besides, anyone who is willing to impose their moral standards on an animal probably shouldn't have pets at all, because that's just selfish.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Adult always say that they wish today's children lived how they themselves live as children. Was their way of living really the best possible and will today's generation say the same about future generations as adults?
Answer: I think there were aspects of childhood in the pre-internet era that were much better than today, and I think there were aspects that were worse. Look, the internet is a marvelous thing, but it's also a horrible thing. Propaganda is everywhere, and image has become all-powerful. Instagram models, TikTok stars, YouTube famous, the cesspools of Facebook and Twitter. Impossible beauty and living standards are on display every day, and while those of us who are more seasoned may realize that most of it is smoke and mirrors, kids are more impressionable, and much more apt to try to emulate these false realities they see on social media. If you can't be as beautiful as these beauty YouTubers or Insta models, your life sucks. Kylie Jenner had to buy herself a new face, because the one she was born with wasn’t good enough for a life lived in public; now she's what, 24?, and looks like she's 35. The rise of TikTok has everyone trying to gain clout, go viral, and become internet famous. When someone as devoid of talent or charm as Logan Paul can become rich and famous overnight, something isn't right. The technology era has also eaten away at interpersonal relationships among kids, and a lot of visceral experience is lost. Instead of talking to your friends on the phone, it's texting. Instead of going outside and exploring the woods, or playing baseball or soccer, or riding their bikes, kids are inside on social media or playing video games. Many kids today live largely virtual lives, which is very isolating and affects social skills negatively. Even at parties and social gatherings, nine out of ten kids will spend half their time or more staring at their phones, and documenting experiences for Instagram or Snapchat seems to be more important than actually living the experience. Shit, look at any random photo from a concert — 90% of the people are watching it through their phone cameras. Bullying has also been turned up to eleven thanks to social media. I was bullied all through school, but once I got off the school bus at the end of the day, the bullies couldn't get me. I was safe. Today there's no escape, and the number of kids who have committed suicide because they're being bullied online, or someone takes embarrassing photos of them and shares them, is alarming. Kids in my era did commit suicide due to bullying and ostracization — my friend Pete was one of those kids — but not nearly to the degree that they do now. Sexual predators also have much easier access to children thanks to the web. Anyone can pretend to be anyone online, and kids are naive. Having said all this, today's kids also live in a world where diversity is valued more highly and it's much more acceptable to be who you are than it was back in my day. I can think of at least three friends of mine from elementary or high school who were closeted back then and didn't come out until years or even decades later. One of them, whom I've known since the sixth grade, only came out last year — at age 49. She married a man, had two kids, tried over and over to live the life she thought she was supposed to. In the Bronx in 1984, if you were a girl who liked other girls, you just didn't come out and say it, even to yourself. (And forget telling someone you're non-binary or asking them to use neopronouns.) LGBTQ+ people in media were portrayed as oddballs or stereotypes; prior to the 1990s, there were very few genuine and compassionate portrayals of LGBTQ+ in the entertainment industry, especially the mainstream. So today's LGBTQ+ youth do have it better overall than those of my generation did. In that sense, the world is more accepting now. I think we live in a weird time where kids are in some ways much more jaded than kids of past generations, yet at the same time are much more sheltered and have less privacy and freedom. Damn right I'm glad there were no cell phones or social media when I was a kid. The lack of those things meant I was able to just be a kid. I didn't have to try to measure up to some impossible standards, my mom and dad couldn't reach me at any given moment or know exactly what was going on in my life every minute of every day, my bullies could only bully me to my face. Maybe you don't think that's better, but I do.

Question: Why does Colorado have so many more people than Wyoming? (Don’t say it’s weed, because Colorado has had way more since long before that)
Answer: None of the other answers have mentioned that almost half of all the land in Wyoming is federally owned, compared with about 30% of the land in Colorado. A lot of the rest of the available land features rugged terrain and harsh climates, and there aren't any big cities, nor is there much in the way of attractions outside those of the natural variety (which Colorado has as well). The lack of any big cities is a huge factor. Denver alone (pop. 715,000) is more populous than all of Wyoming (pop. 576,000), and if you throw in Colorado Springs (pop. 484,000) and Aurora (pop. 374,000), that's about a quarter of Colorado's total population, without even counting metro areas. In other words, most of Colorado's people are concentrated in the metro areas of its larger cities; the rest of the state is not heavily populated at all. (Almost 80% of Colorado's population lives just in the Denver and Colorado Springs metro areas.) The largest city Wyoming can boast is Cheyenne, with just 65,000 people (despite showing steady population growth over the last 50 years). States without any larger cities (200k or more) usually have smaller populations. Vermont's largest city is Burlington, pop. 45,000. Fargo is North Dakota's largest city, with 125,000. Maine has Portland, with 68,000, while Delaware has Wilmington, with 70,000. If you look at the least populous U.S. states, they're all states without any larger cities in them, and thus no larger metro areas, which will also translate to fewer jobs.

Question: Do US citizens still treat the movie Reefer Madness like it's a factual documentary on how horrible marijuana is supposed to be, or is it now considered high comedy of the lowest kind?

Plenty of American senior citizens were potheads themselves 40 or 50 years ago (and some still are). Almost 90% of American adults support the legalization of marijuana, and obviously, not all of them smoke pot themselves. There may be some exceptionally puritanical folks or religious fundamentalists who view the film seriously, but I would bet they're pretty few and far between. Weed is one of those things that just isn't viewed that negatively by most Americans anymore, and rightfully so.

This is why multiple people, including Collins and backing vocalists Leslie Hawkins and Cassie Gaines, did not want to board the plane the day of the crash, and only did so upon being chewed out by Ronnie Van Zant. Even with a failing engine, if the remaining fuel hadn't been dumped from the other engine, they may have either made it to the county airport 10 miles away in McComb, Mississippi, or at least to the grassy field they had been aiming to make an emergency landing in, which may have resulted in fewer injuries or deaths.

Question: Are some people too big to ride horses?
Answer: Yes. The general rule is that a rider should weigh less than 20% of the body weight of the horse, including tack (saddle, etc.). Whether you're too big to ride a horse depends not so much on your size, but on the size of the horse. A 350lb Shetland pony probably shouldn't carry anyone over around 60 pounds. A 500lb Welsh pony needs a rider under 100lbs. A 1,000lb quarter horse shouldn't carry anyone over roughly 180lbs. A 1,300lb Friesian can carry a rider up to about 250lbs. And so on. Basically, the absolute limit is going to be around 350 pounds, and a person of that weight would need to be riding a draft breed like a Clydesdale or Percheron. Horses are not machines, nor are they mythical creatures that can carry anything you put on them. Riding a horse if you're too heavy for it can cause permanent damage to its back and musculoskeletal system, in addition to causing a lot of pain. It's not discrimination, and it's not even about fat or thin; someone who is 5′10″ and weighs 170lbs is not overweight, but they're still too big for any horse under around 950 pounds. A person who weighs 150 pounds at 5′0″ IS overweight, but can ride a smaller horse than the 5′10″, 170lb person. (The rider's skill level is also a factor in the equation, as a good rider who knows how to sit a horse properly will put less stress on its back, but the 20% rule still applies.) Short answer is, yes, some people are too big to ride horses, and most reputable facilities, at least in the United States, have a weight limit for riders and will ask you what you weigh (or possibly even weigh you) before allowing you on one of their horses. It's not about you, it's about the health and safety of the animal.

Question: How can I cure my OCD? Do you have any experiences?
Answer: There is no “cure” for OCD. Your brain works differently than those of people without the disorder. OCD can be managed, usually most effectively with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and sometimes also with medication, but there is no magic cure. Personally, I learned good coping mechanisms from CBT. I still have intrusive thoughts, but they're less severe and frequent than they used to be, and I've reached a point at which I can usually control compulsions pretty well. (I'm primarily a checker — stove, door locks, light switches, etc. — and also a counter.) There are aspects of the disorder that I may never be rid of; my mind is still always moving, I still count pretty much everything (steps, sips, etc.), I still have a thing for symmetry, but my OCD does not disrupt my life to nearly the same degree that it did before CBT. At this point my OCD symptoms have mostly just become my “normal”. So, my advice would be to find a therapist who specializes in cognitive behavioral therapy for OCD and anxiety. Depending on how severe your OCD is, they might also recommend an appointment with the psychiatrist to see about medication. But I'd start with CBT.

Question: What is "sasperilla" as seen in old Western movies?
Answer: It's properly called sarsaparilla, and it's a soft drink similar to root beer, flavored with a plant called Smilax ornata (commonly also called sarsaparilla), which is native to Central America and Mexico. Sarsaparilla is still widely available in many places, including the U.S., and is very popular in some East and Southeast Asian countries like China and the Philippines. Unlike root beer (which was historically flavored with the sassafras plant, native to the eastern United States), there is no mass-market sarsaparilla in the U.S.; it's typically a microbrewed or craft beverage. (Also, I should add that modern root beer is artificially flavored, because there are components of sassafras that are carcinogenic and its use has been banned. Sarsaparilla is more likely to be naturally flavored.)

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Do Certain animals have more rights than others?
Answer: In Western human society? Of course. Our “favorite" animals, namely dogs and cats, are often put on a pedestal, and injustice done to a dog or cat is seen as a horrific thing. But the mistreatment of other domestic animals doesn't evoke the same level of indignation and outrage for some reason. Horses, for example, are mistreated all the time, often under the guise of “training”. There are still people who use the term “breaking” a horse, which literally means breaking its spirit. If a horse is mistreated and lashes out, it's often deemed “dangerous” and put down. People still put metal bits in horses' mouths, which causes great pain, even though there are bitless bridles readily available these days. Horse racing is inherently animal abuse; racehorses die all the time, and most of them are also given PEDs. Tennessee Walking Horses are sored, with caustic chemicals applied to their legs to enhance their gait. Saddlebreds are also sored and forced to wear heavy shoes and chains on their feet. (Soring is illegal in the U.S., for the record, but people still do it and unethical vets are paid to sign off on the horse's health.) Carriage horses in major cities like New York live horrible lives. They never get to run in a pasture or just be horses; they're either on the streets pulling dumb tourists around or they're locked in a stall. When they collapse from exhaustion, they're whipped and beaten. (For the record, horses have thinner skin and more nerve endings than humans do, meaning it's more painful for them to be whipped than it is for us.) These aren't animals to their owners, they're machines and commodities, that exist only to make their owners money, and they get nothing whatsoever in return for it. People also routinely ride horses that are not big enough to safely carry them; I've seen videos of people weighing over 200 pounds riding miniature horses that probably weigh less than they do, when the general rule is that a rider should weigh no more than 15 to 20% of the horse's body weight (and 20% is pushing it). That means if you're 200 pounds, you shouldn't be riding any horse less than 1,100 pounds (most saddle horses are between 800 and 1,100 pounds). Many horse riding facilities have weight limits in place for riders, usually around 220 pounds. There was an incident awhile back where a plus-sized TikTok model, whom I think weighed around 250 pounds, raised a stink because a horse riding facility on Long Island wouldn't allow her to ride, because they didn't have any horses big enough to safely carry her. She called them fatphobic and discriminatory. For not letting her abuse an animal. (One of the employees at the stable did later fat shame her in a TikTok, which was 100% wrong, and I believe he was fired over it, but that doesn't change the fact that this girl thought it was somehow her right to ride a horse, even if it could injure the animal. It's not about being fat, it's strictly about weight. A 5′9″, 150lb person is not likely to be overweight, but they're still too heavy to ride a 500lb Welsh pony, just as a 250lb person is too heavy to ride a 1,000lb Quarter Horse or Morgan. By the same token, a 5′0″, 160lb person IS overweight, but can still ride a 1,000lb horse.) Other animals are also abused and mistreated all the time, often just for clicks and views on TikTok or Instagram. Fish are routinely abused on TikTok. Rabbits are abused on TikTok. Hamsters are abused on TikTok. Birds are abused on TikTok. Reptiles are abused on TikTok. Horses are abused on TikTok. And these videos often have millions of likes and views. We're talking blatant animal abuse, and nobody cares. People think it's funny to see a rabbit thrown into a swimming pool and forced to swim, even though they can die of shock or hypothermia. It's hilarious to see a plus sized person riding a 200lb mini horse that's in pain, panting, and wheezing from the weight on its back. Watching goldfish gasp for breath out of water, or hamsters forced to run Squid Game-like obstacle courses? OMG, sooo funny! Do some animals have more rights than others? You bet your ass they do, and it's wrong on so many levels.

Question: Is it possible for a movie to have no script if it has experienced actors on it?
Answer: Pretty much all of Christopher Guest's mockumentaries — Waiting for Guffman, Best in Show, A Mighty Wind, etc. — had no actual script, just a basic story outline. The dialogue was improvised by the actors on the fly. Guest typically filmed over 60 hours of footage to make each movie, which ultimately ran on average around 90 minutes. This is one of the reasons these films tended to feature the same core cast members (Eugene Levy, Catherine O'Hara, Michael McKean, Fred Willard, Parker Posey, Michael Hitchcock, Bob Balaban, Jane Lynch, etc.) — because they're all actors with great improvisation skills and experience.

Question: Are rabbits scared of their owners or just shy? Why do they dislike being handled or carried?
Answer: Rabbits in general are timid and cautious by nature because they're prey animals. Dude, practically every animal that eats other animals wants to eat rabbits. If you spent your life with other animals trying to eat you all the time, wouldn't you be cautious and alert? A complacent rabbit is likely to be a dead rabbit. (Rabbits also have excellent memories, so if they are abused or mistreated by humans, they will not forget it and will be less likely to trust you.) Having said this, not all rabbits are especially shy or timid. My Eddie is very confident and outgoing, and he's not scared of new people at all; when a new person comes over, Eddie is highly curious and actively seeks their attention and investigates them. But a sudden loud noise will still scare him, certain smells stress him out, and he hates being picked up or carried. Rabbits don't like being picked up because, again, they're prey animals. To them, being picked up and held feels like being caught by a predator, and it also means they can't run away if they sense danger, so they feel trapped. Rabbits are not dogs or cats, both of which are predatory animals, and they can't be expected to act like those animals. Simply put, rabbits are most comfortable with all four feet on the ground. It doesn't mean they're not tame, or even necessarily that they don't like or even love you. My rabbit loves to be petted, I can touch his belly, his tush, his tail, I can even give him a little hug while he's next to me on the couch, and he loves both giving and getting kisses, too. He absolutely trusts me and knows I'm not going to hurt him. But he still hates being picked up, because he's a rabbit, and that's just how rabbits are. If you want something soft and fluffy to carry around with you, get a teddy bear. Nobody should get a rabbit if they're looking for a pet they can just randomly pick up and cuddle. That's not how rabbits are built.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is your favorite horse breed?
Answer: All around, it's 100% the Morgan. I've ridden and known a variety of breeds, but most of the best horses I've ridden in my life have been Morgans. I learned to ride at 7, taking English lessons on a Morgan gelding named Star, who was the gentlest and most patient horse imaginable. When I was a teenager, I regularly rode a Morgan mare named Joy, who was 22 years old and blind in one eye, and yet still one of the best saddle horses you could find; she had all the heart in the world and no problem keeping up with the younger horses. Morgans are maybe the most versatile of all horse breeds; they can excel at almost any discipline, English or Western, from hunting to jumping, driving, trotting, dressage, cutting, and endurance racing. They're strong, with incredible stamina, but they also love people, are intelligent and eager to please, and generally speaking, are gentle enough in temperament for the youngest or most novice riders. They're also beautiful horses — compact and muscular, but with that naturally arched neck, wonderful, expressive face and big, beautiful eyes. And, of course, they're a true American original, maybe the oldest of all horse breeds developed in the U.S., and Morgan blood has contributed to other terrific American breeds like the American Quarter Horse, Standardbred, American Saddlebred, and Tennessee Walking Horse. Yep. The Morgan is definitely my favorite breed.

Question: Is there really such thing as a "bad" actor? If an actor performs poorly, isn't it the fault of the director? Actors can easily and impressively transform into anything the director asks for?
Answer: Of course there are bad actors. Saying there are no bad actors, only bad directors, is like saying a chef must be able to make a great meal with spoiled ingredients or he's a bad chef. It's also an insult to great actors. Do you really think actors like Meryl Streep and Daniel Day-Lewis and Denzel Washington became so acclaimed because they just never had a bad director? Also, a good actor can shine even in a poorly written or poorly directed film — see Loose Cannons as an example, an utter shit show of a movie that still saw solid performances by Gene Hackman and Dan Aykroyd; it was the script and direction that killed the film. Blaming poor direction for a poor performance is a copout. They're two different elements of a film. (Poor writing/dialogue can affect an actor’s performance, but that's not necessarily a reflection on the director, but rather the writer.) Francis Ford Coppola, a great director and perhaps Hollywood's king of nepotism, tried his damnedest to make an actor out of his daughter Sofia. He cast her in a minor role in The Outsiders as an annoying kid bugging Matt Dillon for money; she had like 3 lines amounting to “do you have a dime?” and she still managed to be terrible. She was no better in Peggy Sue Got Married, and worse in The Godfather Part III. Given her connections, if Sofia Coppola was even a so-so actor, she would have had a successful acting career. She didn't because she was a shit actor. (She's a much better director than actor, thankfully.) Bad direction can absolutely ruin a movie, but it doesn't turn a good actor into a bad one, and suggesting that anyone could be a good actor if a director knows what he's doing is naive at best. The best director in the world can't turn Megan Fox into Ethel Barrymore.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What zoos, if any, in the Dallas area have baby exotic animals such as tigers, monkeys, etc. that you are allowed to pet?
Answer: None that are legitimate or ethical. If you find a place that allows you to pet cubs or monkeys or other wild, exotic animals, you can be guaranteed that the animals are not properly cared for and that the owner doesn't give a shit about their well-being. Cub petting is illegal under U.S. law, and as much as Texas likes to think it's its own country, it's still subject to federal law. The U.S. Senate and House unanimously passed a bipartisan bill called the Big Cat Public Safety Act last year, which makes it illegal nationwide to breed big cats or allow the public close contact with them. The bill was then signed into law by President Biden. Whether they're cubs or not is irrelevant. It's not legal to pet them, and anyone who lets you do it is breaking the law. I don't get this obsession people have with treating wild animals like pets. What's wrong with dogs, cats, rabbits, ferrets, etc.? You know, animals that are probably not going to claw your face off or rip off your testicles? And consider the impact on the animals themselves, who are almost invariably mistreated. Cub petting is not good, and it's not legal in Texas, or anywhere else in the U.S.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why do native English speakers like Americans laugh at people who don’t speak English very well or to those people who doesn't have a perfect American English accent? is their english really the standard or are they just being racist?
Answer: I'm American and I've never once laughed at someone for their accent or for not speaking perfect English. Never. (That includes fellow Americans with different regional accents or poor speech.) Someone who speaks even so-so English as a second language is definitely more advanced than I am, seeing as I only speak English (I do understand some Spanish, but I don't speak it), so personally, I have great respect for those people. There have been moments of frustration when I found it difficult to understand someone due to their accent (and I'm not sure where racism would come in; this has happened to me with white people, like Poles and Russians, as surely as it has with brown people), but I've never laughed at or berated someone over it. Communication barriers are just inherently frustrating, for all parties involved. Anyone who laughs at or makes fun of someone who is actively making an effort to learn or speak another language is just a jerk. It doesn't matter what the language is or where the person is from or what color their skin is. Like, if you're French or Japanese or Italian and you laugh at someone making an effort to speak that language, you're also a jerk. And you will find jerks in every country, unfortunately.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why do Americans always equate England to London. Do you not know we have other large cities?
Answer: As if the average Englishman could name any major U.S. cities other than New York City, Los Angeles, and maybe San Francisco or Chicago. Philadelphia has a larger population than any English city other than London, and most Brits who've even heard of it probably only know it because it's the title of a Tom Hanks movie. Houston, Phoenix, San Antonio, Dallas, and San Diego are also bigger than any city in England aside from London, and San Jose, Austin, and Jacksonville are not far behind. There are nine cities in the U.S. with populations greater than one million (and that's the city proper, not the metro area), and ten more with populations between 700,000 and one million. Yet I'd wager that a majority of English people couldn't name more than 4 or 5 of them at most. Many, maybe even most, Americans have heard of cities like Manchester, Liverpool, and Birmingham. I personally also know cities like Sheffield, Cambridge, Milton Keynes, and Nottingham. (For the record, Nottingham’s population is roughly the same as that of Stockton, California, which even a fair number of Americans have never heard of.) But when almost one fifth of your country's entire population lives in the greater London area, and most of the movies and media we see set in England are set in or around London, what do you expect? Cut us some slack, man. I don't care if you've heard of Indianapolis or Louisville or Albuquerque. EDIT: Folks, being able to name Stamford, Connecticut or Durham, North Carolina because they're named after English cities doesn't make you well-informed about American city names. Connecticut has a ton of cities and towns named after places in England, and kids who grow up in Danbury and surrounding areas are well aware that there's a Danbury in England that the city is named after.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Who was the most dangerous serial killer in the US history?
Answer: How do you quantify “most dangerous”? I mean, what makes one serial killer more dangerous than another? They're all serial killers. If you're asking who the most prolific serial killer in U.S. history was, it's Samuel Little, who is confirmed to have killed 60 women between 1970 and 2005, and confessed to killing 93. He was apprehended in 2012, convicted on four counts, and died in prison in 2020 at age 80. The American serial killer with the most convictions is Gary Ridgway, AKA the Green River Killer, who was convicted of killing 49 women, mostly sex workers, in Washington state between 1982 and 1998, confessed to killing 71, and is suspected to have killed over 90. Ridgway, who is now 74, accepted a plea deal in 2002 in order to avoid the death penalty, and remains incarcerated at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla. (Samuel Little was a pretty creepy looking guy, but Gary Ridgway is actually scarier to me, because he basically looks like your goofy uncle who sells life insurance in Des Moines and goes bowling with his buddies every Friday night. A wolf in sheep's clothing.)

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: I lost my hamster a few months ago and I'm still a little sad, but people say it's not that big of a deal. Should I just learn how to get over the death faster?
Answer: No, you are 100% entitled to still feel grief over the loss of your pet, and the people telling you this are insensitive jerks. It doesn't matter what species the pet was, and one of my biggest pet peeves is people assigning more importance to some pets than others. (There are a few notable dog people on Quora who do this regularly, and make insensitive posts about small pets. I downvote and report every one I see.) If the pet you lost had been a dog or cat, I guarantee that nobody would be telling you it's not a big deal. Unfortunately, there are a lot of ignorant people out there who think pets like hamsters, guinea pigs, rabbits, rats, etc. aren't “real" pets like cats and dogs, or are disposable, throwaway pets. This is why so many small animals live unhappy, miserable lives, and end up either neglected or abandoned. It's almost as if it's okay to mistreat these animals, because they're “just hamsters", or “just guinea pigs”, or “just rabbits”, and that's really fucked up. They are no less capable of suffering than any dog or cat, and they are just as able to work their way into our hearts (if we're not ignorant, that is). If you're still sad about losing your hamster, allow yourself to feel sad. There's nothing wrong with you missing your pet. You're not the one with the problem here — the dumbasses telling you it's “not that big of a deal” are. I'm sorry you lost your little friend.

Question: Are pet albino rabbits rare?
Answer: Yes and no. Certain breeds of rabbit, like the New Zealand and the Florida white, are very frequently albino (pink-eyed white); both are very often used for laboratory testing, and also raised for fur, since white fur is easily dyed. (Most commercial rabbit meat comes from New Zealands of all colors.) So albino domestic rabbits are not rare at all. New Zealand white: Florida white: (The Florida white was basically bred to be a smaller laboratory animal than the New Zealand, and was first bred by crossing that breed with albino individuals of smaller breeds, mainly the Polish and Dutch.) However, albino rabbits are less common *as pets* than as production or lab animals because a lot of people are put off by their pink eyes and/or see them as “boring” or “ordinary", and when they show up in shelters and rescues they're usually the last ones to be adopted for this reason. It's entirely unfair, and New Zealand rabbits actually make great pets due to their calm and docile temperaments. (It's also kind of ironic that people don't want them because they think they're too ordinary, yet they're actually more exotic as pets than the average lop or Lionhead.) So, albino rabbits aren't necessarily that rare in general, they're just rarer as pets than non-albinos, because they're considered less aesthetically pleasing by a lot of people.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How good was Lynyrd Skynyrd technically?
Answer: Better than they get credit for being. Most of the original members of Skynyrd were self-taught musicians without any formal training. Allen Collins' stepmother was a country guitarist and taught him some basic chords, but beyond that he taught himself. Gary Rossington was entirely self-taught. Technically, I'd say the best musicians in Skynyrd were Billy Powell (who was a classically trained pianist from childhood), Ed King, Steve Gaines, Leon Wilkeson (for my money one of the most underappreciated bassists in rock history), and Artimus Pyle. Pyle's predecessor, Bob Burns, was a good drummer with a distinct, laidback style, but technically speaking, Artie was the better drummer. Steve Gaines was a tremendous talent, with a natural gift that neither Collins or Rossington had. Had he not died at 28 after only making one studio album with the band, he might be a legend today, and he was as good a guitarist as pretty much any of his contemporaries. Skynyrd have the misfortune of constantly being compared to the Allman Brothers, a band comprised pretty much entirely of musical virtuosos (although I would put Billy Powell ahead of Gregg Allman on keys). It's not fair to compare anyone to Duane Allman, who was one of the best blues/rock guitarists who's ever lived. These were two different bands with different strengths and sounds, and the ABB definitely made more complex music, but that doesn't mean Skynyrd weren't fine musicians. They were.

Question: Is there anything bad that you shouldn't feed your pet rabbit?
Answer: There's a metric shit ton of things you shouldn't feed your rabbit. Rabbits' digestive systems are designed to primarily digest fiber. Not simple carbs, not starches, not fat, not sugar, not protein. They're built in such a way as to be able to extract all the nutrients they need from hay and leafy greens. Among the plethora of taboo foods for rabbits: Grains. Bread, crackers, cereal, all of them are no good for rabbits. Dairy. Pet stores often sell processed treats for rabbits and other small animals that are made with yogurt. Never ever ever feed these to your rabbit. Rabbits can't properly digest dairy and it will also mess up their gut flora. Most processed treats are terrible for rabbits; avoid anything with seeds, nuts, honey, grains, sugar, etc. Just because there's a picture of a rabbit on the package does not mean it's healthy or safe. Simple carbs, especially sugar. A small piece of carrot, strawberry, banana, or apple, a blackberry or raspberry, or a couple of blueberries, maybe two or three times a week, should be the extent of your rabbit's sugar intake. Avocado — it's toxic to rabbits and should never be fed to them. Mushrooms are also toxic to them. Iceberg lettuce. It's mostly water and can give rabbits diarrhea, and it has no nutritional value for them. Cruciferous vegetables, e.g. broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, etc. These will make a rabbit gassy and more prone to G.I. stasis, in which the digestive system slows down or stops, and which can be fatal in less than 24 hours. Starches. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash (acorn, butternut, pumpkin), corn, peas, etc. (Summer squashes like zucchini and yellow squash are lower in starch and can be fed in small quantities as a treat. Always raw, obviously — rabbits should never have cooked foods.) Non-leafy veggies in general. A small piece of carrot, bell pepper, cucumber, zucchini, etc. is fine as a treat a few times a week, but these should not be fed daily or in excess. Excessive pellets. Pelleted rabbit food was originally designed to feed to rabbits being raised for meat, in order to fatten them up quickly, and too much can cause obesity and/or digestive problems. Healthy adult rabbits do not need pellets at all as long as they're being fed a proper diet, and most rabbit vets advise feeding either no pellets or a very small quantity of them. My rabbit, who is 4.5lbs, only gets 1/4 cup a day, split into two portions, and I buy the healthiest brand as recommended by vets and rabbit experts. I would not feed him pellets at all except that I know how much he loves them, he's very active, and I don't feed enough of them to make him overweight. If you do feed pellets, buy plain Timothy-based pellets — none of that junk food-y crap with dried fruit, nuts, or colorful bits in it. (The exceptions when it comes to pellets are baby rabbits under six months old, who should be fed unlimited alfalfa-based pellets to aid growth, and elderly or underweight rabbits who need to gain or maintain weight.) The ideal diet for a pet rabbit consists of unlimited grass hay (Timothy, oat, meadow, or orchard grass), which should be 80% of their diets at a minimum, one cup of fresh, leafy greens per two pounds of body weight daily, one teaspoon of fruit or non-leafy veggie two or three times a week as a treat, and no more than 1/4 cup of plain, high-quality pellets per day per 5lbs of body weight. Chew toys made from willow or apple wood make a good supplement. Good greens for rabbits are red and green leaf lettuce, romaine, spring greens/mesclun mix, escarole, arugula, radicchio, bok choy, basil, dill, cilantro, mint, watercress, chicory. Others that are okay but should be fed in moderation are spinach, parsley, kale, mustard greens, and Swiss chard. Rabbits also tend to appreciate forage in the form of dried flowers such as rose, chamomile, hibiscus, and cornflower, but this is more of a treat — you can sprinkle some into your rabbit's hay so they can dig and forage for it. Rabbits also need fresh water available at all times — they can drink as much water as the average dog — and their water should be provided in a heavy ceramic or stoneware bowl that they cannot tip over, NOT a gravity feed water bottle, which does not allow a rabbit to get enough water at a time. Rabbits are built very differently than other pets like dogs and cats, and while no species should be fed an improper diet, the wrong diet can kill a rabbit in a fairly short period of time, or have lifelong detrimental effects, so you need to be very careful that you feed your rabbit right if you want them to live a long and healthy life.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why shouldn't hoarders be allowed to have children or pets?
Answer: Because children and pets shouldn't have to live in spaces like this: They didn't make the decision to hoard out the house, and they shouldn't be forced to live in squalor, under unsafe conditions, because the parent or pet owner has a mental illness. If you can't even properly take care of yourself, you cannot properly take care of children or animals. Kids who grow up in hoarded houses are often ostracized at school, because they tend to smell like the hoarded home — I've seen numerous children of hoarders say this happened to them — and they can't have friends over because of the conditions in the house, so their social development is often stunted. Hoarded houses are also usually extremely unsanitary and hazardous to the health of both humans and animals. In hoarding situations, children and pets are innocent bystanders, at the mercy of the hoarder. It's not fair, it's bad for their physical and mental health, and they shouldn't have to live like that. If you want your kids and pets in your home, get therapy and clean up.

Question: Do atheists try their hardest to not believe in God?
Answer: In my experience it's closer to the other way around. Admitting that I didn't believe anymore was scary, especially since my dad was extremely devout, and God was so important to him. So, this atheist, at least, tried very hard to keep believing in God, even after I realized that I no longer did. Eventually I had to face the facts and admit that I just didn't believe anymore. 32 years later, I still do not believe, and I doubt that's going to change at any point in the rest of my life. I have no reason to believe.

Question: What buildings currently survive from the Dutch colonial period in New York (state and city)?
Answer: Columbia County, a short jaunt south of Albany, was settled by the Dutch and has a number of Dutch Colonial homes still standing. The Luykas Van Alen House, in Kinderhook, was built in 1737 and is considered one of the finest surviving examples of Dutch Colonial architecture in New York state. (It's been used in several movies, too.) The Peter Sander Van Alstyne House, better known as the Tory House, is also in Kinderhook and was built in 1758. (It's currently on the market for the very reasonable price of $900,000, if you're interested.) Also in Kinderhook is the Benedict Arnold House, built in 1770. It's so named because it's said that legendary traitor Benedict Arnold was brought there to recuperate in 1777 after being wounded in the Battle of Bemis Heights. The Jan Van Hoesen House, in Chatham, was built between 1715 and 1724.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What are some of the most morally justified crimes ever committed?
Answer: The murder of Dee Dee Blancharde. 48-year-old Dee Dee Blancharde was found stabbed to death in her home in Springfield, Missouri, in June of 2015. Her disabled and terminally ill 19-year-old daughter, Gypsy Rose, was missing. Friends and neighbors feared the worst for Gypsy, who had developmental problems, leukemia, and muscular dystrophy, among other illnesses. Her wheelchairs were all still in the house, and Gypsy couldn't walk. Then Gypsy was found, safe and sound, in Wisconsin. She was also perfectly healthy — no leukemia, no muscular dystrophy, no developmental problems; nothing wrong with her at all. Gypsy and her boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn, were arrested and charged with Dee Dee's murder. But if anyone was justified in committing such a crime, it was Gypsy. Dee Dee Blancharde, as it turned out, was a con artist and an abusive mother. Dee Dee had Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another, formerly known as Munchausen Syndrome By Proxy — a disorder that causes people to either feign or induce illness in a child or other loved one with the hope of gaining attention, sympathy, or financial rewards. From the time Gypsy was an infant, Dee Dee had been conjuring up various illnesses for her and subjecting her to medical treatments and surgeries that she did not need. She routinely shaved Gypsy's head, to mimic the effects of chemotherapy, and had her salivary glands removed, which led to Gypsy losing most of her teeth before she was even a teenager. She also convinced Gypsy that she was four years younger than she actually was. Whenever one of Gypsy's doctors became suspicious, Dee Dee found a new doctor. Gypsy's father, Rod Blanchard (Dee Dee added the “e" at the end of her surname for unknown reasons after her divorce) was seven years younger than Dee Dee, and only 17 when Gypsy was born; he and Dee Dee split shortly thereafter, and while Rod tried to stay in Gypsy's life, and faithfully paid child support each month, Dee Dee kept finding reasons to keep him away from his daughter. She moved Gypsy from Louisiana to Springfield, Missouri, where she told new friends and neighbors that Gypsy's father was a deadbeat, a lowlife drug addict who did nothing for his daughter — a bald-faced lie. Dee Dee also had everyone convinced that Gypsy was mentally disabled, and Gypsy was not allowed to spend time with anyone without Dee Dee present. She was trapped, and her only escape from her mother's domination of her was using the internet after Dee Dee fell asleep. (Dee Dee did catch her once; her response was to smash Gypsy's computer and chain her daughter to her bed.) When Gypsy met Godejohn online on a Christian dating site, the plans began to come together. In June of 2015, Godejohn, who was autistic and had an IQ of 82, traveled to Springfield. While Dee Dee was sleeping, Godejohn stabbed her 17 times while Gypsy waited outside, covering her ears so she did not have to hear her mother's screams. The couple then fled to Godejohn's native Wisconsin, which is where they were apprehended a few days later, and the truth came out that there was nothing physically wrong with Gypsy at all — everything had been fabricated by her mother. Gypsy herself learned that she was not actually 19, but 24. Although otherwise healthy, she was also significantly underweight, and subsequently gained almost 15 pounds in jail. Gypsy accepted a plea deal and was sentenced to 10 years in prison for second degree murder. Godejohn was convicted of first degree murder and sentenced to life without parole. Rod Blanchard and his wife Kristy have been supportive of Gypsy, who is now 31 and will be eligible for parole in December of this year. One thing Gypsy said in an interview will never leave me: I feel like I'm more free in prison, than living with my mom. Because now, I'm allowed to just live like a normal woman.

Question: Should I surrender my guinea pig if the other died and is sad? I got them when I was younger and now that I am older I just don’t have time for it anymore.
Answer: If your pig is lonely and you aren't interested in having it anymore (because let's be honest, when someone says they “don't have time” for an animal anymore, that's usually what they mean), then yes, you should absolutely find a rescue or shelter near you that takes guinea pigs. No reason to condemn the poor animal to a lonely life of neglect, even if he or she is older. Please do not just give the pig away for free to some random stranger — there are a lot of sickos out there who will harm animals, he could be tortured, fed to a snake, etc. If you decide to rehome your pig yourself rather than surrendering him to a rescue or shelter, charge a rehoming or adoption fee of at least $30 USD and vet anyone who shows interest, to make sure he goes to a good home. While I appreciate you thinking of the pig's happiness, the question illustrates a very common occurrence, and why I don't think kids should have pets, aside from family pets like a dog or cat. A guinea pig's lifespan is about five to seven years on average. That's something you should know before you get guinea pigs, and it needs to be considered where you're going to be in 5 or 6 years. While a pig's lifespan is longer than that of most rodent pets, 7 years is just not that long, and yet you suddenly “don't have time" for your pig anymore, because you were younger when you got guinea pigs, and now you're older and you have more important things to do. So this animal that I assume you've had for at least several years is now unwanted and going to be tossed out like an old toy that you've outgrown. Please, people, I'm begging you: do not get your kids pets that are their pets. If it's not going to belong to the entire family, don't do it. The vast majority of the time, this is the end result. They're not toys, they're living beings.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is fun about having rabbits?
Answer: Their personalities. Anyone who tells you that rabbits are boring pets isn't treating their rabbits right, because when you have a happy and contented rabbit, there's rarely a dull moment, and rabbits are loaded with personality. While some rabbits are inherently more timid than others, they can also be very sassy animals. They will tell you in no uncertain terms if they're miffed at you — if a rabbit flicks its hind feet at you, congratulations, you've just been given the lapine equivalent of the middle finger — and they rule the roost. (We rabbit people have a saying: dogs have masters, cats have staff, rabbits have slaves.) On the flip side, they can also be incredibly loving and affectionate animals, and once a rabbit loves you, it's forever. Because they are prey animals, it takes patience and effort to form a bond with them, and that makes it incredibly rewarding when it happens. Add to this zoomies, binkies, flops, and sploots, and the fact that they are clean, quiet, soft, and much more intelligent than they are usually given credit for being. They can be litter trained like cats, usually very reliably, and with proper care can live a very long time — longer than many larger breeds of dog. Having said all this, they're fairly high maintenance pets, they're not for everyone, and definitely not for young kids. I strongly advise doing very thorough research on rabbit care and behavior before getting rabbits. Way too many people fail to do this, and way too many rabbits end up abandoned or surrendered in very short order because of it.

We get Newark, the northern suburbs, Trenton, Camden; The Sopranos, factories, the Jersey Turnpike, and “New York City's redheaded stepchild”. Question: Do you have the rights to kill an endangered animal if that animal killed a family member?
Answer: I guess you've never heard of the Zanesville animal massacre, which happened in Zanesville, Ohio, in 2011. A man named Terry Thompson, who kept a private “zoo" full of exotic and endangered animals, opened the pens of all his animals before committing suicide. 50 animals escaped and were roaming the countryside. Sheriff's deputies ultimately killed 49 of them: 18 Bengal tigers, 17 African lions (9 males and 8 females), 6 black bears, 3 cougars, 2 grizzly bears, 2 wolves, and one baboon. The only survivors were 3 leopards, one grizzly, and one monkey that did not escape, and one monkey that escaped was never found. These animals didn't even attack or kill anyone, which is why the incident was so controversial. Many, many people protested the killings of the animals, some endangered and most protected to some degree, and the local police department received numerous complaints about the animals having been killed instead of captured. Bengal tigers are obviously one of the most endangered species of mammal in the world, and 18 of them is a decent percentage of all the living wild Bengals on Earth, but if they're deemed a danger to the public, they're still going to be killed. Is it fair? No, I don't think it is. It's not the animals' fault that Terry Thompson set them free. But apparently capturing them proved very difficult, and the primary responsibility of law enforcement officers is public safety. Any animal that's known to have killed a human will be euthanized, at least in the U.S. In Alaska, it's illegal to kill grizzlies without a permit, but the one that killed Timothy Treadwell and Amie Huegenard was still killed. However, I'm pretty sure you as a private citizen are not allowed to go out and start randomly blasting away at grizzly bears if a grizzly killed a family member. Self defense is one thing, hunting down an animal is another, and that's usually left to the authorities to handle.

Question: Has anyone lost their pet rabbit to a hawk?
Answer: Has anyone? Yes, I'm sure. Hawks will absolutely prey on rabbits if they have access to them, and domestic rabbits kept outdoors will usually be in some kind of run that makes it difficult for them to evade predators. (EDIT: I should note that the size of your rabbit will affect its overall vulnerability to raptors. A 15lb French lop or 20lb Flemish giant is going to be very hard for the average hawk to prey on, but a 2lb Netherland dwarf or 4lb Lionhead is a different story.) Have I? No. My rabbit lives indoors where it would be very difficult for a hawk or any other predator to get him. He doesn't have an outdoor run, doesn't play in the grass, doesn't go outside except in his carrier when we need to either go to the vet or travel somewhere. He doesn't even like to go outside. Rabbits, especially domestic rabbits, are incredibly vulnerable animals. Hawks, eagles, foxes, coyotes, bobcats, owls, weasels, raccoons, in North America, all of them will prey on rabbits given the opportunity. Other perils of the outdoors for rabbits are toxic plant life, pesticides, fly strike, diseases, traffic, and inclement weather (including extreme heat or cold). I love my rabbit. He's a part of my family, just as much as any dog or cat would be. Not only would I not subject him to the dangers of the outdoors, I have a strong bond with him and would miss him (and constantly worry about him) if he didn't share my living space. Watching a movie without Eddie next to me on the couch or lounging on the rug just wouldn't be the same. No hawks anywhere in sight, and as you can see, he's a relaxed and happy rabbit. Very healthy, too, as my vet confirmed last week. I never have to worry about a hawk or other predator taking him away from me. This is a hill I am fully willing to die on. Pet rabbits should be housed indoors. They are not livestock and they are not wild animals. They're pets.

Question: Are guinea pigs basically tail-less rats? Why don't they have tails?
Answer: No, guinea pigs and rats are not that closely related — guinea pigs and other cavies are more closely related to the capybaras than they are to rats (which is why capybaras basically look like giant guinea pigs). Physically, guinea pigs have little in common with rats other than having vaguely similar teeth. Guinea pigs don't have tails because they don't need them. Rats are climbing animals, and their tails help them with balance. Domestic guinea pigs, which are descended from wild species native to the high Andes Mountains of South America (most likely the montane guinea pig, although we're not 100% sure), typically do not climb and don't need long tails for balance like rats and mice do. Guinea pigs are also herbivores, while rats (specifically the brown rat and black rat, the most common species) are omnivores. It's amusing to me that so many people seem to consider all rodents, rats. The order Rodentia is huge, and rodents make up about 40% of all mammals on earth. It's a pretty diverse group of animals.

Question: Do people primarily turn off comments to their answers to gain a sense of power and control, as people can't have constructive debate, or do they do it so the conversation doesn't devolve into deconstructive argument?

Question: What was it like to grow up in a family with a pet that was older than yourself?
Answer: My family had a Weimaraner named Max when I was little. They got him as a puppy from a local breeder in the summer of 1970, a few months before my brother was born, so Max was about 3 when I came along in 1973. Max was like a part of the furniture. A constant in my life from my earliest memories. He was a gentle, dopey dog; my brother and I could use him as a pillow. If he got annoyed with us he’d just grunt, get up, and go lay somewhere else. Although he had no aggression in him at all, he was an excellent watchdog, and his breeding showed whenever a cottontail showed up in the yard — he would point, although he usually didn't chase them. He also always listened when you gave him a command, even to us little kids. One time I gave him a chicken leg bone, not knowing they were bad for dogs, and when everyone started freaking out and trying to catch him to grab the bone I started bawling. I was so afraid that he was going to die and it would be all my fault. (He was fine. Dad caught him and took the bone away.) When I was ten and Max was 13, he became crippled with arthritis. It happened pretty suddenly — he'd been slowing down, then one day he just couldn't get up anymore. The vet told my dad that his health was otherwise okay, and he could live longer like he was, but he couldn't walk, and Dad didn't think it was fair to make him live like that. So he decided to put him to sleep. (I'll never forget the last time I saw him — my brother bundled him up in a blanket and put him in his car to take him to the vet. Max was looking at us with his earnest Weim face like he was wondering where he was going.) It was very, very hard to say goodbye to that dog. I had never known the world without him, and I loved him. When Dad told me the news, I threw myself down on my bed and just cried and cried. Even though I never knew him as a puppy, and he was around 7 years old before I could really remember him, he was the ultimate “good boy". I'm glad I got to have him as my dog even though he was older than me.

Question: Do rabbits get along with dogs? What was your experience?
Answer: It depends on the rabbit and the dog. If your dog has a high prey drive, it will probably want to kill the rabbit. If your rabbit is especially timid, it will likely be afraid of your dog even if your dog isn't aggressive toward it. But despite their reputation, some rabbits are not especially frightened of dogs and cats. (My rabbit Tenacious B used to dominate my friend's big orange tabby, Calvin, who would run away from him every time.) There's a popular Instagram account called A Puppy and a Bunny, starring a golden retriever named Bear and a Holland lop rabbit named Hugs Bunny (AKA “Mighty Smols”), who are best friends. Hugs regularly grooms Bear, they nap together, etc. (Their owner also recently got another golden puppy who has joined the fold.) However, not all dogs are going to be like Bear, and being raised with rabbits is likely to lessen the chances of aggression. If you know your dog has a tendency to go after smaller animals, don't let it near your rabbit; if your dog doesn't have a high prey drive, and you do want to introduce them, do so very carefully and in stages. It only takes a second for tragedy to strike.

Question: Why do actors blame the director for a bad film and not their performance?

Question: What is a rabbit proof heating mat? I want 2 rabbits and I would keep them in an insulated shed outside. It gets quite cold where I live so they would need it to be heated.
Answer: Please don't get rabbits if you're planning on keeping them outside. They will not be happy living outdoors in a cold climate, and subject not only to extreme cold and heat, but to predators, parasites, toxins, insects (especially fly strike) and diseases like tularemia, myxomatosis, and RHD. Even a predator that can't actually get into a rabbit's hutch or enclosure can still frighten it enough to kill it via a heart attack. Studies have shown that outdoor rabbits have an average lifespan of about 3–4 years, whereas indoor rabbits average 8–12. I will never understand keeping pet rabbits outdoors. What's the point of even having them? You're not going to have the kind of bond with them that you would if they lived indoors, because you'll be living in separate spaces. I mean, why do you want rabbits? So you can stick them in a shed in your backyard and just leave them there? Maybe visit them once or twice a day? I just don't see the fulfillment in that setup. Pet rabbits are not livestock, they don't take up that much space, and they're no less hygienic or more destructive than the average dog or cat. (In fact, they're significantly cleaner than the average dog.) Housing rabbits outdoors is a holdover from their days as livestock; it's outdated and unnecessary. In the 21st century, pretty much every animal welfare organization, especially in the U.S., advises keeping pet rabbits indoors. Otherwise they're not really pets. They're just animals that live in your yard. Keep them indoors and you don't need to worry about keeping them warm in cold weather. If you can't keep them indoors, don't get rabbits, especially if you live in a cold climate. (EDIT: I just want to add that I know there are cultural differences in different countries, but the general attitude has absolutely been changing. In recent years I have seen terrific indoor rabbit setups in many countries where it's usually more common to house rabbits outdoors, including the UK, Australia, India, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, U.A.E., and Sudan.)

Question: Why do some people choose not to spay or neuter their pets? What are some of the arguments they give and what are the benefits of spaying or neutering animals?
Answer: So, Eddie went to the vet today. I've been considering neutering him, because all the rabbit websites and YouTubers say it's imperative, and I wanted a full exam done. (My vet is a rabbit specialist recommended by the House Rabbit Society, among other rabbit organizations, for the record.) Well, after the exam, the doc told me that he seems to be in excellent health, and that as long as he's happy, healthy, and not showing the negative behaviors associated with not being neutered — which in male rabbits usually means aggression, humping everything in their general vicinity, and spraying urine all over the place — that it's not worth the risk of the surgery and anesthesia. (She did also stress that if he was a female, she would insist on spaying, because unspayed female rabbits are at risk of serious health conditions, especially uterine or ovarian cancer, as they age. Unaltered male rabbits are not subject to the same health risks, as testicular/prostate cancer is extremely rare in rabbits.) I told her I know he can't ever have a rabbit companion unless he gets neutered (although I am not in a position to be able to get a second rabbit at present), and she said some rabbits can be fine without another rabbit, that bonding often fails, and as long as he doesn't seem to be lonely or depressed, he's probably okay being alone provided he gets enough attention and love (and I assure you, he does). Because he is still young, I can also opt to neuter him later if I decide to get another rabbit. I'll be honest — I was incredibly relieved to hear her say this. Eddie is my whole world, and if I put him through an elective surgery and something went wrong, I would end up in a padded room. I've read so many horror stories of male rabbits who are holy terrors due to hormones — biting, lunging, charging, humping everyone and everything, spraying urine on everyone and everything, etc. That just isn't Eddie. He's a super mellow, ridiculously sweet little guy, and the worst of his hormonal behavior (which invariably comes in spring) amounts to him circling my feet, and pooping and maybe dribbling a little pee on the couch here and there for a month or so (my couch is covered by a waterproof couch protector). Then he's back to not peeing or pooping anywhere but in his litterbox, and even when he's hormonal, he's as sweet as ever. (I even got him a stuffed animal, figuring he could vent his sexual frustration by humping it, but he never has. He mostly just ignores it.) So for me, the reason I am not currently planning on neutering my rabbit is that the potential benefits of doing so do not outweigh the inherent risks that come with surgery. Rabbits are delicate creatures, and putting them under anesthesia carries more risk than it does with a dog or cat. If he is happy, and my very qualified and experienced rabbit vet advises against neutering him at this time, I see no reason to do it.

Question: What is the missing report of Warlock actor Julian Sands?
Answer: Somehow I only heard about this the other day. Sands, who had just turned 65, was an experienced and avid hiker, but the area he was last known to be hiking in — Mount San Antonio, also called Mount Baldy — was hit by severe weather shortly after he was last heard from, which impeded the initial search for him (a search his three children took part in), and avalanches were reported in the region. I understand that as long as no body has been found, we don't know for sure that Sands is dead, but it's been nearly three months since his disappearance, and the odds that he's somehow still alive are almost nil. So while I've enjoyed a lot of his work, and I'd love a miracle, I'm pretty sure that Julian Sands is dead, and I feel terrible for his family and friends. I hope they get closure one way or the other.

Question: What are some good forgotten obscure TV shows from the '80s, '90s and '00s?
Answer: Brothers. I was thinking about this show recently, and it seems to have fallen through the cracks of television history, which kind of sucks, because I remember it being a really good show. Brothers was a Showtime series set in Philadelphia and focusing on the Waters brothers — oldest brother Lou (Brandon Maggart), a construction foreman, middle brother Joe (Robert Walden), a retired NFL player, and youngest brother Cliff (Paul Regina), an aspiring chef. It was pretty groundbreaking for its time, as Cliff comes out as gay in the first episode; the series centered on his and his brothers' adapting to this, and dealt with homosexuality in a fair and realistic way. Cliff becomes more confident and self-assured for having come out, and while his two conservative brothers react differently to the news that he's gay — with Joe being more open-minded and accepting, while Lou is accepting, but believes Cliff might be going through a phase — both continue to love and support him. Cliff also becomes friends with Donald (Philip Charles MacKenzie), an openly gay, flamboyant man who helps the more masculine (and until recently, closeted) Cliff adjust and navigate his new, out world; Donald often gets the last laugh on Lou, who finds his flamboyance unsettling. The show ran for five seasons, from 1984 to 1989, and was critically acclaimed, but for some reason almost nobody seems to remember it now. (Maybe because it was a premium cable series, and fewer people had premium cable channels back then?) Disappointingly, Showtime has declined to offer it for streaming or on DVD, and there are actually online petitions urging them to do so. I hope they do someday, because I would love to get to watch it again. Clockwise from top left: Walden, Regina, MacKenzie, Maggart.
