Question: Should I separate both my rabbits until they're fixed? Will it be stressful to them? 1 male, 1 female, 4mths old frm the same litter. I wanted to get them fixed but the vet said to wait til abt 6mths old, and my male has started mounting the female.
Answer: Unless you want lots of kits, separate them immediately. Your female could potentially already be pregnant, although males reach sexual maturity somewhat earlier than females (around three to four months, as opposed to four to six months). Pregnancy is also stressful to does, and will be more stressful in one so young. (Having your brother constantly trying to mount you will also stress you out.) Also be advised that once they are adults and both have been spayed and neutered, they may not get along. Juvenile rabbits, both bucks and does, form “baby bonds" that can very well be broken once they reach adulthood, as a rabbit's behavior and personality can change from kittenhood to adulthood. A lot of people think that spaying or neutering changed their rabbit's personality, but often it's just that they're typically altered right around the time they're becoming adults, and their behavioral or personality differences are just due to growing up. But yes — separate them ASAP. And you may want to take your doe to the vet to make sure she isn't already pregnant.

Question: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein emerged from a story-telling competition among a group staying by Lake Geneva in the cold, wet summer of 1816. Did any of the other stories told by Byron, Percy Shelley and others ever come to anything?
Answer: The Vampyre, by John William Polidori — Lord Byron's personal physician — was the first modern, English-language vampire story, and is generally regarded as the progenitor of the vampire fiction genre; it set off a craze around Europe for more vampire stories. It was initially credited to Byron, but Byron himself confirmed that Polidori was the author. Polidori never repeated the success of The Vampyre. Suffering from depression and owing deep gambling debts, he died in August of 1821 at the age of 25. While his official cause of death was listed by the coroner as “natural causes", it's believed he actually committed suicide by taking prussic acid. Polidori has been portrayed onscreen at least four times: by Timothy Spall in Gothic (1986), by Alex Winter in Haunted Summer (1986), by Jose Luis Gomez in Remando al viento (1988), and by Ben Hardy in Mary Shelley (2017).

Question: Why do the best dog breeds have the shortest life spans? Breeds like English Mastiffs, Boerbuls, and Great Danes are very good family dogs but they don’t last around long enough. Why is this?
Answer: Because all the breeds you mentioned are giant breeds, and giant breeds don't live as long as smaller breeds. They grow and age faster than smaller breeds, their hearts and other organs have to work harder due to their size, and their size also causes more strain on their systems. (However, a bit of research shows that the average Boerboel lives about 10 years, which isn't bad for a 150lb dog.) It's the same with large and giant breed rabbits. A 2lb Netherland dwarf can live 12 to 14 years if well cared for, a 5lb Dutch 10–12 years, but a 20lb Flemish giant is unlikely to make it 8 years, no matter how well its taken care of. (And the Flemish, like a lot of giant dog breeds, is renowned for its gentle and loving temperament, while dwarf breeds tend to be much more high strung, like many toy dog breeds.)

Question: Is it legal in the United States to keep hamsters, goldfish, rabbits, guinea pigs, gerbils, and chinchillas as pets? Are they victims of the pet trade?
Answer: Yes, it's legal to keep all of those animals (including chinchillas, for those people who answered and weren't sure), although specific laws vary by state and location. All of those animals are bred as pets, so if by “pet trade", you mean animal trafficking, no. These are domesticated animals, and most of those species can be purchased at the average pet store. (Chinchillas and rabbits are the exception; chinchillas are seen as exotics and most pet stores do not sell them — they're also extremely expensive — while more and more cities and states are banning the sale of rabbits at pet stores. New York City is one such place, and is also considering a ban on the sale of guinea pigs at pet stores, because so many were purchased and then abandoned during the pandemic.) The problem with animals purchased at pet stores is that they usually come from mass breeding facilities — the equivalent of puppy mills, where the animals are overbred, overcrowded, and not bred with health or temperament in mind. Reputable breeders want to know who's bringing home their animals. Rabbits and guinea pigs are commonly found at many animal shelters and rescues, and that's the best avenue for obtaining them. Second best would be a reputable breeder. Some shelters will also adopt out hamsters and gerbils, although those species are short-lived and not surrendered as often, and there are rescues for them, too. There are also specialty shops for aquaculture, where you can buy goldfish and other aquarium fish that were ethically bred. In short, the pet store should not be your go-to place for getting a pet, regardless of species. Their animals are not trafficked like other species, e.g. many parrots and turtles, but they almost invariably come from mass breeding mills that don't treat their animals well, and buying those animals only supports unethical breeders and animal cruelty.

Question: Why don’t other rabbit owners provide fresh green chew sticks & grass? I cut grass & chew sticks for my bunnies & they like it much better.
Answer: Because most rabbit authorities in the U.S. advise against giving your rabbits grass from your yard, or sticks cut from trees you're not entirely familiar with. Pesticides used on grass and trees are toxic, lawnmowers can deposit gas and oil in the grass, and you have no idea how many animals have pissed or pooped on the grass you're feeding your rabbits. And even if no pesticides are used on your grass, what about your neighbor's? Those chemicals leach into the soil and can contaminate your lawn even if it's not treated. (Also, chewing on fibrous hay helps to keep a rabbit's teeth healthy.) True story: about 15 years ago, I adopted a pair of rats from the Humane Society in Longmont, Colorado. They told me that they had had a bunch more, but one of the volunteers had picked some dandelion leaves as a treat for them, and it turned out they were sprayed with pesticide. The rats died, and dying from pesticide poisoning is not a pleasant way to go. My rabbit and guinea pig get premium Timothy hay, premium pellets, organic greens and herbs, and fresh fruit as treats. I buy them willow toys and baskets designed for pets. They are not deprived; they're healthy and happy. You do you, but other people don't have to feed their rabbits the same way you do.

Question: What kind of bunnies can you find on Rabbit Island?
Answer: Assuming you're talking about Ōkunoshima in Japan, mostly sick and malnourished ones. The original Ōkunoshima rabbits were domestic rabbits (descended, like all domestic rabbits, from the wild European rabbit) intentionally released on the island decades ago, and the thousand or so rabbits there now are their descendants. But while hunting the rabbits is illegal, and predatory pets are not allowed on the island, the Japanese government also doesn't feed the rabbits, nor are they provided veterinary care. They're entirely dependent upon the tourists to feed them, and if they get sick or injured, oh, well. (Remember that these are not wild rabbits, which can mostly fend for themselves in the wild. As a rabbit lover, the idea of an island full of bunnies is lovely, but the reality is not so pretty. Here's a video made by rabbit YouTuber Lorelei Carlson after visiting Ōkunoshima. Question: Do you know songs in which the singer (band) talks about himself, maybe even about his job as a musician? (Example in the first answer)
Answer: Ronnie Van Zant of Lynyrd Skynyrd did this all the time. A lot of his songs were autobiographical. “Gimme Three Steps” was written after he, Allen Collins, and Gary Rossington stopped at a bar in Jacksonville and Ronnie started dancing with a girl, only for her boyfriend to confront him with a gun. Ronnie's reported response to the man was “gimme three steps and I'm gone", hence the song's title and chorus. “Am I Losin'" is about the ejection of original drummer Bob Burns following a mental breakdown, and the impact of fame on his life in general. “Whiskey Rock-a-Roller" is about life on the road as a touring band; his “Queenie with the long, brown, curly hair” may well have referred to Ronnie's wife Judy, who did, in fact, have long, brown curly hair. James Taylor also wrote a number of autobiographical songs, the most famous of which is probably “Fire and Rain”, which talks about his struggles with mental illness and heroin addiction, and the loss of his friend Suzanne Schnerr to suicide. Question: What actress, never concerned with glamor or ageism, continued to give finely etched performances?
Answer: Frances McDormand. She was a lovely 31-year-old when she garnered her first Oscar nomination for Mississippi Burning in 1988. She then won her first Oscar in 1997 at 39, for her unglamorous role in Fargo. McDormand worked steadily into her 40s, then her 50s and 60s, and unlike most female actors in Hollywood, she refused (and still refuses) any and all cosmetic surgery. No Botox, no fillers or facelifts, no covering up her grays, no liposuction or butt lifts. Her decision to age naturally didn't negatively impact her career at all. She was nominated again for acting Oscars for Almost Famous in 2001, aged 43, and North Country in 2006, aged 49, then won her second Oscar for Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri in 2018, at age 60, and her third for Nomadland in 2021 at 63. (The latter film also garnered her the Best Picture Oscar as the film's producer, an award she was again nominated for this year, for Women Talking.) In Three Billboards: In Nomadland: Frances McDormand has embraced the aging process, rather than fighting it. Maybe she's not as beautiful as she was at 31 — most of us aren't once we reach our 60s. But she's among the greatest and most acclaimed American actors of all time, and she got where she is not by being beautiful or glamorous, but based entirely on her own talent. Where so many female actors find their careers languishing after 40, McDormand has bucked the trend even while embracing her age. One thing I find infuriating is the tendency of many — usually men — to give McDormand's husband, Joel Coen, credit for her success. “Oh, well, she's married to Joel Coen, that helped her career. She'd never have gotten this far without him". McDormand and Coen married in 1984, and she received her first Oscar nomination before anyone knew who the hell the Coen Brothers were, for a film they had nothing to do with. It's really sad that some people feel the need to attribute an incredibly talented and accomplished woman's success to a man.

Question: How do I find my rehomed dog that I used to own? I asked the humane society that I surrendered them to and they won’t tell me her new owner.
Answer: You may not like this answer, but… you don't. You accept the fact that you surrendered the dog and therefore terminated your rights as her owner, and that someone else adopted her. Most Humane Societies in the U.S. have a pretty thorough vetting process for potential adopters, so the chances are good that she went to a loving home. But she's not your dog anymore. The Humane Society is under no obligation to tell you who adopted her, and they may be legally obligated not to do so. I'm sorry if you are now having second thoughts, but if you willingly surrendered the dog, you have zero rights to her now, and unless you happen to see her on the street with her new owners, you're highly unlikely to ever know who adopted her.

Question: I am moving to Denver this summer with 2 dogs and 4 cats. Trying to find rentals with flexible pet policies has been tough. Does anyone know of any spots (I.e., apartments, houses, condos)?
Answer: I hate to break it to you, but Denver zoning laws prohibit having more than five dogs and cats combined per household. So within the city of Denver, it's not legal for you to have two dogs and four cats in one residence (and even if it were, most landlords are unlikely to allow that many, especially in an apartment). The city also requires by law that dogs and cats be spayed and neutered by the age of six months, unless you apply for a special permit, and pit bulls are banned in Denver without a permit, so hopefully your pets are all fixed and neither of your dogs are pitties. You may want to check the surrounding suburbs instead. Again, Denver only allows a certain number of pets per household based on species — I have a rabbit, and you can't have more than two of those in Denver legally. (EDIT: I just want to note that I am in no way knocking Denver. It's a great city, and if I were ever to live in a city again, it would be high on my list. But they do have heavy regulations when it comes to pets.)

Question: Can you recommend some movies like Wednesday, where an actor who previously played the character returns but as another character?
Answer: The original 1962 Cape Fear starred Robert Mitchum as rapist Max Cady, Gregory Peck as Sam Bowden, the attorney who prosecuted him, and Martin Balsam as police chief Mark Dutton. In Martin Scorsese's 1991 remake, Cady was played by Robert De Niro, and Bowden by Nick Nolte, while the Dutton character does not appear, but Peck, Mitchum, and Balsam all appeared in small roles, with Peck and Mitchum's roles as protagonist and antagonist reversed — Peck played Cady's attorney Lee Heller, Mitchum a police lieutenant. (Balsam played a judge.) Also, Kevin McCarthy starred as Dr. Miles Bennell in the original Invasion of the Body Snatchers in 1956, and had a cameo appearance in the 1978 remake (starring Donald Sutherland as Bennell, although his first name was changed to Matthew) as a man running in fear.

Question: If you caught a random rat at the local dump, brought it home and put it in a cage, would it behave the same as a fancy rat?
Answer: No. Fancy, or domestic, rats have been selectively bred for certain physical characteristics and for temperament over the last few centuries, and are domestic animals that don't behave like their wild counterparts. They're not just tame versions of wild rats — they're fully domesticated. That's why their taxonomic name is Rattus norvegicus domestica, while the wild brown rat is just Rattus norvegicus. Wild brown rats are naturally wary of and shy around humans, and unlike domestic rats, a wild rat isn't going to want you picking it up or petting it, any more than a wild squirrel or groundhog would. They would also not be happy in a cage, because it's not natural for them. Might as well catch a coyote, put it in a kennel, and expect it to act like a cocker spaniel. Wild animals are wild, even those that are common around human dwellings, like rats and mice. Capturing a wild animal and locking it in a cage is cruel, and will absolutely not turn it into a pet. If you want pet rats, find a breeder or visit a pet store.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Can dwarf rabbits live outside?
Answer: Pet rabbits, regardless of breed, should not be housed outdoors. Period. All rabbits are vulnerable to predators, toxins, parasites, disease, extreme heat or cold, etc. when they live outside, and dwarf breeds like the Netherland dwarf, dwarf Hotot, etc. are especially vulnerable because of their small size. These are not wild animals, and dwarf breeds in particular have always been bred specifically as companion or fancy animals, not livestock. You really don't have room for a two-pound animal in your home? If that's the case, don't get rabbits. Pets belong inside with their families, and rabbits are just as much pets as dogs or cats. A pair of Netherland dwarfs just doesn't take up a lot of space. A 4′x4′ exercise pen will do them just fine.

Question: Are small towns/villages more crime ridden and impoverished than cities (countryside has less police and more drug use, cities are filled with police and opportunities)?
Answer: I live in a small town in upstate New York. Our annual violent crime rate is 0.41 per 1,000 residents, and our annual overall crime rate is 7.6 per 1,000 residents. (The U.S. average for violent crime is 22.7%, and overall crime, 35%.). And we don't even have our own police department — we have a state police barracks in the village, and the county sheriff's office 15 miles away. The town overall is safer than 98% of localities in the United States, and our highest crime statistic is for vandalism, at 4.2 annually per 1,000 residents — every other crime stat is less than 1, including drug-related crime, which is 0.8 per 1,000 residents. With a total population of 8,300 (that's for my village along with the other two villages in the town) that's around 60 crimes, total, per year, and most of them are vandalism. In terms of safety, the town is rated an A+. Our median household income is $79,000, compared to the New York state average of $75,000 and U.S. average of $70,000, and our poverty rate is 4%, compared to an average of 11% for the U.S. overall and 13% for New York state on the whole. I think my small town is doing pretty well. There simply isn't crime here. There aren't enough people for there to be a lot of crime here, and many of us know each other. I've accidentally left my keys dangling from my door lock overnight on more than one occasion, and forgotten to lock my front door on many occasions. I still do lock the door most of the time, mainly out of force of habit, but I don't really have to. Nobody is prowling my rural farm road looking to break into houses or rape or murder people. I've no doubt there are small towns with more serious crime than here, but my answer should tell you that making sweeping general presumptions like the one in the question is not very smart.

Question: I find the expression: "British" accent confusing. As the UK is comprised of different nations, including England and Scotland. To American ears does Benedict Cumberbatch's RP English accent sound similar to Sean Connery's Scottish brogue?
Answer: I remember when the miniseries Band of Brothers came out, and as it was filmed in the UK, a lot of the cast were Brits — mostly English or Scottish — playing American soldiers in WWII. Do you know how many British people I saw in online forums bragging about how spot on all the British actors' American accents were? A lot. But as a Yank, I saw Marc Warren play a guy from Philadelphia with a deep Southern accent, and Dexter Fletcher play a guy from Ohio who sounded vaguely like he was from New York City, and Ross McCall play a guy from San Francisco with a flat accent reminiscent of a Midwesterner. None of their accents were correct (and in Fletcher's case, he actually met and spoke to the man he was playing, John Martin, and heard his real accent). To those Brits who praised the accents, they all sounded spot on because they all sounded vaguely American. But they didn't sound like the real men they were playing, and their regional U.S. accents were, in many cases, completely wrong for the men they were portraying. (I will give props to the Scottish actor Robin Laing, who at least tried to adopt an authentic Philadelphia accent, even if it had some cracks in it.) While Britain has a wider variety of regional accents and dialects than the U.S. does, the U.S. definitely has its share, especially east of the Mississippi, where English speakers have been settled longer. Yet there are plenty of British people who refer to the “American accent”, as if we all sound the same. No, an RP accent doesn't sound the same to me (or to most Americans) as an Edinburgh accent. I can also hear the difference between other British/English accents, even if I don't necessarily know exactly where each one originates. I have a friend from Cambridge, and another from Birmingham, and they absolutely sound different to me (when I first met Geoff, my Brummie friend, I had a hard time understanding some of what he said, an issue I never had with my Cantabrigian friend Darren). But they also both sound British — in the same way that a guy from Boston and a guy from Chicago both sound American, despite having vastly different regional accents. And that, I think, is what most Americans mean when they refer to a “British accent”.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Do you like Popeye the Sailor?
Answer: I did as a child. So much, in fact, that I accidentally killed our family television set because of him when I was about four. I really, really loved Popeye when I was little. Like, I thought he was the coolest guy around. I always ate my spinach, and always asked for seconds, because I wanted to be super strong like Popeye. If Popeye was on TV, you can bet I was watching, and if my brother wanted to change the channel, I'd fight to watch my Popeye. So one day I was in the family room watching Popeye, with my mom in the next room, and it occurred to me that if I could just break the TV screen, I could get in and hang out with Popeye and Olive. How cool would that be?? My brother's ski poles happened to be leaning against the wall, so I grabbed one, poked the glass screen of our 19″ Sony as hard as I could, and… ***CRRRACCKK*** A spiderweb of cracks radiated out from where the ski pole had hit the screen. My mom came running in. The TV was still working, even with the cracked screen, like if you crack your phone screen, but the picture wasn't very good, and to my great disappointment, it appeared that I couldn't, in fact, get in to see Popeye and Olive, nor could they get out to hang out with me. Shattered dreams (and TV screens)… Mom couldn't believe a kid as young and small as I was had managed to actually break the screen, but to her credit, she didn't really yell at me after I explained why I had done it, and in fact was kind of amused in spite of her exasperation. I guess she knew I was too young to know better. Dad went out and bought us a new TV, and I don't recall him ever yelling at me, either, even though television sets were really expensive back then — this was the late 70s, when a new color TV ran about $500, or over $2,000 in today's dollars. My siblings weren't mad either, because the Sony was kind of old and our new Zenith was a lot fancier, with a better picture. So thanks to my love of Popeye the Sailor, I learned a valuable lesson — that the people you see on TV aren't actually IN the TV — and my family got a brand new TV.

Question: What are some of the best movie adaptations of all time?
Answer: Note: I'm only mentioning films that I did not see mentioned in other answers, and whose source material I have also read. Jaws. One of the rare film adaptations of a popular book that's actually better than the source material. Peter Benchley's novel suffered greatly from the fact that it had essentially no likable characters at all — pretty much the only one who wasn't a total shit was Martin Brody, and even he wasn't a smidge as likable as he was in the film, as portrayed by Roy Scheider. In the book, you almost root for the shark, because the humans all suck so badly. Also, the novel's ending — the shark suddenly just dies of its wounds right before it eats Brody — is lame as hell compared to the film's (although Benchley reportedly pitched a fit on Steven Spielberg for changing it). Spielberg transformed a mediocre, bubblegum beach novel into the original summer blockbuster film. Stand By Me. Rob Reiner's adaptation of Stephen King's novella The Body is mostly pretty faithful, although it softens things up quite a bit — in the book, our main protagonist Gordie Lachance is still feeling the loss of his older brother Denny, but almost exclusively because of the neglect of his parents since Denny's death. Gordie and Denny didn't have the close relationship in the book that they did in the film, mainly because they had a bigger age gap — ten years, if I remember right, whereas in the film it was more like five or six. Also, in the book, Gordie is the only one of the four young protagonists who is alive in the end; Teddy and Vern are both revealed to have died young, like Chris. But Reiner's adaptation makes for a better film, especially for its target audience of teens and tweens, and is a classic youth adventure and nostalgic coming of age tale. King has called it the best of all film adaptations of his work, and Reiner said in 2017 that it's his personal favorite of his own films. A Room With a View. There have been a few adaptations of E.M. Forster's 1908 novel, but the absolute best has to be Merchant-Ivory's 1985 version. Everything, from the script, to the sets, costumes, cinematography, music, and the mind-boggling cast (Helena Bonham Carter, Daniel Day-Lewis, Dame Maggie Smith, Julian Sands, Denholm Elliott, Dame Judi Dench, Simon Callow, Rupert Graves, Rosemary Leach) is absolutely spot on. I love Forster's book, and James Ivory and Ismail Merchant did it justice. To Kill a Mockingbird. Robert Mulligan's 1962 adaptation of Harper Lee's novel is an enduring classic of American cinema, and perhaps no actor was ever better suited to play dignified Southern lawyer and single father Atticus Finch than Gregory Peck. The child actors in the film — Mary Badham, Philip Alford, and John Megna — were also brilliantly cast, as was Brock Peters as the tragic Tom Robinson. The film also, of course, marked the screen debut of Robert Duvall in the small but pivotal role of Arthur “Boo" Radley. The Black Stallion. As a horse-crazy kid, I had the entire series of Walter Farley's children's books about teenager Alec Ramsay and his wild Arabian stallion, The Black. Carroll Ballard adapted the original 1941 novel in 1979, starring unknown, 12-year-old Kelly Reno as Alec and prized Arabian stallion Cass-Ole as the Black (along with Mickey Rooney, Teri Garr, Hoyt Axton, and Clarence Muse), and it's a glorious film, with a terrific score by Carmine Coppola and absolutely stunning cinematography by Caleb Deschanel (who was inexplicably snubbed at the Oscars, although he did receive a BAFTA nomination). Without question one of my favorite film adaptations of all time. (Fun fact: Reno, who grew up on a ranch in Colorado, did all of his own riding and stunts in the film other than the big race at the end, which used a professional jockey because a racing Thoroughbred stood in for Cass-Ole, and the boy was simply not strong enough to control the horse at full speed.)

Question: Can rabbits live outside their cages? If so, for how long and what precautions should be taken?
Answer: Pet rabbits don't belong in cages at all. Cages are relics of a bygone era, when rabbits were no more than livestock being fattened up for the dinner table. Outdoor hutches are even worse; pet rabbits belong indoors with their family, and rabbits housed outdoors face numerous threats, including predators, disease, parasites, toxic plant life, insects, ticks, and inclement weather. The whole reason rabbits were originally kept in small cages and hutches was to limit how much they could move around, so they'd be easier to fatten up. They were fed diets of almost entirely commercial pelleted food, also designed to help them fatten up, and rabbits raised for meat are typically slaughtered by the time they're six months old, which is equivalent to a human's teenage years. It's a short, miserable life they live, and they are not fed or housed with any regard for their long term health, because they will be dead before they even reach adulthood. Why would you do that to an animal you consider a pet? While for some reason it's still seen as acceptable in the wide world for rabbits to be housed in cages as small as five square feet, in the growing rabbit community, it's not acceptable at all, and those of us who know better WILL judge you for keeping rabbits in tiny pet store cages, feeding them tons of pellets, giving them drip bottles for water, and otherwise not doing research on proper care of pet rabbits. It's 2023 and there is a wealth of information out there. If you have access to the internet, you have no excuse. There are alternatives to keeping a rabbit in a cage. If you're insistent that the rabbit must be enclosed, you can get a 4′x4′, 30″-36″ tall puppy exercise pen — websites like Amazon and Chewy sell them for around $50 USD, much cheaper than the average 2′x3′ cage from a pet store — that will give them 16 square feet of living space and allow them to run around and exercise even while enclosed. Rabbits can be litter trained much like cats, and a plush blanket or cotton area rug used for flooring. They also need unlimited grass hay and fresh, leafy greens (about 2 cups per five pounds of body weight) every day, and a five pound rabbit should only get about 1/4 cup of pellets daily at most, unless otherwise directed by a rabbit-savvy vet. They should also be given water in a heavy ceramic or stoneware bowl, not a drip bottle, as those bottles don't dispense enough water at a time for rabbits — they're rabbits, not hamsters. Rabbits are also intelligent animals who need toys and enrichment or they can become bored and depressed. Rabbits can also, with a little effort, be free roamed in your home like a cat or dog. Once they're litter trained, you simply need to cover your electrical cords and baseboards to protect against chewing, protect wood furniture, and perhaps also carpeting if your rabbit is a digger (females are more likely to be big diggers than males). My rabbit lives in a pen at night and when I'm working, but he has free roam of my living room every evening from about 6 or 7pm to 11pm or 12am. He has not destroyed anything, nor has he ever peed on my rug or otherwise outside his litterbox. Again, rabbits don't belong in cages. Period. If you wouldn't make a dog or cat live in a tiny cage, you can't justify doing it to a rabbit, especially when some breeds of rabbit are bigger than the average cat or small dog. I will repeat, there is no excuse in this day and age, with a ton of information available right at your fingertips, to be ignorant of proper rabbit care.

Question: Do you think it's sad that kids today don't have an innocent childhood like old school kids back in the 80s, 90s and 2000s had and now, kids have to grow up with corrupted politicians and modern day liberals?
Answer: Well, as someone born in 1973, let's see. When I was five years old, I had nightmares after an older neighbor showed me the photos of the Jonestown massacre, when Pentecostal preacher Jim Jones had a U.S. Congressman murdered and forced over 900 of his followers to commit mass suicide by cyanide. In 1980, Mount Saint Helens blew her top in Washington state, killing 57 people and causing an ecological disaster. When I was 6, John Lennon was murdered by an obsessed fan. Then, when I was 7, John Hinckley Jr. attempted to assassinate President Ronald Reagan, his motive being to get the attention of actor Jodie Foster, on whom he had a crush. Two months later, Pope John Paul II was shot and nearly killed by a member of a Turkish fascist group, and 5 months after that, Egyptian president Anwar Sadat was assassinated. The following year, the IRA attempted to assassinate British PM Margaret Thatcher, and just weeks after that, Indian PM Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her own bodyguards. When I was nine, some lunatic in Chicago poisoned a bunch of bottles of Tylenol, killing 7 people, including a 12-year-old girl. I refused to take Tylenol for years after that, even when they introduced tamper-resistant packaging. The perpetrator was never apprehended. After my parents divorced when I was nine, my brother and I became latchkey kids, and were home alone after school every day until my mom got home from work. When I was ten, I watched two television films about nuclear holocaust, The Day After and Testament, and every night I went to bed terrified that the Russians were going to bomb us and we were all going to die. When I was 12, the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine had a massive meltdown, killing 47 people, displacing 300,000 more and spreading radioactive material across parts of Europe. Many people who survived the incident later developed terminal cancer. This did not assuage my fears of nuclear war. When I was 13, I watched the space shuttle Challenger explode upon takeoff, killing all 7 astronauts on board. When I was 16, the Exxon Valdez oil tanker ran aground in Alaska and spilled roughly 11 billion gallons of crude oil into Prince William Sound. This resulted in the deaths of 200,000+ seabirds, 2,800 otters, 300 seals, 247 bald eagles, 22 orcas, and an uncountable number of fish, and the area still hasn't recovered ecologically today, 34 years later. When I was in the 5th grade, kids were already jaded, already making out and talking about sex, and three of my male classmates cornered me in the schoolyard of P.S. 83 in the Bronx and tried to pull my clothes off and assault me. These were 10-year-old boys, and I only got away because some older boys playing baseball stepped in and made them leave me alone. Very innocent, indeed. Let's not forget the AIDS epidemic and the crack epidemic of the 1980s. All of this is on top of the fact that Ronnie Reagan and his trickle down economics removed tax burdens from the wealthy, making Gen X the first generation to earn less money than their parents. Also, by 1985, U.S. divorce rates had risen from 34% in 1970 to 52%, and most of my friends came from broken homes like I did. I could go on, but I won't. Children today actually have longer and more innocent childhoods than we did back then. Why do you think Generation X became known for being jaded, apolitical, and apathetic? Because we grew up under Reagan and Bush, and watched the hippies of the 60s and 70s become the “greed is good" yuppies of the 80s and 90s. There was nothing innocent about my childhood. The only positive was that we had more freedom, and the lack of social media meant that bullies could only bully us in person.

Question: What actor/actress deserves an Honorary Oscar?
Answer: Given the results of this year's Oscars, I'm going to say Judd Hirsch. Hirsch was nominated for Best Supporting Actor in 1981 for his performance as psychiatrist Dr. Tyrone Berger in Ordinary People, but lost to his own costar Timothy Hutton, despite Hutton's role actually being the film's lead. Then he was nominated this year for his performance in Steven Spielberg's The Fabelmans — at 87, he was the second-oldest acting Oscar nominee of all time, and the 42-year gap between his nominations is an Academy record. But he lost to Ke Huy Quan, for Everything Everywhere All At Once. Judd Hirsch just turned 88 years old, and while he still continues to work, and I hope he stays with us for a long time yet to come, the chances of him getting a third nomination are slim to none. He's been a solid and reliable actor, both in film and television, for over 50 years, and is also a supremely likable guy. (Plus, he's a Bronx boy.) Give him the damn honorary award before he dies.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: If a word is mispronounced by an entire community, does it become the proper pronunciation?
Answer: Not in the case of Mahopac, New York. My hometown (sorry to say), Mahopac is actually a hamlet within the town of Carmel in Putnam County, about an hour north of New York City. The name “Mahopac” comes from the Munsee language spoken by the Wappinger people, the area's original inhabitants, and reportedly means either “great lake" or “lake of the great serpent”. (There is a large natural lake in the town, Lake Mahopac, but if, as the Natives may have believed, there's a giant lake monster in it, I never saw it in my decades of swimming and boating on the lake.) Anyway, the correct pronunciation of the name is “Ma-HO-pack", but ever since the influx of migrants from New York City who turned it from a summer resort town to a residential community in the mid-20th century, everyone has pronounced it “MAY-uh-pack". And when I say “everyone", I mean pretty much everyone I have ever known except for my dad, who always insisted on using the correct pronunciation. (Possibly because he first heard of the town when his brother Jimmy vacationed there in the 1940s, and most people did pronounce it correctly then.) So if everyone pronounces it “MAY-uh-pack”, then that's become the proper pronunciation, right? Nope. In 2007, the Carmel Town Board voted by a margin of 3–2 that the correct and official pronunciation is “Ma-HO-pack”. So my hometown is populated entirely by people who pronounce the town's name wrong, know they're pronouncing it wrong, and just keep doing it anyway. Old habits die hard.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What actor/actress’ film career came undone due to blacklisting?
Answer: Anne Revere. I just mentioned her in another answer, so she's fresh in my mind. A native of New York City (and a direct descendant of Revolutionary War icon Paul Revere), she began her acting career on Broadway in the early 1930s, and then in film in 1934. She became known for playing mothers, and won the Best Supporting Actress Oscar for her fantastic performance as Elizabeth Taylor's mother in National Velvet. She had previously been nominated for playing Jennifer Jones' mother in Song of Bernadette, and was nominated again for playing Gregory Peck's mother in Gentlemen's Agreement (despite being only 13 years older than Peck). With Taylor in National Velvet: Revere was a lifelong Democrat, a self-professed “damn Yankee", and a vocal critic of the McCarthy hearings and the House Un-American Activities Committee. When she was called to testify before the committee in 1950, she invoked her Fifth Amendment rights and refused, leading her to be blacklisted at the height of her career, aged 47. She would not appear in another film until 1970’s Tell Me That You Love Me, Junie Moon, when she was 67. Revere, who was married to theater director Samuel Rosen for nearly 50 years until his death in 1984 (although the couple had no children, perhaps somewhat ironically given her history of playing mothers), died in 1990 at age 87, with only three acting credits on her resume since 1951. One of film's best, most reliable, and most popular actors simply disappeared overnight.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Can you become a great Hollywood movie star without being particularly beautiful?
Answer: Sure. Of course the first person who came to mind was the great Kathy Bates. She's not an ugly woman, but perhaps best described as “plain", and she became a star as a middle-aged, overweight woman at a time when the term “body positivity” didn't exist in Hollywood. Judy Garland wasn't a great beauty, either. That's partly why her life became so tragic, because she spent so much time trying to be that great beauty. Perhaps one of my all-time favorite character actors was the legendary Anne Revere, who was among the most sought-after actresses of the 1940s and landed an Oscar, along with two other nominations, before being blacklisted in 1950 for refusing to testify before the House Un-American Activities Committee during the Red Scare. The most one could say about Anne's appearance would be to call her “handsome” — she was never beautiful. I'll also mention Frances McDormand, who was absolutely a beautiful woman in her younger years, but has aged naturally, with no fillers, facelifts, hair dye, teeth whiteners, etc., and has had probably her greatest success as an actor in her 60s. How many female actors pick up their Oscars with messy hair and not a smidge of makeup on their faces? Lastly, there's THE great Hollywood movie star, Meryl Streep. I think Meryl is stunning, but she is and was not a conventional beauty, and in fact she was rejected many times early in her career for not being beautiful enough, most famously by Dino DiLaurentiis when she auditioned for the female lead in the 1976 remake of King Kong. DiLaurentiis basically called her “it", as well as “so ugly". Didn't stop her from becoming probably the most acclaimed American actor of all time. I'll also note, Hollywood beauty also has its share of smoke and mirrors. The average person walking down the street doesn't have a team of hairstylists, makeup artists, waxers, manicurists, nutritionists, personal trainers, etc. to keep them looking glamorous. If you look at Jennifer Lopez back when she was a Fly Girl on In Living Color, she was obviously attractive, but nowhere near as sleek and glamorous as we know her now. Just a cute girl from the Bronx. And if you were to see J. Lo even now when she wakes up in the morning, you might not recognize her.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is it normal for someone to be depressed when they have everything in life that they could have?
Answer: Depression doesn't give a flying fuck how much you have or don't have. Look at guys like Chris Cornell, Anthony Bourdain, and Chester Bennington. All of them had successful careers, plenty of money, children they adored. I've seen people say that all of them had everything, and therefore no reason to be depressed or to take their own lives. People who ask those questions don't seem to understand that depression is a disease. It's not being bummed for a week because you got passed over for a promotion, or your boyfriend broke up with you. It's a lot deeper than that, it's biological, and it can affect you regardless of whether you're homeless on the streets, middle class in the suburbs, or wealthy beyond measure and living in a mansion.

Question: It's the 1920s in New York and I am walking through Brooklyn or the Bronx. Would it be dangerous for me to be in these neighbourhoods, or were the crime rates of this era not as severe as what is portrayed in film and television?
Answer: Neither Brooklyn nor the Bronx is a neighborhood. They're boroughs made up of a lot of neighborhoods. In the 1920s, the Bronx had a population of roughly a million people, while Brooklyn had over two million. My father grew up in the Bronx in the 1920s and 30s. He and his brother Jimmy used to go to Yankee Stadium on their own as young kids to watch Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig play for the Yanks. The old Yankee Stadium was in the South Bronx, which has historically been a relatively high crime area — when my stepdad lived near the Stadium in the 80s it was bad — but Dad never reported any problems back then. They also lived in the Bronx but went to elementary school at Our Lady Queen of Angels in Harlem, so they had to take the train into Manhattan and back every day for school. There were street gangs in his neighborhood of Eastchester (which is in the northern part of the borough) when he was a teenager, he told me about that, but according to him, if you didn't cross them, they usually left you alone. Beat cops patrolled the neighborhoods on foot — Dad told me one of them whacked him across the back with his baton when he saw my dad smoking a cigarette, which was illegal if you were under 16. Except it was a menthol cigarette, which were not illegal, but oh, well — cops could get away with hitting kids for no reason back then. The cop said “sorry” and went on his way, leaving my dad with an aching back. Having said all this, YMMV. My dad was a slightly built, Italian-American kid who was fairly meek and unassuming. Not someone anybody would think to rob or who was going to pick fights, and also not female. “Walking through Brooklyn or the Bronx in the 1920s" is an incredibly vague and broad scenario. How safe it would be is going to depend on a number of factors.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Was an actor ever fired for reasons other than their acting talent?
Answer: Sometimes actors are fired simply because the filmmakers figure out too late that they aren't right for the role they were cast in. I can think of at least three examples off the top of my head: Eric Stoltz, in Back to the Future. Stoltz was cast as Marty McFly after Michael J. Fox, Robert Zemeckis' first choice, was initially unable to take the role due to his starring role in the sitcom Family Ties. But Stoltz — who is a fine actor, no question — had an approach to playing Marty that was not in line with what Zemeckis envisioned. He was a method actor, who had mostly done drama up to that point, and played it much more serious than Zemeckis wanted. So when Fox became available upon the return of his Family Ties costar Meredith Baxter from maternity leave, Stoltz was fired, something Zemeckis said was extremely difficult to do, because he genuinely liked him — just not as Marty McFly. (I'll also note that Stoltz really got the shaft here, because they continued filming with him even after Fox accepted the role and signed a contract; he wasn't fired until weeks later. Zemeckis later said, “I broke [Stoltz's] heart, and it was all my fault”.) John Cusack, in The Breakfast Club. At 17, Cusack won the role of tough guy John Bender over Judd Nelson, mainly because Nelson, at 24, was considered too old to play a high school student. But it soon became apparent to John Hughes that Cusack was just a little too cuddly-looking to be appropriately intimidating. So he got the boot, and Nelson played the role after all. Cusack is an excellent actor — I've been a fan since I was a teenager — and overall he's had far greater career success than Nelson has, but again, he just wasn't the right guy to play John Bender. Stuart Townsend, in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. Townsend was 26 when he was cast as Aragorn in Peter Jackson's adaptation of LotR, but he was fired shortly after filming began, and replaced by 40-year-old Viggo Mortensen. The primary reason was simply his age — Jackson realized that a guy in his 20s was just too young to play the 87-year-old Númenórean Aragorn. Again, not a matter of him being a bad actor, just not right for the part.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What Hollywood couple continues to thrive and blossom?
Answer: Samuel L. Jackson and LaTanya Richardson Jackson. They met in 1970, when they were 21-year-old students in Atlanta (Richardson at Spellman College, Jackson at Morehouse), and married in 1980; their only child, daughter Zoe, a producer, was born in 1982. She also says this was “very, very hard", but as of 2023, they've been together 53 years, married 43, and still show genuine love and warmth toward each other.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: I'm living in an apartment. Is it a good idea to get a bunny/rabbit as pet?
Answer: That depends. As long as you do your research beforehand to make sure a rabbit is the right pet for you — rabbits are long-lived and fairly high-maintenance animals, and do not behave like dogs or cats — and have enough space for at least a 4′x4′ exercise pen, apartment life is fine for rabbits. Certainly it's much better than keeping them in hutches outdoors. I live in a 700 square foot apartment. My rabbit's pen is in my living room, and in the evenings he has free roam of the entire room. (I've recently given him the option of going into the bedroom, but he hates the hard floors and mostly stays on the rug or his blanket, although I suspect he will eventually get curious enough to venture in.) As long as you rabbit-proof by protecting baseboards, carpeting, electrical cords, etc., and litter train the rabbit — neither of which are very difficult — you'll be fine. I would actually suggest getting two rabbits if you're not home all the time, as rabbits are social and need company. Having said that, if you're thinking a rabbit might be a good option because you live in a small space and can keep it in a cage — meaning the sort of small cage generally advertised for rabbits — I would say don't do it. Rabbits don't belong in cages, and the aforementioned 4′x4′ ex pen is the smallest recommended enclosure for one rabbit. Here's Eddie hanging on the couch with me and enjoying a lollipop made for bunnies.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why do people assume that something is better quality just because it is expensive?
Answer: It depends on what you're talking about. Things like OTC pain relievers are just as effective in generic form as brand name, and at my local supermarket, Advil costs $10 for 100 tablets, while the store brand is $2.50. That's a no-brainer. Generic ibuprofen kills a headache just as well as Advil. So I have no idea who it is that's paying through the nose for Advil, or why. Many food products are similar, and you'll often see the same exact ingredient list on store brands as on name brands. In those cases, you're better off saving the money, but some people are going to simply assume that Campbell's soup must be better quality than store brand. Paper towels and toilet paper, though — most of the time, generic brands are not as good as more expensive name brands. Especially paper towels; I always pay the extra for Bounty or Scott towels, because you use less of them. Many supermarkets have their own generic brand of “premium” paper products, but they're usually not much cheaper than Bounty or Scott tissue anyway. In my days of poverty, I bought Angel Soft toilet paper, because it was $1.50 for four rolls, where Scott was $4 for four rolls. But the Scott lasts three or four times longer, so you're not really saving in the long run. What about cars? I'll be the first to admit that my sister's $50,000 BMW drives more smoothly, handles better, and accelerates more quickly than my $20,000 Honda Civic, but Honda has a much higher reliability rating than BMW. That BMW is only a couple years old and has had more issues than my 10-year-old Honda has. So I'll stick with the cheaper option when it comes to cars; reliability matters more to me than performance. I'm not Steve McQueen, I just need it to get me where I'm going and not cost an arm and a leg in repairs and maintenance. But that's me. Some people (like my sister) want that German engineering, and bully for them. But let's not even talk about shoes. Given a choice between a $35 pair of vinyl boots from Walmart, or a decent pair of leather boots by, say Steve Madden, which is not an overly expensive brand, for $100, I'm going with the Maddens every time. Shoes are one of the worst things to go super cheap on, because cheap shoes are bad for your feet, and they don't last. I used to buy shoes at Target when I worked there, because I was poor (I worked at Target, after all), and all of them ended up in the trash within a year or two. Most of my shoes, aside from sneakers, cost between $100 and $250, and most have already lasted me for years. When it comes to footwear, the vast majority of the time, you absolutely get what you pay for. So, some things that are more expensive are absolutely better quality. Others are not worth the extra money. But it's not a black and white issue. Again, it depends on the item in question.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What are some good movies that realistically portrayed life in nuclear post-apocalypse?
Answer: Testament. It started life as a PBS American Playhouse film, based on a short story by teacher Carol Amen, but it was so well-received that it was given a theatrical release by Paramount. It stars Jane Alexander and William Devane as middle-class Northern California couple Carol and Tom Wetherly, and Ross Harris, Roxana Zal, and Lukas Haas (in his film debut) as their children, Brad, Mary Liz, and Scottie. (Kevin Costner and Rebecca DeMornay also have small, early roles as a young married couple who are friends with the Wetherlys, Oscar nominee Mako is the local gas station owner, and veteran character actor Leon Ames is a local ham radio operator.) The film is unique among nuclear apocalypse movies of its time (e.g. The Day After, Threads, etc.) in that there is no mushroom cloud, no scenes of destruction or devastation. We don't even know who started it, or why, and that ultimately doesn't matter. That's not the story that Testament wants to tell. It starts with a normal, suburban American family living their lives in the fictional town of Hamelin, California — breadwinner Tom is a cheerful exercise nut, his wife Carol a good-humored, if somewhat harried, stay at home mom. 13-year-old Mary Liz is an aspiring pianist, 12-year-old Brad both idolizes his father and resents his own perceived inability to measure up to him, and Scottie is an adorable preschooler. Tom heads off on a business trip to San Francisco, and as the kids are watching TV, suddenly the screen goes dark, only to be replaced by San Francisco news anchor stating that the East Coast has been hit with multiple nuclear devices, and the New York feed has been lost. Then there's a sudden, blinding flash of yellow light outside the windows, and the town air raid sirens begin to wail. That's all we see of the nuclear war. Hamelin itself doesn't look much different than it did the day before, but everything has changed, and the Wetherlys begin to notice little things, like specks of radioactive dust on their cereal bowls. Tom never returns from San Francisco, and a neighbor boy, Larry, moves in with them when his parents also fail to come home from the city. At a town meeting, the local doctor advises that there will likely be fallout, and if it's significant enough, people will get sick and die. And that, of course, begins to happen. When the cemetery fills up, people are buried in their own yards and gardens, and finally, bodies are burned. In one scene, Mary Liz asks her mother what love and sex are like, knowing without saying it that she herself will never get to experience them. Brad tries to take Tom's place as the man of the house, still seeking his father's approval even after he's gone. Scottie tries to understand what's happening, but he's too young to fully grasp it. The story is mostly told from Carol's perspective, via her journal entries, and is largely about the efforts of the people of Hamelin to maintain some sense of calm and normalcy, and to stick together, even knowing that what future they have will almost certainly be dark and brief. They ration their food, and everyone turns in their batteries from non-essential devices. The young children had been rehearsing a stage production of The Pied Piper of Hamelin, and the parents decide not to cancel it, apocalypse or no. The entire cast is effective, but the film belongs to Alexander, who is just marvelous (and thanks to the film's limited theatrical release, she received an Oscar nomination as Best Actress). It's a subtle film in its portrayal of nuclear holocaust, and one that shows what happens to the people who don't die in the initial blast, but have to keep going, even knowing that their future is so bleak.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is there an action movie that examines philosophical issues?
Answer: Runaway Train, that overlooked gem of 80s action films. Directed by Andrei Konchalovsky, with a screenplay by Eddie Bunker and Paul Zindel, and a story by Akira Kurosawa (who initially planned to direct in 1966, but couldn't get studio backing in the U.S. and so abandoned the project), it stars Jon Voight and Eric Roberts, both of whom received Oscar nominations for their performances. Voight — a hulking powerhouse here — is Oscar “Manny" Manheim, a vicious bank robber and hardened career criminal, who was welded into his tiny cell in Alaska's Stonehaven Prison after two escapes. Those escapes, and his three years in solitary, have made him a hero to his fellow inmates, none more so than Buck McGeehy (Roberts), a dumb, naive young prizefighter in for statutory rape. After a court order deems Manny's confinement unconstitutional and he is returned to general population, the brutal warden, Ranken (John P. Ryan), attempts to have him shanked, leading Manny to plot another escape in the dead of the Alaskan winter. He enlists Buck, a laundry trusty, to help, and the starstruck youngster convinces Manny to take him along. Buck and Manny hop a train consisting only of four locomotives, intending to ride to freedom, but unbeknownst to them, the engineer suffers a heart attack and falls from the train, leaving it speeding through the wilderness at higher and higher speeds. They eventually learn that there's one other person on board, locomotive hostler Sara (Rebecca DeMornay), but she, too, is powerless to stop the train, whose emergency stop is located on the inaccessible first engine. While the action sequences are dynamite, it's also on the train that the film waxes most philosophical. Manny is institutionalized; even if he earned a legal parole, he wouldn't know how to live a normal life. He's beyond redemption. Buck is not so far gone, but he romanticizes both Manny and the criminal lifestyle, testing Manny's patience. Manny envies Buck, in a sense, because Buck still has a chance, still has most of his humanity, something Manny jettisoned a long time ago, and Buck's seeming determination to ruin his life beyond repair frustrates Manny. However, at the same time, Manny's viciousness becomes only too evident in this desperate situation, and the film asks the question, is Manny an animal? Or is he only too human? I won't get into further detail about the plot, or the epic ending, but I'll leave you with the same Shakespeare quote (from Richard III) as the film does: No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity. But I know none, and therefore am no beast.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why did Diane Keaton have top billing over Jane Fonda in Book Club? Jane Fonda was a much bigger star in her heyday and has 2 Oscars to boot to Diane's 1.
Answer: The key word in your question is “heyday”. Jane was a bigger star than Diane in the 70s, maybe also in the early 80s, but she was entirely absent from film through the entire decade of the 90s following Stanley & Iris, and even since returning to the screen in 2005, most of her films have flopped. (Monster-in-Law? Georgia Rule? Peace, Love, and Misunderstanding? Ugh.) Diane Keaton has had a much more successful career — and I mean sustained, consistent success — over the last 35 years than Fonda has. Whereas Fonda made no movies in the 1990s, they were a big decade for Keaton, and she continued that success into the 2000s. She's just a bigger and more bankable star at this point. Jane runs more on legacy than anything else. Oscars are ultimately irrelevant. Dianne Wiest has two Oscars; when was the last time you saw her get top billing? Most people under age 40 have probably never even heard of her. Jane Alexander has four Oscar nominations, and most people under 50 probably only know her from that shitty Terminator film with Christian Bale, if they know her at all. Fonda's last Oscar win was also 45 years ago, for a film most people have never seen. (That's not to knock Coming Home, it's a great film, and Jane gave a great performance, as did Jon Voight, but it's fallen into obscurity.) The bottom line is, it doesn't matter who was the bigger star 40 years ago. Keaton is a bigger star now.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How can someone be “priced out of their home” if they already own their home?
Answer: My friend Rita sold her house a few years ago, and bought another, smaller one in the same neighborhood. Her old house was a gorgeous, 19th century lakefront colonial, with a custom chef's kitchen (Rita does custom kitchens for a living), vaulted ceilings, stone fireplace, and a window wall overlooking the lake, and she owned it outright, having purchased it with her ex-husband over 30 years prior. It was property taxes that drove her out. Her property taxes were in excess of $33,000 a year, because she lived on prime real estate — there's only so much lakefront property on any given lake — in a fairly affluent town in the NYC metro area. In addition to that, local school taxes were $14,000 annually. That means that even without a mortgage, she was paying $4,000 a month just in taxes, and although she does well for herself, she is getting to an age where she's considering retirement, and that was just too much money. So as much as she loved her house, she sold (and she got a million dollars for it, which was less than her asking price, but still made her a nice profit). Her property taxes in the new house? $8,500 a year. Again, it's a smaller house, with no lakefront property, and on a smaller lot, but she still has lake rights, and especially with the profit she made from the sale of her old house, she also has a lot more financial room to breathe.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: If someone should rent an apartment that's intended for a non-smoker, is it okay if their friends come over and happen to smoke? That's allowed of course, so not to be rude to your guest.
Answer: First of all, even as a longtime smoker (who switched to vaping last year), nobody smokes in my home, whether or not it's allowed by the landlord. Cigarette smoke stinks, especially once it's in your upholstery and curtains and rugs and goes stale, and even in apartments in which smoking isn't forbidden, you can be charged for repainting or replacing carpeting damaged by smoke. (It's also rude to any upstairs neighbors who don't smoke, because they WILL smell it.) I also won't have my pets inhaling secondhand smoke, as rabbits and guinea pigs have sensitive respiratory systems. If I don't smoke in my own home, I'm damn sure not going to let anyone else do it. My current lease forbids smoking anywhere on the property, and guests in my home need to respect that. The only person I see regularly who smokes is my sister (who doesn't smoke much anyway), and she wouldn't dream of even asking if she could smoke in my place. The bottom line is, check your lease. If it says no smoking, that means no smoking, whether it's you or a guest. Are you really willing to risk eviction because you don't want to tell guests to go outside if they need a smoke that badly?

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What are the biggest waterfalls in the United States near NYC near the New York area or Northeastern United States?
Answer: Kaaterskill Falls, in the eastern Catskill Mountains of Greene County, is a double-drop waterfall with a total height of 259 feet. It's about a two and a half hour drive from NYC. High Falls, near the city of Hudson, has a 150 foot drop, making it the tallest waterfall in Columbia County, and is also about two and a half hours from the city. (Hudson itself is also a very trendy weekend destination for NYC residents, and its Amtrak station makes it relatively easy to access even without a car.) The Dover Stone Church Cave Falls, in the town of Dover Plains in Dutchess County, are not necessarily very big, but seeing as they are inside an ancient stone cave, they're still pretty cool and worth visiting. About 2 hours, maybe a tad less, from NYC. Less than an hour from NYC, in the village of Croton-on-Hudson, is Croton Gorge Park, home of Croton Dam and an accompanying 297-foot waterfall. If you're willing to jaunt a bit farther from NYC, you can visit picturesque Taughannock Falls, in the small town of Ulysses in Tompkins County (near Ithaca) in the Finger Lakes region. It's the U.S.'s tallest single-drop waterfall east of the Rocky Mountains, at 215 feet. I have personally visited all of these lovely falls, and all are well worth a visit.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is the fastest known creature?
Answer: Relative to its size, it's paratarsotomus macropalpis, a species of mite endemic to California and about the size of a sesame seed. It set the record as the world's fastest land animal in 2014, when one was recorded running at 322 body lengths per second, about half a mile per hour. 1/2 mile per hour may not sound fast, but for reference, a cheetah running at top speed runs about 16 body lengths per second, and a human running at an equivalent rate to paratarsotomus macropalpis would have to reach a speed of approximately 1,300 miles per hour. Even Usain Bolt can't manage that.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is Duchess County, New York known for?
Answer: Dutchess County — you forgot the “t" — is home to Hyde Park, the birthplace of Franklin Delano Roosevelt and death place of Frederick William Vanderbilt, as well as to their respective homes — Springwood and the Vanderbilt Mansion, both national historic sites. It's also home to Poughkeepsie, a small city (pop. 32,000) on the Hudson River whose name has nonetheless become well-known simply because it's so damned hard for people to pronounce. The name comes from the Munsee dialect spoken by the Wappinger people, its original inhabitants, and means “the reed-covered lodge by the little-water place". It's pronounced, roughly, “pe-KIP-see”. Some notable natives or residents include inventors Samuel Morse (Morse code) and Alfred Mosher Butts (Scrabble), film director Ed Wood, and veteran character actor Bill Duke. Poughkeepsie is also notable for being the top destination for New York City residents who fled the City and relocated due to the pandemic, I guess because it's fairly diverse, and big enough to have some conveniences, but small enough to be safer in a pandemic situation.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What do you think of people who never go abroad?
Answer: I think that I'd have to have a pretty shitty life and an extreme lack of self confidence if I spent my time even remotely pondering what kind of traveling other people do, let alone judging them for it. Seriously, how big an asshole would I have to be in order to spend time thinking about that? What bearing does other people's level of travel experience have on my life? Judging people negatively because they're not world travelers is the absolute height of arrogance, and to me, a sure sign of a shallow, shitty person that I don't want to be around. I mean, does a person have to have visited 17 countries in order to be a good person? An intelligent person? An educated person? Apparently so, according to some of the answers to this question. Talk about a first world issue. Questions like these seem to invariably be asked by Europeans, who apparently don't realize that not all places in the world are laid out in such a way that you can drive or take the train from one country to another in a matter of hours. European countries are mostly pretty small (at least as compared to places like the U.S., Canada, and Australia). It's easier and faster to travel from London to Vienna (925 miles) or from Dublin to Rome (1,490 miles) than it is to travel from Boston to Denver (1,970 miles), or from Sydney to Perth (2,440 miles), or from Toronto to Vancouver (2,700 miles). So don't pat yourself on the back too much because you took a summer holiday to Prague in 2017. I get plenty of vacation time, and I make a decent salary. If I really wanted to travel to Europe or Asia or Australia, I could do it. But international travel is expensive, and there are other things I would rather spend my money on, especially with everything I see on this site about how many Europeans feel about Americans in general and American tourists in particular. Why would I hand my money to such people? Just to see Stonehenge or the Colosseum or the Eiffel Tower, or to eat pizza in Naples? And why do I need to travel to another country when there is so much of my own that I still haven't seen? The bottom line is that I don't concern myself with how much anyone else has traveled. It doesn't affect my life. Judging people for such things speaks volumes about your character, and what it says isn't pretty.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What happened to Lynyrd Skynyrd's founding member Gary Rossington?
Answer: He died. But you already knew that, didn't you? Probably nothing else about him, but that he was famous and he died, and that's all you needed. I hate these questions whenever someone famous dies. What do you mean, what happened to him? He died. He was 71 years old with a long and very public history of severe heart problems. He had at least three heart surgeries that I'm aware of just in the last ten years, and multiple heart attacks over the course of decades. It's probably a miracle that he lived and was able to perform for as long as he did and was. What you probably don't know about Gary is that he wrote “Simple Man”, and “I Ain't the One”, and “Things Goin' On", and “What's Your Name?”, among other Skynyrd classics. That he played the slide guitar on “Free Bird”, and the killer solos in “Call Me The Breeze”, “Gimme Three Steps”, “Don't Ask Me No Questions”, “Poison Whiskey”, and others. That he almost died in the plane crash in 1977, only a year after almost dying in a car wreck. You probably don't know that he was married to his wife Dale for over 40 years and had two daughters and several grandkids, all of whom are mourning him today. And you also probably don't care. His cause of death hasn't been released by his family, but the obvious assumption is that it had something to do with his heart. He was playing shows as recently as last month, and I'm glad he was able to keep playing up until the very end, because that's all he knew and all he ever wanted to do from the time he was a kid (and he was a kid, just 13, when he formed Skynyrd with Ronnie Van Zant and Bob Burns in the Burns family carport in Jacksonville). Gary Rossington was a legend, the last surviving founding member of Skynyrd. He died, and those who appreciated him, be they family, friends, or fans, are mourning that loss. Rest easy, Gary.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why is mini lop rabbit shaking it's head frequently when there is no visible difference to ears?
Answer: Ear mites or an ear infection, most likely. Lop-eared rabbits are highly prone to ear infections and also to severe mite infestations, due to the unnatural shape and position of their ears. (This is why I think it's ethically wrong to breed them.) You need to get your him or her to a rabbit-savvy vet for an examination and, most likely, medication.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What are some of the best scene-stealing performances by a supporting actor/actress in a film?
Answer: I scanned the other answers, and I'll name two I didn't see mentioned. Candy Clark, in American Graffiti. Clark was primarily a model, who had only appeared in one other film, John Huston's Fat City, before being cast as Debbie Dunham, the “bitchin' babe" picked up by lovable loser Terry “the Toad" Fields (Charles Martin Smith) in George Lucas's 1973 nostalgia-fest. The scenes between Toad (or Tiger, as Debbie comes to call him) and Debbie are probably my favorite in the whole movie. As Debbie, Clark manages to convey a level of sweetness and innocence even though the film makes it pretty clear that she's probably “been around the block" a few times, and she is certainly more worldly than the naive Toad. Clark received an Oscar nomination as Best Supporting Actress for her performance — the only acting nomination the film received — but I still don't think it gets mentioned enough when scene-stealing supporting performances are brought up. James Whitmore, in The Shawshank Redemption. Unlike Clark, Whitmore was a veteran of stage and screen — aged 72 and in his 6th decade as a professional actor — when he was cast as elderly con and prison librarian Brooks Hatlen in Frank Darabont's adaptation of Stephen King's novella. If Whitmore's performance doesn't make you cry, you're probably made of stone. It's a smallish but key role, illustrating how long prison sentences lead to institutionalization, and even though we know Brooks committed a heinous crime, Whitmore makes us not only love him, but sympathize with him. I've seen Shawshank quite a few times, and Brooks — whether on the bus after his parole, gripping the seat in front of him, his face a mask of fear, or sitting on a park bench, feeding the birds and hoping to see Jake the crow, his only friend on the outside — still makes me weep. Every. Damned. Time.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What celebrities have the most uncanny resemblance to other family members?
Answer: Jim Hanks is the younger brother (by 5 years) of Tom Hanks, and also an actor. Jim not only looks a lot like Tom — he was in fact Tom's body double in Forrest Gump — he sounds so much like him that he frequently does voice substitution work on Tom's films when Tom is unavailable, and he has provided the voice of Woody for a number of Toy Story videos as well as for quite a bit of merchandise.

Question: What Hollywood stars shared the same birthday?
Answer: Michael Gross and Meredith Baxter played husband and wife Steven and Elise Keaton on the 80s sitcom Family Ties. Coincidentally, they were born on exactly the same day: June 21, 1947. Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why did Tom Cruise not win an Oscar for Magnolia?
Answer: Because the Academy voters opted to vote for Michael Caine in The Cider House Rules. (People are saying Roberto Benigni, for Life is Beautiful, but that's a different award — Benigni won Best Actor, Cruise was nominated for Supporting Actor.) I have to think the people who ask these questions are somehow unaware that multiple actors are nominated in each category every year, and also that Oscars are awarded based on number of votes received from Academy voters. No, the person you think deserved the Oscar doesn't always win. The person *I* think deserved the Oscar doesn't always win. I thought Jackie Earle Haley deserved to win Best Supporting Actor for Little Children in 2007, but the voters chose Alan Arkin for Little Miss Sunshine. In 1987, I'd have given Best Supporting Actor to Tom Berenger for Platoon, but Michael Caine (again) got more votes for Hannah and Her Sisters. And so on. Such is life. Tom Cruise didn't win an Oscar for Magnolia because there's only one Oscar awarded each year in each category, and Michael Caine got more votes that year. (Personally, I thought Cruise's performance in Magnolia was overhyped anyway. I was watching Tom Cruise give a performance, he never fooled me for a second.)

Question: Which actors who were considered too young or too old for a role and were ruled out for the part, still managed to get the role anyway?
Answer: Judd Nelson, in The Breakfast Club. John Hughes liked Nelson's audition for the role of John Bender, but balked at actually casting him as a high school student, because Nelson was 24 when he auditioned — Molly Ringwald, whose character Claire would ultimately be Bender's love interest, was only 16 during filming. (Anthony Michael Hall was also 16, while Emilio Estevez and Ally Sheedy were both 21.) So Hughes cast 17-year-old John Cusack as Bender, but shortly before filming began, he decided Cusack didn't look intimidating enough to play the metalhead “criminal" Bender. So Cusack got the axe, and Nelson got the part after all. (Fun fact: Canadian actor John Kapelos, who played lovably kooky janitor Carl, is only three years older than Nelson.)

Question: What are some peculiar requests that actors or actresses make?
Answer: Back in the 1960s and 70s, when he was perhaps the biggest movie star in the world, Steve McQueen had a habit of demanding free items in bulk from studios as a condition of appearing in their films, usually regular, day-to-day items like blue jeans, electric razors, and other common hygiene products. McQueen would then donate the items to the California Junior Boys' Republic (today just called Boys' Republic), a reform school in Chino Hills, California. As a troubled youth who had endured a tumultuous, abusive childhood, and had numerous brushes with the law beginning as early as age 9, McQueen had been remanded to the school by his mother and stepfather as a teen, and credited it with helping him turn his life around. He was also known to visit the school periodically to spend time talking to the boys and playing pool with them, even after becoming an A-list star. McQueen was not a saint — he absolutely had his vices and his unlovely character traits — but he wasn't all bad. EDIT: To the people asking why he didn't use “his own money” for charity, um, he did. The items were part of his negotiated salary, and none of the studios had to provide them if they didn't really want to. More importantly, you negative Nancies don't seem to grasp that McQueen also donated his time to the boys at the school, which to me is more valuable than money. Any rich asshole can throw money at a cause, they do it every day. They don't all actually hang out with troubled kids and try to make a personal, positive impact on them.

Question: How did my rabbit get GI stasis when I always fed him grass and fruits?
Answer: Fruit is terrible for rabbits. Their digestive systems aren't designed to digest sugar. Too much sugar will give a rabbit a stomachache and upset their gut flora, and that will make them stop eating, leading to stasis. Fiber. Lots and lots of fiber, preferably from grass hay and chew toys made from safe woods like willow and apple. That, plus a daily serving of dark, leafy greens and herbs, is a proper rabbit diet. Fruit should only be given in very small quantities — half a strawberry, a few blueberries, a small slice of banana, etc. — a couple times a week as a treat. Like it or not, rabbits have very sensitive digestive systems, that can be thrown out of whack very easily if they're not fed the proper diet.

Question: How are single season non-fictional and fictional programs on TV a series? I mean they only have one season, so how are they series?
Answer: These types of shows are usually called “limited series" these days. They're classified as longer than a miniseries, but with a predetermined, limited run that tells a complete story — say, The Haunting of Hill House, or Latin American telenovelas — and still with the potential to be renewed and for the story to be extended. They're classified as series because they are — the story is told in a series of episodes, it's just a preset number of episodes. Also, not sure where you are, but I know that in the UK, what we in the U.S. and Canada call a “season" of a show is itself called a “series”. Instead of season one, they call it series one. (As an example, look at the British and American versions of The Office — in Britain they're called series, in the U.S., seasons.)
