Question: How does one know if he is a hoarder or if he needs to live in a bigger space? Should everything a person owns mid-life fit into a studio/one-bedroom apartment? And, if it does not seem to fit neatly anymore, should perfectly-good things be expunged?
Answer: It's not necessarily about how much stuff you have, but whether you actually use/need it or not. Hoarding is usually defined by people keeping things they don't actually need or don't use (sometimes can't use, e.g. trash) when they don't have the space for it, and just because something is “perfectly good" doesn't mean you personally can use it or need to keep it. (Similarly, an animal hoarder is one who keeps more animals than they can properly care for, pay attention to, or clean up after.) I know there's a stereotype, but a hoarded home doesn't have to be dirty — I think the cleanest hoarded home I've ever seen was a lady named Nora on Hoarders, a retired teacher who hoarded books and school supplies. Everything was neatly binned up in plastic storage tubs, and her house was quite clean — no trash, no bugs or cobwebs, no dirty dishes, etc. — but it was packed with over 3,000 storage bins. She just cleaned and vacuumed around the stacks of bins. Three thousand storage bins is too much stuff for anyone, so even though Nora's house was relatively clean and neat despite the clutter, she was still a hoarder. She didn't need 3,000 bins of notebooks, pencils, rulers, etc., nor could she use any of them. She was a shopaholic who couldn't resist a deal, and never wanted to part with anything. I am not a hoarder, but in my last move I downsized from a two-bedroom with several closets and a large attic, to a one-bedroom with a single, very large, walk-in closet. When I went through that attic I was amazed at the amount of crap I had that I had no need for whatsoever, much of which I had forgotten I even had. The only reason I had so much stuff is that I had the room for it without it being obviously hoarded (read: out in the open). When I got new stuff, other stuff I still liked went into the attic. Because it could. That was an eye-opener for me, and I realized that on that path, maybe I could eventually become a hoarder. So I donated, sold, or threw away at least 60–65% of my belongings. Clothing, shoes, furniture, housewares, candleholders and knickknacks, all kinds of things. I did get some new furniture in my new place, to replace pieces that were in poor shape, but today I don't own anything more than what can fit in my huge walk-in closet, kitchen cupboards, and small bathroom linen closet. (I actually just donated another box of housewares to the Salvation Army last week, including my blender — a blender I bought at least four or five years ago and recall using exactly once — and I have an old quilt and a couple of blankets bagged up to donate to the local Humane Society.) If you have a lot of stuff that you don't use or need, you can't bring yourself to part with any of it even though it's not useful, and it's cluttering up your space, you're probably a hoarder. A bigger place isn't going to change anything; if you're a hoarder you'll just compensate by getting more stuff to fill the extra space.

Question: I think Gary Rossington (Lynyrd Skynyrd’s lead guitarist) is underrated. Does anyone agree?
Answer: I must correct a falsehood in the question: Gary was (and is) not Skynyrd's “lead guitarist”. They didn't have a “lead guitarist”, they had three of them. All of Skynyrd's guitarists played both lead and rhythm, sometimes within the same song. It's one of the things that, in my opinion, made Skynyrd special, because each had his own style and their different styles complemented each other. With that out of the way, I think it kind of depends on how you define “underrated”. In a sense, all of Skynyrd's guitarists were underrated; the only one of their four pre-plane-crash guitarists I've ever seen on any list of “greatest guitarists” is Allen Collins, and that's probably mostly because he was the guy behind the “Free Bird” solo, although he had other solos I actually like better (see “The Needle and the Spoon” or “I Ain't the One”). The fact that none of them was a proper “lead guitarist”, ala a Jimmy Page or Eddie Van Halen, probably has something to do with that; there isn't one guy to single out as the star. I think Gary is a fine guitarist, I love his sound and style, but if I were ranking Skynyrd guitarists — again, pre-crash — I would put him at the bottom of the list. I just think Collins, Ed King, and Steve Gaines were better guitar players. From a technical standpoint, I would rank them in the order of Gaines, King, Collins, Rossington, although all four were creative and had great feel. (Allen was my personal favorite overall, even though he didn't have the level of technical skill that Steve or Ed did.) But that doesn't mean I think Gary is bad, or even average, and I don't think I've ever heard anyone call him a bad guitarist. Again, like all of Skynyrd's guitarists, he's just overlooked, because they all played both lead and rhythm, and there was no one guy who got all the attention or praise.

Question: Is Timothy hay a treat or a food for guinea pigs? Is there a danger in giving too much in a day?
Answer: If you have to ask this question, you probably shouldn't have guinea pigs. No offense. Hay — Timothy, orchard, meadow, or oat — is the bulk (80%) of a guinea pig's diet, and there is much more danger in not giving them enough of it. You literally can't give them too much, and they should always have access to fresh hay. As hindgut fermenters, guinea pigs' digestive systems must always have food moving through them, or they will be at risk of going into gastrointestinal stasis, which can be deadly. Pelleted food should be no more than a supplement, about 1/8 cup a day per pig. A 2lb guinea pig should also have about one cup of fresh greens per day, and can have small pieces of fruit and veg like apple, banana, bell pepper, or carrot as treats. They also need a vitamin C supplement. But the single most important part of a healthy diet for a guinea pig is hay, and Timothy is the standard.

Question: Are bunnies good house pets? Do they make a lot of mess?
Answer: If they're properly housed and given the right enrichment, overall I don't think house rabbits make much more mess or have more potential for destructiveness than dogs and cats. I mean, my brother Eddy's dog Keats caused so much mayhem in their house that Eddy and his wife had to start keeping the trash can on the kitchen counter whenever they went anywhere, so he couldn't reach it to scatter it all over the house, and his cat Eliot was fond of shredding curtains, knocking things over, and randomly pissing outside the litterbox, sometimes on people's belongings. (I adored both Keats and Eliot, for the record, but facts are facts.) Rabbits are also cleaner animals overall than either cats or dogs, provided they live in a clean environment. They groom themselves constantly, they have no inherent smell, they never need to be bathed (and in fact bathing can be harmful to their health), and they really, really don't like being dirty. Rabbits do chew. It's not “naughty” behavior, and it's not something you can train them not to do; they need to do it, because their teeth never stop growing. They also tend to explore their environment with their teeth. But just because they chew doesn't mean they're inevitably going to destroy your home. You just need to rabbit-proof, and to make sure they have appropriate things to chew on as well as enrichment toys to keep them from getting bored. Rabbits are intelligent animals, they need mental stimulation or, like dogs, they're more likely to be destructive. I recently got a new piece of furniture, an end table/cabinet made of solid wood. Eddie took one little nibble on the first night — it was a new thing in his environment, and those will always be investigated — but then he hopped away, and since then, he hasn't touched it. I can live with this: Rabbits can also easily be litter trained, especially if they're spayed or neutered. My rabbit never pees outside his litterbox. He'll scatter a few territorial poops here and there, but rabbit poo is inoffensive stuff — dry and odor free even when it's fresh. It's very different than if your cat or dog takes a dump on the rug. The messiest part of having rabbits is hay, which makes up 80% of their diet. Hay is messy, and can't be made not messy; I sweep at least twice every day and there will always be stray bits of hay on my floor. That just comes with the territory when you have a rabbit, so if you can't handle it, then choose another pet. But overall, rabbits make just as good of house pets as cats or dogs. There is just still this annoying stereotype of them as farm animals or livestock, especially in Europe where eating rabbit meat is much more common than in the U.S., where they're mainly viewed as pets. But that seems to be dying out, slowly but surely, as more people realize that rabbits make lovely house pets.

Question: Why is it said that the Amityville horror movie is all fake when there were reports of a real family getting killed?
Answer: Nobody has ever disputed the murders of the DeFeo family in the house. The case was notorious across the whole country; it's not every day a guy slaughters his entire family for no apparent reason. What's fake are the accounts of haunting and demonic possession in the house. Ronald DeFeo claimed he heard demonic voices in his head telling him to kill his family; his own defense attorney has stated that this was a total fabrication. Several other families have owned and occupied the house since the so-called paranormal events allegedly experienced by the Lutz family, with none reporting anything unusual or sinister whatsoever, and most of what the Lutzes claimed they experienced has either been debunked or cannot be proven. They made it up, maybe thinking that the house's history would make the story more plausible. Probably they thought they could get some money out of it. I wouldn't want to live in a house in which six people were brutally murdered, but not because I expect it would be haunted or possessed, just because I would always be thinking about the terrible events that occurred there. Anyplace where a bunch of kids got slaughtered is going to give me bad vibes.

Question: Why don't famous authors collaborate on books? Why haven't JK Rowling and Rick Riordan co-written a book? Wouldn't it become very popular?
Answer: Stephen King and Peter Straub — two giants of American horror fiction — became friends after meeting in London in 1977 and discovering that each was a fan of the other's work. They would subsequently collaborate on The Talisman. It spent 12 weeks at #1 on the New York Times Bestseller List when it was released in 1984. Indeed, it was popular enough with fans that seventeen years later, King and Straub decided to write a sequel, which was critically lauded and also a #1 bestseller. Authors will collaborate with one another, but it's not going to happen willy-nilly — like, “oh, you're popular, I'm popular, let's write a book together!” They have to have something to work with other than both simply being popular. Otherwise it's just a gimmick.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why did Stephen King come out publicly against Stanley Kubrick for "The Shining?" It is my fifth (5th) favorite horror film of all time.
Answer: Because King's novel was intensely personal to him — Jack Torrance represented King — and Kubrick bastardized it. I'm not sure King even actually thinks it's a bad movie, necessarily, he just thinks it's a bad adaptation of his book. And he's absolutely right. Look, in King's novel, Jack Torrance was a flawed person, no question, but he was also a tortured person, a man who deeply loved his wife and son, but was psychologically frail and thus easy for the evil at the Overlook Hotel to exploit. It wasn't Jack the hotel really wanted, it was Danny, but Jack was weaker and easier to get to than Danny or Wendy. So the hotel used him as a tool, and for most of the story, Jack fought against the hotel, because he did love his family. Jack was a human being in the book, a fleshed out person, as were Wendy and Danny. Kubrick jettisoned the human element of King's story, and of Jack Torrance. Did you actually give a real flying fuck about any of the Torrances in the movie? Because Kubrick didn't. He was interested only in showing Jack go batshit. Who the Torrances were didn't matter. That's why we know almost nothing about who any of them are as people, and in addition to that, Kubrick's Jack Torrance didn't really seem to have much love or affection for either his wife or son even before they got snowed in. The only time you see him show any warmth whatsoever toward either of them is when other people are present, which makes it seem disingenuous and phony. A false face. King himself summed up his feelings on Stanley Kubrick thusly: “he thinks too much, and feels too little". And so does Kubrick's The Shining.

Question: What is the lifespan of pet rabbits? How can it be prolonged?
Answer: The lifespan of a rabbit depends largely on breed, size and quality of care. Because we know more now about how to properly care for them, pet rabbits are already living much longer in general than they did even 30 years ago. Rabbits are like dogs in that smaller breeds live longer on average than larger breeds. If properly cared for, small and average sized rabbits like the dwarf breeds, Dutch, Lionhead, mini lop, Havana, etc. can live 12 years or more. Large and giant breeds like the English and French lops, Flemish giant, checkered giant, and New Zealand usually live more like 6 to 8 years. Question: What do you prefer, rural or urban life?
Answer: Rural. 100%. That wasn't always the case, although I grew up in a “semirural" town in the NYC metro area. When I was in my teens, 20s, and 30s, the city and city life appealed to me. I was in New York City almost every weekend in my late teens and early 20s, and I lived in Denver in 2011–2012, on a very busy street just a few blocks from a hospital, and I quite liked it despite the constant traffic and noise. In Denver, I didn't need a car, because I could either walk, bike, or take the bus or light rail everywhere. (Well, almost everywhere.) Close to city parks, restaurants, shopping, theaters, even walking distance from the zoo. But now, nearing 50, I'm all about rural life. I like quiet. I like green things growing. I like songbirds and rabbits and woodchucks, and the sound of the wind in the trees. The people are friendly in the country. I know this doesn't appeal to everyone, and some people would rather everyone ignore them, but I like that people out walking or jogging wave when you pass them, and that you can have a random conversation with a stranger at the supermarket. It gives a sense of community, and there is so much distrust and division in the U.S. these days, it's nice to just be able to chat with people about mundane shit. I like the access to fresh, local produce, eggs, and meats that living in farm country provides. Local baked goods, too. I don't have to buy factory farmed meat, I can get ethically sourced food that also supports local farms and businesses. Pretty much anything I want, I can get. Local honey, jams and jellies, maple syrup, sausages, cheese, pasta sauce, whatever. (My herbivorous pets also appreciate the abundance of organic local produce.) Now, I should clarify that my rural living is probably a little different than what most people think of when they hear that term, at least in this country. This is still New York, not the vast expanse of Montana or Texas or Wyoming, and as small as my town is, I'm not “in the middle of nowhere". The supermarket is five minutes away, and there are several big shopping centers pretty close by. In my village we have a wine bar, and a restaurant that serves locally made artisan cheeses and salamis, as well as a great pizzeria (run by a transplant from Brooklyn) and an excellent, authentic Mexican restaurant. We have an art gallery, and a few museums and historic sites, too, and ten minutes up the road is a fine craft brewery. But make no mistake: it's still rural — cornfields, cows, old farmhouses, dilapidated barns, pickup trucks literally everywhere, tractors cruising down the road, sunburned old men in suspenders, ball caps, and gumboots shuffling through the supermarket, and a population of 1,200. If I want a taste of the city, Albany is not that far a drive, and while it may not be a metropolis, Albany is still a city, and offers the choice and convenience of a city, should I so desire it. (I'm also still close enough to NYC to take the train down and make a day of it if I want to.) My county — which has an overall population density of less than 100 people per square mile — has also voted Democratic in the last 8 presidential elections, so as much as some people want to believe that all rural people are far right wing doomsday preppers with arsenals in their sheds, that's definitely not true. Along with Denver, the city I'm most familiar with is New York City, where both of my parents were from. I lived in the Bronx for several years as a kid, and worked in the Financial District for most of 2013. I know NYC fairly well, I'm comfortable on the subway, fine walking at night, whatever. New York is a great city, but it seems a lot of people who live there think it's the entire universe. That's kind of sad to me, because there is so much more to be seen and experienced even just in the state of New York. And that's something nobody seems to talk about when it comes to urban living: it can be quite insular, maybe as much so as rural living. Just as some people in small towns in Tennessee or West Virginia may never leave their town or county, there are people in big cities who never, or at least rarely, leave those places. People who never even get a driver's license. (I understand not owning a car if you live in a big city with ample public transport, I didn't own one in Denver or even for much of my time in Boulder, a much smaller city, but I don't know how anyone could be okay with not even knowing how to drive, or being able to do so legally. To me, driving is a life skill everyone should have.) My other issue with urban life is the crowding. While I enjoy talking to people here and there, I'm a pretty introverted person, and I really value my personal space. Taking the subway from Grand Central to Wall Street (and back) every day at rush hour sucked ultimate ass. Squished in a subway car with a hundred strangers, all doing our damnedest to pretend we didn't even see each other, jostled on the platform and stairs. I hated it. On top of that, most cities are way more expensive to live in than smaller towns are. The apartment I live in would rent for probably around $4,000 in Manhattan. I pay $1,400. I am not rich, nor do I have any interest in living in what equates to a walk-in closet. If I want to live in 300 square feet, I'll get myself a tiny house, rather than pay $2,000 or more a month for a micro studio apartment. So, that's pretty much where I'm at on the subject. I know everyone has their own preferences and priorities for their way of living, and that rural life isn't for everyone, but at this stage of my life, it's absolutely my preference.

Question: Why do people in the New York area seem to know so little about other suburbs in different parts of the region?
Answer: When you say “New York area", are you actually talking about New York City? Because people in the NYC suburbs are usually, in my experience, fairly familiar with their surrounding suburbs (and my experience comes from having lived the bulk of my life in the NYC suburbs and metro area). People in Yonkers know about White Plains, and vice versa. People in Harrison know Rye, people in Pleasantville know Tarrytown, etc. Frankly, the question isn't very clear. Just as I don't know what “New York area" means, I also don't know exactly what you mean by “other suburbs in different parts of the region". If by region you mean the metro area, the question is based on a false premise. Obviously people in a city like Mount Vernon, which is just north of the Bronx, may not be super familiar with Peekskill, which is on the far northwestern end of Westchester County. The two cities are over 30 miles apart, so not exactly neighbors. But people in the metro area are usually reasonably familiar with other localities in their general area. If you mean that people in the NYC suburbs aren't familiar with other suburbs in the tri-state area, well, why would they be? Outside of the places they border, what do Bayonne, New Jersey, or Greenwich, Connecticut matter to people in New York? If by “New York area”, you're talking about New York City, well, a lot of people in the city seem only vaguely aware that anything exists north of Yankee Stadium. New Yorkers tend to be rather insular, in my experience, and many of them are also transplants from elsewhere who may have never even been farther north than the Bronx.

Question: What were popular music artists before the Beatles?
Answer: Are you talking about rock artists? Or just popular music artists in general? Rock and roll started in the U.S., with artists like Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley, Buddy Holly, Jerry Lee Lewis, Gene Vincent, Eddie Cochran, Little Richard, Bill Haley and His Comets, The Big Bopper, Ritchie Valens, and Dion. Bob Dylan also hit before the Beatles, but he started out as a folk singer before transitioning to rock in the mid 60s. Pete Seeger (solo and with the Weavers), Joan Baez, the Staple Singers, and Odetta were all popular folk artists, as was Woody Guthrie, although he came earlier. Country had Hank Williams, Patsy Cline, Roy Acuff, Jimmie Rodgers, Earl Scruggs, Gene Autry, and others. Pop music before the Beatles saw the popularity of Frank Sinatra, Bing Crosby, Perry Como, Vic Damone, the Andrews Sisters, and Matt Monro. This is hardly a comprehensive list, but there's a sampling for you.

Question: What billionaires were not born into wealth and privilege?
Answer: Oprah Winfrey. She was born in Kosciusko, Mississippi, to an unwed teenage mother, Vernita Lee, and for the first six years of her life, was raised by her maternal grandmother, Hattie. They were so poor that her grandmother made Oprah's dresses out of potato sacks. At six she moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin with her mother, who worked as a maid, and also lived for a time with her father, Vernon Winfrey, a barber, in Nashville, Tennessee. She started high school in Milwaukee at Lincoln High School, but participated in the Upward Bound program, and excelled in academics, so was transferred to Nicolet High School, a more upscale school in the affluent suburb of Glendale. However, she was surrounded by wealthier children, and frustrated with her family's poverty, began stealing money from her mother in an attempt to “keep up with the Joneses”, leading her mother to send her back to Nashville to live with Vernon. Her father was much more strict than her mother, as well as more encouraging, and insisted that her education be top priority. She became an honors student, and was voted “most popular” in her senior class at East Nashville High School. She was also on the speech team, and won an oratory contest that earned her a full scholarship to Tennessee State University, where she studied communications. However, by the time she actually got her bachelor's degree, she was in her thirties and had already become a successful television personality. Love her or hate her, Oprah Winfrey started with absolutely nothing, and overcame tremendous odds to become the richest African-American of the 20th century, all by virtue of her own intelligence and hard work. Today her net worth is $2.5 billion.

Question: Can I give my guinea pig vitamin C tablets meant for people?
Answer: No, don't do that. Vitamin C tablets made for humans are going to be way too high in dosage for a guinea pig. This is an animal that weighs two pounds on average. You can either give your pigs safe, C-rich foods like bell peppers, parsley, and dill, buy a supplement made for guinea pigs, or both. I recommend Oxbow Natural Science Vitamin C biscuits. They're relatively inexpensive (about $8-$10 for 60 biscuits, or a one month supply for two pigs) and my pig (who will not eat bell peppers) absolutely loves them — as far as he's concerned, they're just treats. One a day, coupled with two tablespoons of C-enriched pelleted food (I feed Oxbow Garden Select), will provide all the C your pigs need to stay healthy. But please don't give them human C tablets. They're not formulated for guinea pigs and it's not safe. (One thing I'll note about the Oxbow C biscuits is that although the package says for all small animals, pets like rabbits, rats, and chinchillas do not need a C supplement. Guinea pigs, like humans, cannot synthesize their own C, but all of those other species make their own C and do not need it provided to them.)

Question: How do you decide which pet to get for your kid?
Answer: First, immediately disqualify any pet whose care you're not willing to take responsibility for, which is basically every pet if the child is under age 10 or so. Kids under, say, five or six shouldn't have any pets — at that age, pets should be family pets. A five-year-old can help — they can feed the cat, the fish, the hamster, the budgie, etc. — but cleaning tanks and cages is going to be your job as the parent. It's just not something young kids can do properly. Other small pets, like guinea pigs, have more specialized diets, and a young kid can't be responsible for feeding them. (Guinea pigs, while delightful, are also messy little poop machines, so their cages need to be cleaned often.) And for the love of all that's good in the world, never get a rabbit for a child until the kid is at least 10 or 11. Rabbits are possibly the worst pets you can get for small children. They're complicated to care for, they're long-lived, and frankly, they generally don't like kids very much, because kids want to cuddle and carry them around, and rabbits almost universally hate both of those things. For young kids, a family pet like a dog or cat is probably best, although they still need supervision while interacting with them. Really the only small animal pet I recommend for kids aged 5–10 are rats, kept in same-sex pairs since they're social. Rats are intelligent and fairly sturdy, they rarely bite or nip, they can be very affectionate, they're relatively easy to care for, and with a lifespan of about 3 years, they're not a long-term commitment. Whatever pet you're thinking of getting your kid, don't do it before doing thorough research on the animal's behavior and proper care. In the internet age, there is no excuse not to know what you're getting into before taking on the responsibility of another creature's life.

Question: In The Breakfast Club (1985 movie), what would happen if John Bender reported Vernon to the police for threatening him, and why doesn't Bender hit Vernon when he tells him to take a shot at him?
Answer: As to the first part of your question, probably nothing, especially if Vernon had no history of other such complaints. It's right there in the movie: John asks Vernon if he's threatening him, and Vernon says, “what are you going to do about it? You think anyone is going to believe you over me?” John Bender wasn't some nice boy who always did his homework on time and called his teachers sir and ma'am. He was known to be a liar and a troublemaker, and for all we know, he may have already had some kind of criminal record. Hell, pulling the false fire alarm may have been a prosecutable offense. In other words, Bender had a reputation, and like the boy who cried wolf, he probably wouldn't have been believed. He had no proof, it was his word against Vernon's, and while the kids knew who Vernon really was, there's nothing to suggest that he had a similar reputation among adults. Also, the movie is set in 1984, not 2023. If it had happened today, there may have been an investigation, but things were different then. (The very fact that Bender harasses and abuses Claire throughout the whole movie and not only faces no repercussions, but ends up dating her at the end — despite not even offering an apology for his inappropriate behavior — should tell you things were different then.) If it had been Andy or Brian, maybe something would have been done. Andy and Brian were basically “good kids" without history of trouble or lies. But Bender? Who's going to believe him? As to why he didn't hit Vernon, it's pretty much for the same reason. Vernon didn't assault him, so it wouldn't be self-defense, and it would be his word against Vernon's again. (And anyway, “he dared me to" isn't really a valid excuse to clock your school principal.) Bender would have been arrested for assault. And both he and Vernon knew that, otherwise a turd like Vernon never would have dared him to take a swing in the first place.

Question: How can white/Caucasian people show their pride yet not seem racist?
Answer: White person here. The very idea of “white pride" is inane to me. “White" isn't a culture or ethnicity, so how is it something to be proud of? Take a lobsterman in Maine, a lawyer in New York City, an insurance salesman in Des Moines, a rancher in Texas, and a shop owner in Seattle. Say they're all white. What else do they have in common? Other than all being Americans, something Americans of every race and skin color have in common? What on earth are the lobsterman and the insurance salesman going to talk about? They're unlikely to like the same sports teams. Iowa is 1,200 miles from the nearest ocean. Okay, maybe they both love Bruce Springsteen, or are into horror movies, but that's nothing to do with being white, any more than liking the same sports teams is. Their ancestors are unlikely to even have come from the same place; the largest ethnicity in Iowa is German, in Maine it's English. The local culture is different in those two states, too; you're throwing a New England Damnyankee in with a Midwesterner. There are millions of white people in my country that I have absolutely nothing in common with other than a general lack of melanin in my skin. Stick me in some dusty town in Oklahoma, or the wilds of Alaska, and I'm going to be a fish out of water no matter how many white people I meet. I certainly can't see myself bonding with the locals over our shared whiteness. I am not proud of being white. I don't see it as anything to be proud of; my race has very little to do with who I am as a person, and I didn't ask to be white, nor is it something I somehow achieved — it just happened that way. (EDIT: I should clarify, I'm not ashamed to be white, either. I don't derive either pride or shame from it.) And that's another thing. I understand racial and ethnic pride in marginalized groups. That's how St. Patrick's Day and Columbus Day first became widely celebrated holidays among Irish-Americans and Italian-Americans, respectively — because both of those ethnic groups were at one time marginalized in U.S. society. My own father experienced that discrimination firsthand in the 1920s and 30s. Irish pride and Italian pride were those people asserting their right to celebrate their own culture despite others discriminating against them and trying to keep them down. Saying, “I'm Irish/Italian, and that's okay.” And that's what black pride and LGBTQ+ pride are today. But white pride? I don't know what that even means outside of the white supremacy movement. So, what's the pride you feel in being white? It's not an accomplishment. It's not a culture. It's a broad term for people of all or mostly European ancestry with fair skin. So I'm afraid I'm stuck at the whole “show their pride” thing, because I don't see anything inherent in simply being white to feel pride in.

Question: Are rabbits hygienic?
Answer: Yes. There's this misconception that rabbits are dirty animals, but that could not be farther from the truth. The idea of them being dirty probably comes mostly from their history as livestock, how they were/are kept for that purpose, and, as pets, from the outdated practice of keeping them in small cages filled with litter. If you were forced to live your life in what's essentially a giant litterbox, would it be easy for you to keep clean? This goes double if the cage isn't cleaned regularly. Rabbits are very clean animals who bathe themselves more frequently than cats do. They also have no inherent smell to them — an evolutionary benefit, as prey animals, that helps them avoid detection by predators. Rabbit poo is also pretty much entirely devoid of odor. The only thing that will cause a smell is their urine, which is very high in ammonia, but even that won't smell if you litter train them, use the right litter, and clean their litterbox regularly. I use pelleted pine litter in a regular cat litterbox and clean it every other day, and never have an issue with odor. The average cat litterbox stinks a lot more. Allergies to rabbits do exist, but they're less common than people think. You're more likely to be allergic to the hay they eat than to rabbits themselves (in which case you can use a different type of hay; there are several varieties to choose from). Keep your rabbit indoors, in a spacious exercise pen — cages are cruel, and rabbits don't belong in them — litter train it, and keep it clean, and hygiene will not be a problem. The simple fact is that rabbits are cleaner animals than either cats or dogs, as long as they are given the proper care and environment.

Question: Which musicians are really good at connecting with their audience during a concert?
Answer: James Taylor impressed the hell out of me when I saw him at what was then called the Paramount Theater, in Madison Square Garden, in 1993. The theater holds 5,600 people, and it was full, but you'd have thought he was performing for a room full of his friends. He was warm, charming, engaging, as well as self-deprecating and funny. He told stories and jokes between songs. When a woman yelled out, “I love you!”, JT looked at the floor, shuffled his feet like a little kid, and said, “aw, shucks". I think it helps us not to know each other.”) When people started yelling for “Fire and Rain", he waved a hand and said, “oh, you don't want to hear that, it's sooo old”. When they kept yelling, he grabbed the setlist from behind an amp, turned it around to show the crowd, and said, “it's not until the next set, you're just going to have to wait!” But there was nothing mean or snotty about the way he said it, it was still charming and touched with humor. On top of this, the man put on a hell of a show. He sang his face off, and his band and backing vocalists were outstanding. I was on my feet for the whole thing. Of all the concerts I've been to in my life, that was easily one of the best, if not the very best, and that's as much because of how well he connected with the crowd as because of the music. He's going to be touring in the U.S. this summer, and I would love to see him again. JT knows how to work a crowd, and he gives his audience their money's worth.

Question: What non-actor was cast in an acting role and did an amazing job?
Answer: Jason Lee in Mallrats. Lee was a professional skateboarder, not an actor, but in 1995, at 25, he wanted to retire from skating and try something new. Casting director Don Phillips brought him in to audition for Kevin Smith, and Lee won the role of slacker manchild Brodie Bruce in Smith's sophomore effort. In the film, Brodie was the best friend of T.S. Quint, who was played by established actor Jeremy London, but Lee acted circles around London, and pretty much stole the whole movie. Brodie is obnoxious as fuck, but Lee is so charming and funny that the audience loves him anyway. (This is reflected in the film, where Brodie is ultimately offered his own late-night talk show.) His performance in Mallrats kicked off a very successful acting career. To date, he has over 70 credits on his filmography, including memorable roles in the films Chasing Amy, Dogma, Almost Famous, Enemy of the State, and Vanilla Sky, and his Golden Globe and SAG Award nominated role as the title character in the sitcom My Name is Earl. Kevin Smith told the story of Lee's casting in a 2020 interview with Entertainment Weekly: Our casting director was the great Don Phillips. Don was famous in town for casting Fast Times at Ridgemont High. He had discovered Sean Penn. For us, he discovered Jason Lee. Jason Lee was a professional skateboarder who had never really acted before. So, Don Phillips goes, "I got a kid coming in today, and he’s never acted before, and he’s a professional skateboarder." I didn’t know much about the skate game. He comes in and he's green as hell. He's never really acted. We’re making chit-chat and I was like, "So I understand you’re a skateboarder." And he’s like, "Well, I just retired." And he looked like he was f---ing 23. So, I’m like, "You retired?" He goes, "I’ve been skating at a professional level for ten years, yeah. I want to put it aside now and I want to concentrate on a different discipline." He was so well-organized. I loved his delivery. It was so not-polished and so real and rough and funny. All the guys came in to read for TS (the role ultimately played by Jeremy London), all the girls that came in read for Brandi (who would be played by Claire Forlani). So, when Jason was done with his audition, Don Phillips was like, "Do you want him to come back?" And me and Scott Mosier (Smith's regular producer) were like, "Well, he's a really good guy, I don’t think he’s right for the part, but bring him back, because he’s fun to talk to." We kept bringing him back because we didn’t know anybody in Los Angeles and we just thought he was a nice guy. Eventually, he wound up being better than everybody else. I said, "Listen, I think we’ve figured it out, we want you to play Brodie." And I’ll never forget, he was eating, and he looks up for a brief second, and he goes, "Yeah?" and he goes right back to eating his sandwich, looking back down. Eating was more exciting than being cast in his very first movie at that moment in time. But he came out and absolutely crushed, man, and he was a delight.

Question: If "Upstate New York" is the northwestern part of the state, what would you call the area Albany is in?
Answer: Upstate New York is not the “northwestern part of the state". Ask people from there, they will tell you. Buffalo is in Western New York, and Rochester is in either Western New York or the Finger Lakes, depending on who you ask. Binghamton and Elmira are in the Southern Tier. Syracuse is in Central New York. Saratoga Springs, Ballston Spa, Lake George, Schenectady, and yes, Albany, would be categorized as “upstate", but they're also in different geographical regions. Geographically, New York state is informally divided into a number of regions that nobody outside of the state (and apparently plenty of people in New York City) seems to know exist. To most people, there's “New York City” and there is “upstate". (I never know where this leaves Long Island, which is east, not north, of the city, and not a part of it.) Albany is in the Capital District, along with Rensselaer, Troy, and Schenectady. Below the Capital District is the Hudson Valley, which extends from Yonkers — which borders the Bronx — as far north as Columbia County, although Columbia, along with Greene, is an “in-between" county that can be placed in either the Hudson Valley or Capital District. Everything below Columbia, Greene, Ulster, and Sullivan Counties is “downstate” and part of the NYC metro area.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is the rarest bird species in the world and what is being done to protect it from extinction?
Answer: Could be the Florida grasshopper sparrow, which lives only in the prairie regions of south central Florida, U.S.A. As of 2017, the total population was only 50 birds (down from over a thousand in 2004), and it was predicted to become extinct by 2019. However, captive breeding was begun in an effort to save the species, although its results have been mixed. The current population is about 120, making it the most endangered bird species in North America. Its main threats are habitat loss, nest destruction from flooding, and competition from invasive bird species. The kakapo is also one of the most endangered bird species, with only 249 in existence. They are ground-dwelling and flightless parrots, native only to New Zealand, who evolved without natural predators, so the introduction of invasive predators like stoats and domestic cats has devastated the species. Conservation efforts have been ongoing for over a century, and include providing feeding stations for the birds to help them with reproduction, and monitoring of nests to help protect them from predators.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What is the most insidious bird?
Answer: I don't think I've ever heard the word “insidious” used to describe a bird before, but there is one I think the word fits, and that's the house sparrow. Looks cute and harmless, right? Think again. It's native to Eurasia and parts of north Africa, but has been introduced in the Americas, southern Africa, and Australia, and here in North America, it's one of our most numerous birds as well as one of our worst invasive species. House sparrows literally murder and mutilate our native bird species like bluebirds, swallows, and martins, and destroy their eggs and nests, as well as competing with them for food. They wreak havoc on our crops, and also spread disease among humans and domestic animals. And there are millions upon millions upon millions of them, despite them not being protected as most of our native species are. The house sparrow is believed to be the most widespread bird in the world, and also possibly the most numerous — its worldwide numbers are estimated at about 1.4 billion. I am a bird lover and avid birdwatcher, but even I can't muster any love for the house sparrow. I wish we could eradicate them from the entire continent. Every last one.

Question: Are hamsters or guinea pigs better as small pets? Why?
Answer: They're totally different behaviorally, and require different care, so it depends what you want in a pet. Personally, my opinion is that if you want a pet that's more interactive, guinea pigs are the way to go. They're dear, sweet little creatures who usually become accustomed to handling pretty easily. But note that they're a longer term commitment than hamsters because of their longer lifespan, and I will stress again that they're very social and should not be kept alone, or they can become depressed. So always get at least two guinea pigs of the same sex. And also always remember that the vast majority of commerical cages sold at pet stores for both species are too small and thus inadequate. Proper cages can be found online.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why do bunnies die when you bathe them?
Answer: Please disregard the answers about how bathing rabbits is fine, blah, blah, blah. There is literally no reason to bathe a healthy rabbit; rabbits are among the cleanest animals you can keep as a pet. Do you make a habit of bathing your cats? No? Well, rabbits are cleaner than cats, so why bathe them? Rabbits don't automatically die when they're bathed, but because they're easily stressed as a general rule, it's a possibility. Sudden and/or extreme changes in temperature can shock a rabbit's system and cause a heart attack. Being restrained and doused with water is stressful — rabbits can swim if they have to, but given a choice, they will always avoid getting wet. Also, rabbits have extremely dense fur, much more so than the average dog or cat, so it takes a very long time to dry, which leaves the rabbit highly susceptible to hypothermia. Again: bathing a rabbit is completely unnecessary. They're not dogs. Keep your rabbit's environment clean and your rabbit will be clean. They are fastidious animals who can't stand being dirty, and they take care of their own hygiene.

Question: Do some girls bully other girls because they are prettier than them, or because they have better boyfriends?
Answer: Michele “Missy” Avila was actually murdered by her two so-called best friends strictly because she was prettier and more popular than they were, and they were jealous of her. Karen Severson had been best friends with Missy since they were 8 years old, but after they hit puberty, Missy blossomed, while Karen did not. Further complicating things, when they were juniors at San Fernando High School in Los Angeles, Karen began dating Missy's ex-boyfriend, a boy named Randy, and while still dating Karen, Randy tried to get back together with Missy. Missy told Karen, and advised her to dump Randy, but Karen instead took out her anger on Missy. In October of 1985, when the girls were 17, Karen and another friend, Laura Doyle, made plans to hang out with Missy after school. But Missy never came home, and Doyle later called Missy's house looking for her, claiming that she had dropped Missy off to talk to some boys in a Chevy Camaro before going to get gas. Laura said when she returned after getting gas, Missy, the boys, and the Camaro were gone. This was a lie — an elaborate ruse to throw suspicion off of her and Karen. The two, along with another friend, Eva Chirumbolo, had brought Missy into the mountains, where Laura and Karen beat her, cut off her hair, and drowned her in shallow water. Following the murder, and during the investigation, Karen even moved in with Missy's family, feigning support, when what she really wanted was to stay informed on the case. It was Eva — who was not involved in Missy's murder, and was initially threatened into silence by the other two — who ultimately told the police, leading the two girls to be apprehended. Severson and Doyle were each convicted of second degree murder, and sentenced to 15 years to life. Karen was paroled in 2011 after serving 21 years, and Laura was paroled the following year. Question: Why do most Americans have such a strong passion and bias for the Italian culture?
Answer: We don't. I'm not sure where you've developed this obsessive thinking that Americans are obsessed with Italy or Italian culture, David, but you're certainly persistent with it. Americans of Italian ancestry total about 16.6 million, or 5% of the U.S. population, and that includes people of mixed ancestry, like myself. For perspective, there are almost twice as many Irish-Americans as there are Italian-Americans, and most Italian-Americans are concentrated in specific geographical regions of the United States, most notably the Northeast and New England, but also places like Chicago, New Orleans, South Florida, St. Louis, and Cleveland. In the Western half of the U.S. you will find very few people of Italian ancestry (comparatively speaking). Italian immigrants and Italian-Americans certainly contributed a lot to U.S. culture, especially in terms of cuisine, but this is Italian-American culture, which is separate and distinct from Italian culture, especially modern Italian culture. Most Italian-Americans are descended from people who came here between the 1860s and 1920s, and Italian culture has changed significantly since then. Even what we call Italian food in the U.S. is in large part Italian-American cuisine — sausage and peppers, baked ziti, chicken parmesan, Alfredo sauce, fra diavolo, garlic bread, all of these things are Italian-American, not traditionally Italian, although some are derived from traditional Italian dishes. As an Italian-American myself, I'm certainly not dismissing the cultural contributions of Americans of Italian ancestry, which have been significant, but the so-called “passion and bias for Italian culture” you're talking about does not exist, and Italian-Americans, as well as their contributions, should be recognized on their own merits. They're not Italian, they're American.

Question: How do I get my rescue pet rabbit to stop chewing all my electric and phone cables?
Answer: You can't stop a rabbit from chewing, it's an inherent behavior. Cords and cables look like sticks and twigs to rabbits, things they would chew in nature. You have to a) make the cords and cables inaccessible to your rabbit, and b) make sure he/she has appropriate things to chew on. Buy chew toys designed for rabbits. Lots of chew toys. Toys made from willow tend to be especially popular with rabbits, as willow is very tasty to them. Oxbow makes a few different willow chew toys my Eddie loves, just do a search on Chewy. They need to be replaced often, though, so be warned. You can also make your own toys with cardboard, like empty paper towel and toilet paper rolls — stuff a couple of those with hay, or put a few treats in them, then fold up the ends, so your rabbit needs to figure out how to get them out. Puzzle toys are a great diversion for rabbits, too, and offer good mental stimulation. You can find them designed for rabbits, but some dog puzzles also work for rabbits — Eddie has a dog puzzle he quite likes. You put some pellets in it, and he needs to figure out how to get them out. Also, cover your cords. There are all manner of cord protectors available online, but plastic split flex tubing is probably the cheapest option. In the U.S., Home Depot sells 10 feet of it for about $3 or $4. You can also block off cords and power strips with C&C grids. Also, if you're not using your phone charger, keep it out of your rabbit's reach. You could try a Command hook on the wall, that you can hang the cord over when it's not in use. There are alao a number of YouTube videos on rabbit-proofing that you might find helpful. But it's entirely possible to rabbit-proof in a way that keeps both your rabbit and your stuff safe. Good luck!

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Are humans the only animal that's voluntarily vegan?
Answer: Veganism is a human invention, and it's inherently voluntary (unless you have some rare medical condition that makes it deadly for you to eat any meat at all, which I'm not sure exists). As a rabbit owner, it peeves me when people refer to rabbits as “vegan", because it's an inaccurate term. Rabbits and other lagomorphs (hares and pikas) are obligate herbivores, meaning that they are biologically designed to eat vegetation. They don't usually eat meat because they can't properly digest it and thus can't survive on it. It's nothing to do with ethics or morals, nor with choice. In addition to that, a number of species, including the European rabbit, snowshoe hare, and cottontails, will occasionally eat meat, usually either carrion or insects, for extra nutrients. But everything about herbivores, from their teeth to their intestines to their gut flora, is designed for digesting plant matter, not animal matter. It's just how they have evolved. Humans who become vegan almost always do so for ethical reasons. Herbivorous animals like rabbits, guinea pigs, horses, deer, cattle, rhinos, etc. don't have human morals, ethics, or consciences, and it's wrong to apply such things to them, just as it's wrong to view obligate carnivores like cats and ferrets negatively because they kill and eat other animals, because that is also biological, and has fuck all to do with morality or ethics. So, yeah. Humans are not just the only animals who are voluntarily vegan, we're the only animals who are vegan at all, because 99% of the time, veganism is elective. Animals that don't consume meat are not vegan, they're herbivorous. Assigning human traits, especially when it comes to morality, to animals, is 100% wrong.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why did film director Michael Cimino never rebounded after directing his one successful film The Deer Hunter and his worst film Heaven’s Gate?
Answer: I'm not sure if you understand just how bad Heaven's Gate was, or how big an impact it had on Cimino's career. Heaven's Gate was so bad, such a failure, and also so controversial (featuring numerous instances of animal cruelty, including the deaths of horses, cows, and chickens), that some critics actually changed their view of The Deer Hunter in its wake. Heaven's Gate lost United Artists almost $40 million; the studio very nearly went bankrupt because of it. The film tainted Cimino's reputation as a filmmaker irrevocably. His next film, Year of the Dragon, was slammed for its racist stereotyping of Asians — and this was the 1980s, when films like Sixteen Candles and Revenge of the Nerds struck box office gold with Asian stereotypes — and was nominated for five Razzie Awards, including Worst Picture. Then, on his next film, The Sicilian, Cimino butted heads with producers, refusing to cut the film below 150 minutes, an almost unheard of run time for a theatrical film back then (The Deer Hunter notwithstanding). 20th Century Fox sued Cimino, and won. The final cut of the film was released in 1987 to almost universally negative reviews; it sits at a 10% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes. After The Sicilian, he only made two more films, Desperate Hours in 1990 and The Sunchaser in 1996, and both of those were also critical and commercial disasters. Basically, after The Deer Hunter, everything Cimino touched turned to shit, and in addition to that, he had a widespread reputation as a liar and a selfish egomaniac. He lied about his age, he lied about his education, he lied about his early work in the industry, he lied about having been a Green Beret in Vietnam (he spent six months in the reserves, never saw active service or combat). Lies, lies, lies. Michael Cimino got lucky. He struck gold with one film. Pretty much everything else he did was terrible, and he was seen as an unpleasant person by quite a lot of people. So, rather than asking why his career didn't rebound, a better question is, how the hell did he strike gold with The Deer Hunter?

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What are the best Netflix original series?
Answer: This is subjective, obviously, but my favorite Netflix original series is hands down The Haunting of Hill House (2018). Here you have what is ostensibly a horror series, written, produced, and directed by one of today's most highly regarded horror filmmakers, Mike Flanagan, but what you get in the end is probably one of the best family dramas of the modern era. For the uninitiated, Hill House is a 10-episode series loosely based on Shirley Jackson's 1959 novel, which it tweaks and updates, with the past sequences set in 1992 and the current ones in the modern day (2018). It's about the Crain family — dad Hugh (Henry Thomas then, Timothy Hutton now), mom Olivia (Carla Gugino), and kids Steven (Paxton Singleton/Michiel Huisman), Shirley (Lulu Wilson/Elizabeth Reaser), Theodora AKA “Theo” (Mckenna Grace/Kate Siegel), and twins Luke (Julian Hilliard/Oliver Jackson-Cohen) and Nell (Violet McGraw/Victoria Pedretti). The family moves into the titular Hill House in 1992 intending to flip and sell it, but things go horribly awry. All of the adult Crain children are some level of emotionally and psychologically fucked up, stemming largely from their childhood experiences in the haunted mansion. Their mother died when they were kids, their relationships with one another are fractured, and none of them have anything even approaching a relationship with their father. Starting with the first episode, each Crain child gets his or her own focus episode, starting with Steve, the oldest, and ending with Nellie, the younger twin by less than two minutes. Hugh and Olivia each also get episodes focusing on them. Episode 6, which sees the mostly estranged family reunite for a funeral, is probably one of the best episodes I've ever seen of any show, both from a technical standpoint and an artistic one. It's almost an hour long, yet was filmed with only five shots, the longest of which was a full 17 minutes. And during these long shots, the actors had to deliver some heavy, emotional shit; I can only imagine the fear each must have had of screwing up their lines and ruining the shot. Flanagan called the episode “the hardest thing we've ever done, and the result of the combined efforts of hundreds of people”. The child actors, who ranged in age from 6 to 13, not only look a lot like the adults who play the grown up versions of them, all of them can actually act. I was probably most impressed with little Violet McGraw (who can currently be seen in theaters in the horror film M3GAN), who had some heavy shit to play as a 6-year-old, but all of them were excellent. So were the adults; if there was a weak link, it was Huisman, but given that he's Dutch and English is like his third language, he played American pretty damn convincingly. Pedretti, meanwhile, landed the role of Nell right out of college, and she was absolutely dynamite. Flanagan regulars Annabeth Gish and Robert Longstreet are also customarily excellent as the somewhat mysterious caretakers of Hill House, Horace and Clara Dudley, as are Anthony Ruivivar, Samantha Sloyan, and Levy Tran as the respective significant others of Shirley, Steve, and Theo. I am an unabashed Mike Flanagan fan, and love quite a lot of his work — Hush, Doctor Sleep, Gerald's Game, Midnight Mass, The Midnight Club — but for me, Hill House is his masterpiece. This isn't just a horror series — it's much more than that.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is The Breakfast Club still relevant?
Answer: It's been a long time since I was a teenager, but… Do teens still feel peer pressure from their friends? Do they still feel pressure from their families to succeed, be it at academics, athletics, etc.? Do they still feel misunderstood or ignored by their parents? Do they still feel like their teachers and other authority figures judge them harshly without knowing their individual struggles? Do they still judge kids from other cliques without knowing them? Do they still feel alone and alienated if they don't fit in? If the answer to any or all of these is “yes" then… yeah, The Breakfast Club is still relevant. The whole point of the movie is that teenagers often struggle to feel understood by the adults in their lives, and also are often pressured by their friends and peer groups. Also that once you get past the superficial differences, many teenagers have similar feelings, and feel similar pressures (like Brian with his grades and Andy with his wrestling), and that if kids in different cliques would just take the time to talk — and listen — to one another, they might not feel so different from each other. My experience is that these are things that happen across generations. They weren't specific to Gen X; the film just happened to be made when Gen X were teenagers.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why don’t Americans like to identify with their English ancestry?
Answer: This American doesn't have any English ancestry, at least that I'm aware of. In the case of almost every American I know who does have English ancestry, said ancestry goes back centuries and generations, so there isn't much to identify with. My high school bestie, Amanda, is of Italian ancestry on her father's side, her maternal grandfather was from Germany, and her maternal grandmother was from England, of Irish ancestry. She actually does identify with her English ancestry, even though technically, her blood ancestry is Irish. Her grandmother passed before she was born, but her great-aunt, who has since passed, had lived in England until her 20s and still had a slight accent. (I absolutely loved Aunt Ron, a spitfire with a razor wit even in her 80s.) Her mom also regularly made English-style pancakes — done traditionally, with a sprinkling of sugar and squeeze of lemon — and homemade jam pasties. I had no idea that pancakes were different in England than they are in the U.S., or even that there was such a thing as a jam pasty, before I met her, but both are tasty, and I always wanted her mom to make us pancakes when I slept over. But Amanda is like a lot of Americans: her ancestry is mixed. She identifies with her Italian ancestry as well, her paternal grandparents having been immigrants. But the bottom line is, she is an American, and that's how she most identifies. She's a prime example of the United States being a melting pot, and many of its citizens not being 100% of any one ancestry, especially those whose families have only been here a few generations (mine is another such family; I just don't have any ancestors from England). And those whose families have been here for five, seven, ten generations are more likely to just identify as American than anything else. What does a guy whose ancestors all came here prior to 1850 have in common with a modern Englishman? There just isn't much to identify with.

Question: What are some of the best "winks" to an actor’s former show/movie that you have seen in their newer shows/movies?
Answer: Enemy of the State, in which Gene Hackman stars as a secretive and mysterious surveillance expert (opposite Will Smith), very clearly pays homage to Hackman's previous film The Conversation, which had been released in 1974. Although it's not explicitly stated that Hackman's character Brill is in fact Harry Caul, the paranoid surveillance expert from The Conversation, his office is the same as Caul's — a locked cage inside an empty warehouse — and Hackman even wears the same coat as he had 24 years earlier in the previous film. In a subplot in Kevin Smith's film Mallrats, Ethan Suplee's character Willam spends the entire movie trying, unsuccessfully, to see the hidden image (of a sailboat) in a Magic Eye poster, becoming increasingly frustrated as passers-by see the image with little effort. Toward the end of the movie, Rene, played by Shannen Doherty, walks by, glances at the poster, and says, “oh, cool, a sailboat”. Willam looks at her quizzically and says, “Brenda?” — a reference to Doherty's most famous role, as Brenda Walsh in Beverly Hills, 90210. Rene calls him a dick and storms off.

Question: Why has my rabbit suddenly started peeing outside his litter box since I covered it with mesh wire? He’s always peed in it before.
Answer: Rabbit feet have no padding like dog and cat feet, and wire is not only uncomfortable and painful for them to stand on, it can cause a condition called ulcerative pododermatitis, informally known as sore hocks, that can be crippling if left untreated. In other words, he doesn't want to stand on the wire, because it hurts his feet. So get rid of the wire. It's totally unnecessary anyway. Litterboxes just aren't that hard to keep clean. Rabbits should never be kept in wire bottomed enclosures, either, for the same reason. It's cruel.

Question: If I am armed with a sledgehammer and I am in moderately good physical shape, could I survive an attack by an angry grey wolf? Or would it make no difference (as it surely wouldn’t in the case of a lion)
Answer: Firstly: wolves basically never attack people in real life. So let's not perpetuate negative and false views of them. However, hypothetically… Of all weapons, you choose a sledgehammer? That's not very practical, is it? The average sledgehammer weighs about 10 pounds, and even if you didn't have a large, agile, and angry predator attacking you, there are only so many swings you could expect to be able to take in a short time span. Swinging a sledgehammer isn't like swinging a regular ball-peen hammer, it's a lot slower, and in fact, you'd probably be better off with a regular hammer. At least that you could potentially still swing if the wolf got you pinned or knocked you down, in which case a sledgehammer would be utterly useless. So, a sledgehammer is a terrible weapon for anything resembling close combat. I'm not even an expert on such matters, not even close, but that's just common sense. It's big, it's heavy, it's unwieldy, it's slow and takes both hands to swing, and it only works if you're standing and there's a reasonable amount of space between you and your attacker. By the time you got your sledgehammer raised to deliver a blow, the wolf would likely be at your throat and ready to tear it out.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What do rabbit owners think of Watership Down?
Answer: Love it. Love the book, loved the animated film from 1978. The BBC miniseries from 2018 was okay — great voice cast, but some of the CGI was laughably cheesy and amateurish. (Seriously, that rottweiler!) I'd have thought the BBC could afford better than that. Look, rabbits don't get a lot of books and movies about them, and even fewer that portray them as complex, intelligent, sensitive animals. Richard Adams actually read up on real life rabbit behavior before he wrote the book, which is commendable. I also love that Adams created an entire language for his rabbits. Lapine is pretty cool. (EDIT: forgot to mention also lapine mythology — Frith, El-ahrairah, the Black Rabbit of Inle, etc.) I know some people thought the story was sexist and “anti-feminist", but speaking as a feminist myself: such critics need to calm down. Wild European rabbits are not human beings. There is no such thing as “sexism" or “feminism” in the rabbit world; bucks have their roles, and does have theirs, and both are vital to the health of the colony as a whole. Adams' rabbits are not meant to be humans in rabbit form, they're rabbits humans can understand. Others were taken aback by the violence in the story, and that just shows a lack of understanding of rabbit behavior. We see them as these cute, timid, docile little fluffballs, but male rabbits — both wild and domestic — will absolutely engage in bloody battle, sometimes even resulting in death. This is why unaltered male rabbits can't be housed together. It's not gratuitous, it's reality. So, yeah. I adore Watership Down. I just wish people would stop naming their pet rabbits Fiver and Hazel. I love both characters, don't get me wrong, but the names are worn out at this point.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Who was the very first teen idol?
Answer: The general consensus is that the first artist who could be considered a teen idol was Hungarian composer Franz Liszt (1811–1886). Liszt was a handsome and reportedly magnetic young man, and young women responded accordingly even in the 1840s. There was even a term coined for the phenomenon: “Lisztomania". Women would try to snip locks of his hair, steal his handkerchiefs and piano strings, and one reportedly even snatched up a used cigar butt he had tossed away, which she then enclosed in a locket with his initials on it. Liszt in 1858: The first teen idol in the modern sense may have been Frank Sinatra (1915–1998). Like Liszt, the legions of screaming teenage girls who descended upon his concerts in the early 1940s led a term to be coined, this time “Sinatramania”. He was given nicknames like “Swoonatra”, and his young fans took to calling themselves “Sinatratics". Young women regularly accosted him trying to steal his clothing right off his person, and would bribe hotel maids to let them touch his bed. Ol' Blue Eyes certainly had it going on in the 1940s.

Question: What areas in upstate New York are still affordable and easily accessible to NYC?
Answer: Generally speaking, the closer you are to the city, the higher the rents and cost of living. In White Plains, which is in Westchester County, about 25 miles north of Manhattan, the average one-bedroom apartment currently rents for about $3,000 a month — more than in some parts of NYC. Staten Island is significantly cheaper on average. In Cold Spring, which is in Putnam County, about an hour and a half from NYC, the average one-bedroom rents for about $2,000 a month. In Poughkeepsie, which is in Dutchess County and is probably about as far as you can live from NYC and still reasonably commute there, the average one-bedroom is about $1,800 a month. If you wanted to push it a little farther, you could try Kingston, in Ulster County, where the average is about $1,600 a month. But Kingston is a two-hour drive from the city, and probably two and a half to three hours by train. However, having said all of this, the only location I mentioned that could reasonably be called “upstate" is Kingston. Contrary to what NYC folks might tell you, “upstate" does not start at Pelham Parkway. Westchester, Putnam, and Dutchess Counties are all in a region defined as downstate New York. It's not until you hit Ulster, Sullivan, and Columbia Counties that you can really consider yourself to be “upstate". And the bottom line is, it's expensive to live in proximity to New York City. If you want ease of access to the city, you are going to pay for it.

Question: Do living writers ever choose to withdraw their past books from publication?
Answer: Stephen King did this with Rage, a novel he'd written in 1977 under his pen name Richard Bachman. The novel is about a Maine high school student named Charlie Decker, who brings a gun to school and fatally shoots two of his teachers, then holds his classmates hostage. Six different school shooters in the 1990s were at least partly inspired by the novel, so when it went out of print in the U.S., King opted not to renew it. He later took it out of print worldwide. In 2013, following the Sandy Hook shootings, King published a nonfiction e-book essay called Guns, detailing why he had taken the novel out of circulation, and donated all proceeds from the sale of the book to the Brady Campaign to Prevent Gun Violence.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Which movie have you been able to recognize the location that's being used to shoot a scene?
Answer: Lots of them. I mean, there have been tons of movies filmed in New York City where the locations are recognizable to me, as someone who has spent a lot of time in the city. Peace, Love, and Misunderstanding is a rom-com starring Jane Fonda, Catherine Keener, and Jeffrey Dean Morgan that was filmed in Woodstock, New York, and I recognized the downtown and police station. Martin Scorsese's The Age of Innocence has scenes filmed at the Luykas Van Alen house in Kinderhook, New York; it's a 17th century Dutch colonial and national historic landmark that I've driven by any number of times. (It's also a house museum, and they give tours, but I've never done one.) Stanley Kubrick's adaptation of The Shining was mostly filmed in England, but has shots of the Flatirons — very distinctive rock formations — in Boulder, Colorado, where I lived for 12 years. (The 1997 miniseries adaptation was filmed at the Stanley Hotel in Estes Park, Colorado; I've been there, too.) Eighth Grade was filmed in Rockland County, New York; the exterior shots of the mall in the film are of the Palisades Center in Nyack, and the interiors are of the Galleria in White Plains (which is actually in Westchester County). I've been to both malls numerous times. Parts of At First Sight, starring Val Kilmer and Mira Sorvino, were filmed at the Bear Mountain Inn, an historic hotel in Bear Mountain, New York — my sister had her wedding reception there when she married her first husband. Nobody's Fool, starring Paul Newman, was largely filmed in Fishkill, New York — my brother used to live there, so I recognized that, too. I could probably come up with more, and if I remember any I will update the answer.

Question: Why are rabbits not so common as pet like cats?
Answer: Rabbits are the third most popular pet in both the U.S. and UK, after cats and dogs, but they are still not nearly as common as either of those species for a few reasons. For one, throughout most of their history as domestic animals, rabbits have been livestock, and in some parts of the world, they still are primarily viewed as livestock. Rabbits have been domesticated for over 2,000 years, but it's only in the last 200 or so that they've become popularized as pets (and for most of that time, they've still been housed outdoors like livestock — it wasn't until the 1980s that keeping rabbits as house pets like cats or dogs started to become more common, and in the UK, it's still much more common for rabbits to be housed outdoors than in). Simply put, to many people, rabbits are for eating, not keeping in your home as a pet. (I do wish people would be a little more sensitive to us rabbit owners, though, because the jokes about making stew out of my rabbit are pretty old and in poor taste.) Rabbits are also misunderstood animals. People think they're dumb, which they absolutely are not — Google “rabbit intelligence” and you'll see that — and also that they're cute, docile little “pocket pets", most suitable for children, which they also are not. Kids, especially younger kids, are the last people who should have rabbits as pets, and a majority of rabbits purchased or adopted for young kids are abandoned within a matter of months because of this. They tend to be kept in small cages filled with litter, like hamsters or gerbils, when they need a lot more space and can be litter trained like cats, they're feistier than most people imagine, and many people for some reason think they live three or four years, when they commonly live ten or more. (Also, many breeds of rabbit aren't particularly small, either — the average rabbit is about 5–6 pounds, some popular breeds like the New Zealand and English lop can weigh as much as 12 pounds, and the Flemish giant can weigh over 20. Dwarf breeds are the exception, not the rule.) Also, and I'm going to be frank here, when it comes to bonding, rabbits aren't pushovers. Look, humans generally like our pets to be very hands-on. We want to be able to pick them up and snuggle them at leisure. Cats and dogs are the most popular pets in part because they tend to be pretty amenable to this (with exceptions, of course, and dogs are usually more outwardly affectionate than cats are). Rabbits are different — they're prey animals, and while they can be very affectionate and loving, it takes time and patience to build a relationship with them, and they usually need to come to you. Rabbits, for the most part, just aren't snuggly, cuddly animals. Most of them hate being picked up and held, and have no interest in hanging out in your lap. They prefer having all four feet on the ground, in case of danger, because their only defense against predators is to run. My rabbit loves to sit on the couch next to me and get pets. I can even snuggle him some, and he both gives kisses and is quite tolerant of getting them, but he's never spent more than a minute or so on my lap at any one time, and he absolutely hates to be picked up or held. That's not because he doesn't love me or isn't tame, it's just rabbit nature; however, many people, especially those accustomed to dogs and cats, see this as evidence that rabbits can't love you or are somehow still wild animals. My sister, for example, is a dog person. Even cats are not demonstrative enough for her, so she doesn't “get" rabbits at all, and was frustrated that she couldn't just hold Eddie in her lap and cuddle him. Lastly, proper rabbit care is complicated and expensive. Rabbits cost more to feed than cats if you're giving them a proper diet, they need regular vet care from an exotics vet, and they have pretty specialized diets. You can't just dump a bunch of pellets in a bowl and call it done. Having said all this, rabbits continue to grow in popularity as pets, as more and more people realize that although they are very different than dogs or cats, they are utterly delightful in their own way for the right owner. I would not take any cat or dog over my Eddie.

Question: President Reagan infamously called Born in the USA patriotic, not realizing it was a critique of the treatment of Vietnam veterans. What other songs have ironic titles or lyrics that many people think mean something other than what they really mean?
Answer: I'm not sure Donald Trump understands the lyrics to “Fortunate Son” by Creedence Clearwater Revival. Trump famously played the song at a campaign rally in 2020, which its author, John Fogerty, called “confounding”. Fogerty — who was himself drafted during the Vietnam War — wrote the song to express his frustration with wealthy, privileged young men using their money and status to avoid the draft. Trump himself, whose father was a multimillionaire, received five deferments during the war, four for education and one for his famous “bone spurs”. John Mellencamp's songs “Pink Houses” and “Our Country” have both been used by conservative politicians who mistook them for patriotic songs, when neither actually is, at least not in the way many far right conservatives view patriotism. Meaning people apparently just ignore the rest of the lyrics. But “Pink Houses” is really a scathing critique of the United States, while “Our Country” — which was probably most famously used by the National Organization for Marriage, at events opposing same-sex marriage — specifically calls for diversity, equal opportunity, and inclusion, and decries bigotry and prejudice. Mellencamp himself, who is also a staunch LGBTQ+ ally, has sent multiple cease and desist letters to politicians and organizations for unauthorized use of his songs, including NOM, Mitt Romney, and John McCain.

Question: What can I use to line an indoor rabbit enclosure? We currently use cardboard boxes but ridiculously they're quite hard to get hold of. He will chew carpet. Thanks

Question: What are the differences between European rabbits and Eastern cottontails?
Answer: The European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) and Eastern cottontail (Sylvilagus floridanus) are not that closely related, even if they look somewhat superficially similar. European rabbits are heavier bodied and generally larger than Eastern cottontails, and have plusher fur with more subtle agouti ticking. Cottontails have proportionally larger eyes than European rabbits, and their ears are shaped differently — cottontail ears are almost diamond-shaped, while European rabbit ears are oval-shaped with pointed ends. European rabbits also have broader skulls and longer noses than cottontails, and as their name suggests, cottontails have fluffier tails. While both can run fast, the European rabbit is significantly faster than the cottontail, with an average speed of 25 miles per hour and a top speed of 45 miles per hour, to the cottontail's max of about 20 miles per hour. Both, however, use zigzag running patterns to evade predators. Behaviorally, they're also quite different. European rabbits are social, and live in colonies of up to 30 or so individuals in complex underground burrow systems called warrens. Cottontails are solitary and, being territorial, do not typically tolerate the presence of other rabbits outside of the breeding season. They don't dig warrens, either, but instead will either take over burrows abandoned by other species, such as woodchucks, or dig a shallow nest called a form. Their solitary nature also causes cottontails to be more timid and easily stressed than European rabbits, which is why they have never been domesticated, and also why they are almost impossible to keep alive in captivity.
