Question: Compared to New York City, why does upstate New York get so much more snow?
Answer: Upstate, Central, and Western New York have a humid continental climate, while New York City, Long Island, and the lower Hudson Valley have a humid subtropical climate. Western and Central New York in particular get so much snow because of their proximity to the Great Lakes (Erie and Ontario). Most of the heavy snowfall in cities like Buffalo, Rochester, and Syracuse is lake-effect snow, which occurs when cold air masses move over warmer lake waters and pick up water vapor, which then freezes and falls as snow. Also, the average high temperature in Buffalo in January is 32°F (0°C). In New York City, it's 40°F (4.4°C). That's a fairly significant difference, but given that the two cities are almost 400 miles apart, it's not really that surprising. I'm not sure a lot of people realize how big a state New York actually is.

Question: Why do some animals eat their own feces? Such as Rabbits and pigs?
Answer: I can't speak to pigs, but technically, the “feces" rabbits eat isn't really feces, meaning it's not really waste. Rabbits produce two kinds of droppings: regular feces, and cecotropes. A rabbit's diet is primarily fiber, and fibrous foods are often less nutrient-dense than other foods, so the rabbit needs to maximize the amount of nutrients it gets from its food. After a rabbit eats, the food is separated (in the intestinal tract) into the more fibrous waste and the more nutritious portion. The fibrous waste is excreted as feces — this is largely why rabbit feces is mostly dry and has no real smell to it. The nutritious bits enter the cecum and are formed into cecotropes, which look quite a bit different than regular poo. For optimum health, rabbits need the vitamins, proteins, and minerals contained in the cecotropes, which is why they eat them. (I'll note, in the year and a half that I've had my rabbit, I've never actually seen him eat his cecotropes, but nor have I ever seen any cecotropes themselves, which means he always eats them, just never while I'm watching.) It's not a whole lot different than ruminant mammals like cows, goats, deer, and buffalo chewing cud; the only real difference is that the reingestion by ruminants is done via regurgitation — basically, they throw up partially digested food and re-chew it. (EDIT: I should add, cud-chewing animals are known as foregut fermenters, while rabbits and other monogastric herbivores, like horses, capybaras, and rhinos, are called hindgut fermenters.) But it's a little misleading to say that rabbits eat their own feces, because the excretions they eat are substantially different than their regular feces, and a rabbit that does not consume its cecotropes will be nutrient deficient. They don't do it for pleasure or for kicks, but for their health, and if you have a pet rabbit and notice cecotropes laying around, a trip to the vet is probably a good idea. EDIT: Comments disabled. Question: Are there any specific pet breeds that are more likely to develop certain health conditions?
Answer: Rabbit breeds with lop ears and brachycephalic (short) faces are much more likely to develop certain health problems than breeds with normal faces and upright ears. People tend to love lops — the Holland lop, which is also highly brachycephalic, is presently the most popular breed of pet rabbit in both the U.S. and UK — because they look kind of like stuffed animals, but the harsh truth is that lop ears are totally unnatural for rabbits. The shape of the ears means there is a kink in the ear canal, making it narrower and increasing the chances of hearing impairment or even total deafness. Lops are also more prone to earwax buildup, ear infections, and severe mite infestations than erect-eared rabbits. And while it's not necessarily a health problem, per se, communication with other rabbits is more difficult for lops, because they can't move their ears the way they're supposed to be able to. The position of a rabbit's ears tells you a lot about their mood, but the range of motion in lop ears is limited. The shape of a lop's skull also makes them more likely to have dental problems like malocclusion, molar spurs, and overgrown molars, and lop breeds that are also especially brachycephalic — like the Holland lop — may require the extraction of teeth due to misalignment and overgrowth. This also goes for erect-eared breeds that are brachycephalic. Rabbits' teeth have open roots and never stop growing, so their incisors need to line up perfectly in order not to overgrow. A brachycephalic head in rabbits means the lower jaw is longer than the upper jaw, and that can lead the teeth to become misaligned. One recent study indicated that lop rabbits are 15 times more likely to experience significant discomfort during vet examinations, 12 times more likely to experience molar overgrowth, and 23 times more likely to have incisor disease than erect-eared rabbits. Brachycephalic rabbits also are prone to respiratory problems and eye issues, such as deformed tear ducts (this is also true of brachy cat breeds like the Persian). So brachycephalic breeds are more prone to weepy eye and conjunctivitis. In addition to the Holland lop, brachycephalic rabbit breeds include the Jersey wooly, Lionhead, and Netherland dwarf, while lop breeds include the English lop, French lop, Mini lop, and American fuzzy lop. Rabbits are pretty different anatomically from dogs, but one thing they have in common is that smaller breeds and mixed breeds tend to live longer than large or giant breeds and purebreds. Most importantly, before you decide to run out and get an adorable lop or brachy faced dwarf, remember that these breeds often experience more pain or discomfort in their day to day lives than plain old erect-eared, standard faced rabbits. Personally, I feel it's unethical to breed lops, or to breed for brachycephaly. It's done out of human vanity, with little or no thought as to the well-being of the animals who have to live with what are essentially deformities that we think are “cute".

Question: Which famous films in your opinion received the wrong age rating?
Answer: Eighth Grade. The writing and directorial debut of comedian Bo Burnham, the film, released in 2018, centers on shy, socially awkward 13-year-old Kayla Day (Elsie Fisher), who is about to graduate from her suburban New York middle school and move on to high school. Kayla lives with her earnest single dad Mark (Josh Hamilton) — who finds his daughter way cooler than she will ever find herself — and although she posts YouTube vlogs about “Being Yourself” and “Putting Yourself Out There”, she probably needs her own advice more than her (nonexistent) audience does. In every interaction with her peers, she is a bundle of nerves, her speech awkward, hesitant, and punctuated by “ums", “likes", and “sorrys”. Eighth Grade is a great film, maybe one of the best films about adolescence that I've ever seen. Fisher's performance is note-perfect as an imperfect girl — an ordinary Gen Z teen with bad posture, adolescent acne, and baby fat, who lives through social media and desperately wants to be one of the cool kids, but can barely even bring herself to speak to any of them. Kayla isn't bullied or ostracized, she's just… invisible. She longs to befriend the popular girls, who barely acknowledge her existence. She pines for basketball star Aidan (Luke Prael), who's cute but a total jerk, already seeking nudes and sexual favors at 13. On her high school “shadow day", she's paired with a sweet and friendly 12th grader named Olivia (Emily Robinson), who invites her to hang out with her friends at the mall, but one of those friends, Riley (Daniel Zolghadri), doesn't have the best of intentions towards Kayla. The film is rated R by the MPAA for “language and sexual material”, but that R rating means that the film wasn't accessible in theaters for the demographic who probably needed to see it most: young teens. Yes, there are a few sexually suggestive scenes, and a “truth or dare" scene that's painful in its intensity and sinister implications. But these are not things kids should be sheltered from, and many young teens could also find a lot to identify with. Eighth Grade is an honest movie, one that shows the angst and awkwardness of puberty which is and has always been a reality for so many teenagers. Keeping its message from the very kids who could most benefit from watching it was, in my opinion, a mistake.

Question: What is the most impressive mammal animal you have ever seen?
Answer: I'm going to answer in terms of animals that I've seen a) in person, and b) in the wild, and that would probably have to be moose (what Europeans call elk). It's difficult to comprehend just how big these animals are until you see them up close. A bull moose can stand over 7 feet at the shoulder, weigh almost 1,700 pounds, and have antlers that span over 6 feet in diameter. Even cows — and moose are highly sexually dimorphic — can get to over a thousand pounds. These are animals that dwarf the average Thoroughbred, and if sufficiently provoked, could very easily kill a human being. (They are also not typically afraid of us, and unlike most wild animals, they usually will not flee just due to our presence. It's like they know they could fuck us up if they wanted.) The first time I saw moose in person, in Rocky Mountain National Park, I was in awe. I just wanted to stand there and stare at them all day. I don't know if you'd call them beautiful animals, necessarily, but holy cow, are they impressive. Bull: Cow:

Question: Are air purifiers safe for guinea pigs and rabbits?
Answer: Of course they are, why wouldn't they be? Question: Why do people keep naming their children the same old common names like John, Michael, Anthony, Alex, Sophia, Anne, Sarah and Mary and what kind of name would you choose if you had a kid?
Answer: Some names are timeless and will never go out of style. A name like Michael is classic; you can find Michaels of any age. You can go by Michael, or Mike, Mikey, Mick, or, as my 20-something cousin does, Mickey. Generally speaking, nobody has to ask how to spell or pronounce it. It's a sturdy, dependable name. So are William, Anne, and Sarah. You have to remember that your kid doesn't just have to live with their name as a kid, they're going to be stuck with it all their lives (unless they decide to go to the hassle of legally changing it), so why saddle them with something trendy or, worse, super unusual? Studies have shown that people with unusual names have a harder time finding employment, and even are more likely to be incarcerated. I'm not saying it's fair to allow a name to influence your decision to hire or not hire someone, but it happens nonetheless. Names also go in and out of style like other fashion trends. 30 years ago, nobody outside of Ireland or maybe the UK named their sons Aidan — the only Aidan I'd ever heard of growing up was the actor Aidan Quinn (who is American, but whose parents were from Ireland). In 1990, it wasn't even in the top 1,000 baby names in the U.S. Ten years later, it was in the top ten, while today, it's still top 25, and it's no longer an unusual name at all. Aidan is a more common name for American baby boys today than John, Anthony, or Alex. It's also funny that, at least in the U.S., the only one of the names you listed that's in the top ten most popular for either boys or girls is Sophia. Mary is actually a very uncommon name for American babies these days, not even top 100. Naming your kid Mary is more against the grain than naming her Harper or Amelia — both of which are top ten names in the United States. If I had a kid — I do not and never will — for a boy I've always liked Alexander, James, and Thomas. I'd also have considered Edward, after my dad and brother, although Eddie is my pet rabbit's name. For a girl, perhaps the name I was almost given, Alexandra (assuming I didn't already have a son named Alex), or possibly Kathleen after my mother, although an Irish name like Kathleen doesn't go very well with my Italian surname, and my mom went by Kay, which is another name I like. But you'd never catch me naming my kid Harper or Ava, or that current plague of a name for boys, Liam. I'd sooner go with Mary or John.

Question: Do pretty and skinny girls know they make other girls hate themselves? Do they feel good about it?
Answer: Perhaps you should refrain from laying your insecurities at other people's feet. What would you suggest? That every pretty girl take a razor blade to her own face and disfigure it, or every skinny girl deliberately pack on a hundred pounds, just to make YOU feel better? I grew up with an older sister who was always beautiful. Tall, slim, and beautiful, where I was average height and curvy, and on top of that, she's extroverted and charming where I'm introverted and socially awkward. To this day — I'm now 49, and she just turned 60 — my sister commands attention when she walks into a room, just by virtue of her mere presence. When I was in my 20s and we'd go to bars together, I was like the invisible woman. I resented my sister for years, because I knew I could never measure up. I was never going to be 5′9″ and a size 4; I'm 5′5″ and a size 8 to 10; at my thinnest I was a size 6, and at my heaviest, a size 14. But what I didn't do was suggest that she should be someone or something other than who and what she was in order to ease my own insecurities, or blame her for being beautiful and charming. I never wished ugliness upon my sister, and if I had, I'd be a terrible fucking person. My sister has been forsaken by so many of her female friends over the years, women who couldn't handle the fact that she got more male attention than they did. Many of them told her that to her face — “I don't want to hang out with you anymore, you always get all the attention”. How do you think that made her feel? Was that fair? She was just being herself. And she was a good friend; always there for people, never stabbed any of her friends in the back. Maybe if those women — many of whom were themselves perfectly physically attractive — worked on their own confidence levels and shitty personalities, they'd have gotten more attention. There are average-looking and/or overweight women (and men) all over the world who get plenty of attention, who can command a room. Because they have confidence in who they are, and they don't place responsibility for their insecurities on other people. The only person responsible for your happiness is you. So quit the woe is me bullshit and work on making yourself happy rather than blaming other people for your low self-esteem. It's not their responsibility, it's yours.

Question: How come some people can't live without makeup when it's natural beauty that matters the most?
Answer: It's natural beauty that matters the most to whom? To you? Are you the one who decides what matters most to everyone? What about people who aren't naturally beautiful? And don't give me that horseshit about how everybody is beautiful, because we both know that's not true. Look, I very rarely wear makeup, of any kind. I think the last time I put on any makeup was for my Aunt Jane's funeral in October of 2021. That's my choice. It doesn't affect my life, nor does it affect yours, so why concern yourself with it? Especially if your “concern” manifests as you judging people, as if wearing makeup is indicative of some kind of moral or personal failing? Some people like to wear makeup. Some people view makeup as an art form (and there are people out there who really are artists when it comes to makeup). Some people feel they look better with makeup. Leave them be. It doesn't matter why they wear makeup. It's their life, and they're not hurting you.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why don't you keep your rabbits in cages?
Answer: Why don’t cat owners keep their cats in cages? Or dog owners? I will never understand why it should be morally acceptable to keep a rabbit in a 5 square foot cage for 23 hours a day, when if the same thing was done to a dog or cat, people would be screaming animal cruelty. Rabbits are energetic and athletic animals that need exercise and space to run. Happy rabbits love to do zoomies and binkies, which they simply cannot do in a cage. Keeping them locked in a cage all the time also separates them from you, and makes it much more difficult to form a real bond with them. It kills me when people say rabbits don't bond with their owners or are boring pets. Given the proper environment, attention, and stimulation, that's just not true. It's also possible to litter train rabbits pretty reliably, and spaces can be rabbit-proofed to prevent damage or injury. A large exercise pen is actually considerably cheaper than a cage, and easier to clean if your rabbit is litter trained. I do a full cleaning of Eddie's pen once a week — which mainly involves switching out his blanket for a fresh one — spot clean in between, and empty and clean his litterbox every other day. It's a million times easier than cleaning a cage, which has to be done weekly at a minimum. Cages are even worse if you don't litter train the rabbit and instead force him or her to use their entire living space as a giant litterbox (which also seems cruel to me, especially seeing as rabbits are fastidious animals who hate being dirty). Have you ever seen the feet of a rabbit kept in a cage? They're invariably stained with urine, and that is not the rabbit's fault. Now, I don't free roam my rabbit 24/7, for a couple of reasons, but he lives in a large exercise pen with plenty of room to run around, and gets an average of 5 to 6 hours outside his pen every day in my rabbit-proofed living room. I like having him hang out on the couch with me when I watch movies, and he likes getting to run around and play, snooze on the rug, jump up for cuddles, etc. The question is kind of strange to me, really. Why would I do this to an animal I love? Rabbits are not hamsters or gerbils. There's literally no logical reason to keep them in cages. It's an antiquated and cruel practice that needs to become extinct.

Question: After passing away at age 81, how will David Crosby be remembered within the music industry, by those he played with in the iconic music groups, The Byrds and Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young, and by other industry artists and insiders who knew him?
Answer: Both Graham Nash and Stephen Stills have posted heartfelt tributes to Crosby since his passing. Nash said on Instagram: I know people tend to focus on how volatile our relationship has been at times, but what has always mattered to David and me more than anything was the pure joy of the music we created together, the sound we discovered with one another, and the deep friendship we shared over all these many long years. David was fearless in life and in music. He leaves behind a tremendous void as far as sheer personality and talent in this world. He spoke his mind, his heart, and his passion through his beautiful music and leaves an incredible legacy. These are the things that matter most. Stills took to Twitter to say: David and I butted heads a lot over time, but they were mostly glancing blows, yet still left us numb skulls. I was happy to be at peace with him. He was without question a giant of a musician, and his harmonic sensibilities were nothing short of genius. The glue that held us together as our vocals soared, like Icarus, towards the sun. I am deeply saddened at his passing and shall miss him beyond measure. Look, Crosby's reputation is well known. He himself acknowledged that he wasn't an easy person to get along with — I believe the word he used was “asshole”. I myself have been highly critical of him personally, even while acknowledging his vast talent, and I felt a genuine twinge when I read the news. And that's as a mere fan, not someone who knew him and made music with him for 50+ years. CSN are one of my favorite bands, and there would have been, could have been, no CSN without David Crosby. It's also well known that he butted heads with his bandmates both in The Byrds and CSN(Y), but I think the statements by Nash and Stills make it pretty clear that they had tremendous respect for him as a musician, and love for him like a brother. Sometimes we fight with our siblings, and we don't always see eye to eye, but underneath there is love, and that seems to be how Stills and Nash, at least, see Crosby: he was a difficult man, with a huge ego, and not always the easiest to get along with, but also a huge talent who made fantastic music for a long time. EDIT: Crosby's other former bandmate, Neil Young, has now also released a statement — one that is all the more moving considering the two had not been on speaking terms for almost a decade. (Thank you to Patrick Lewis Van Ness for the link.) It reads: David is gone, but his music lives on. The soul of CSNY, David’s voice and energy were at the heart of our band. His great songs stood for what we believed in and it was always fun and exciting when we got to play together. ‘Almost Cut My Hair’ ‘Dejavu’, and so many other great songs he wrote were wonderful to jam on and Stills and I had a blast as he kept us going on and on. His singing with Graham was so memorable, their duo spot a highlight of so many of our shows. We had so many great times, especially in the early years. Crosby was a very supportive friend in my early life, as we bit off big pieces of our experience together. David was the catalyst of many things. My heart goes out to Jan and Django, his wife and son. Lots of love to you. Thanks David for your spirit and songs, Love you man. I remember the best times!

Question: Which movie villain would be considered a hero in a different film?
Answer: Little Bill Daggett in Unforgiven. In fact, I'd go so far as to say that Little Bill would be the hero in the same movie had the story been told from his perspective. The film is intentionally somewhat ambiguous as concerns its antagonist, Little Bill (Gene Hackman), and its protagonist, Will Munny (Clint Eastwood). It's all about whose perspective you're viewing the story from. Unforgiven tells the story from Will's perspective, so Will is the one we identify with. But the same story told from Little Bill's point of view would look different. SPOILERS AHEAD. It's 1881, and Little Bill is the sheriff of Big Whiskey, Wyoming. One night, two local ranch hands, Quick Mike and Davey Bunting, visit the town brothel, where a prostitute named Delilah (Anna Thomson) makes the mistake of laughing at Mike's diminutive penis, leading him to cut her face and disfigure her in a rage. Little Bill orders that the brothel owner, Skinny DuBois, be compensated for loss of revenue (due to Delilah now being seen as less desirable) with payment in horses, but the two men are not punished other than in the loss of the horses, although a contrite Davey — the one who did not cut her — offers her personally (as opposed to Skinny) his best horse as compensation. Outraged by the lack of punishment, the other prostitutes in the brothel, led by Strawberry Alice (Frances Fisher) secretly pool their money and offer a $1,000 bounty for the two men's deaths. Meanwhile, in Kansas, a cocky young man calling himself the Schofield Kid (Jaimz Wolvett) seeks out infamous outlaw and murderer Will Munny, who is now a widower raising his two kids on a hog farm, and tells him about the bounty, requesting his help. Will, in need of money, recruits his old pal Ned Logan (Morgan Freeman), and they head off to Big Whiskey. Also in pursuit of the bounty is English Bob (Richard Harris), a gunfighter and killer who has with him his own biographer to document his exaggerated tales. Because guns are illegal in Big Whiskey, Little Bill and his deputies disarm and then severely beat Bob and throw him in jail when he refuses to leave town. The Kid manages to kill Quick Mike, but the act overwhelms him with remorse, and he forsakes the mission. Will successfully kills Davey (who, we should remember, committed no actual crime) after Ned also realizes that he doesn't want to kill the man. But Ned is then captured by Little Bill, who tortures him to find out Will's true identity, and then kills him. The Kid, meanwhile, goes back to Kansas with the reward money, which he gives to Ned's wife and Will's kids. Will seeks out Little Bill to avenge Ned's death. He kills Skinny along with three of Bill's deputies before killing Bill himself, then leaves town after promising to come back if any more of the prostitutes are harmed. The epilogue suggests that Will took his kids to San Francisco and became a prosperous dry goods merchant. Now, really, what made Little Bill a villain? Sure, he didn't whip or imprison the man who cut Delilah, instead offering Skinny the only compensation, but if you consider the times, that's not terribly surprising. And that's literally the only thing he does that can really be considered “bad". We see him as savage for the beating of English Bob, but Bob was actually a way worse person than Bill, a murderer and a braggart, and he was breaking the law by trying to bring guns into town. We also hate him for what he does to Ned, because we love Ned, but really, Ned brought it on himself by seeking the bounty in the first place. So did Will — who, by the way, is a man who has killed women and children in his time, not some hero. And is death really a fair punishment for the two men anyway? Especially Davey, who never laid a hand on Delilah, and even tried to compensate her for the actions of his friend? Will is the hero and Little Bill is the villain only because the story is told from Will's point of view. We travel with Will and Ned, we get to know them, and so we sympathize with them, not with Little Bill, who's really just a lawman trying to maintain order in a Wild West town. Little Bill is tough, but he's also mostly fair. The movie even kind of acknowledges this, as right before Will kills him, Little Bill says “I don't deserve to die this way". And Will tells him, “’deserve’ ain't got nothing to do with it”. The ambiguity of the story is one of the things that makes Unforgiven such a great film, but the fact remains that the vast majority of people who watch the movie are going to see Little Bill as the villain — due almost entirely to perspective. EDIT: Comments are now disabled. For one, because there are people who can't agree to disagree and want to turn this into a debate site, which it is not, and for another, because the point of the answer is apparently flying over too many heads. I wrote the answer straight up — related the plot of the film mostly as it's given to us. And everyone is commenting based on the POV we're given in the film — Will's POV. When the answer literally says that if it was told from from Little Bill's perspective, he could well be the “hero". Instead of starting with Will on his hog farm, start with Little Bill trying to finish building his damn house, and follow the events of the film from his point of view. It looks different. I'm not debating this anymore. Anyone who thinks it's a bad answer is free to downvote it, because I honestly don't care anymore. Have at it.

Question: What actor/actress made an unforgettable appearance in a classic Hollywood film, then disappeared?
Answer: Darlene Cates. She wasn't actually an actor, but a Texas housewife and mother struggling with morbid obesity, whom screenwriter Peter Hedges saw on an episode of the Sally Jessy Raphael talk show in 1992, and who was subsequently cast as Bonnie Grape, the housebound mother of Johnny Depp's title character in What's Eating Gilbert Grape. Cates received widespread critical acclaim for her terrific performance, but other than a couple of guest appearances on TV shows, she never acted again, although in 2012 it was reported that she had lost 244 pounds, to drop from 575 to 331 pounds. She died of natural causes in 2017 at age 69. Also, Peter Ostrum. He was a sixth grader in Cleveland, Ohio, when he beat out thousands of other boys to win the lead role of Charlie Bucket in Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory in 1970. After the success of the film, Ostrum was offered a three-movie contract, but turned it down, and eventually went to veterinary school at Cornell University, graduating in 1984. He didn't like to tell people he had played Charlie — he says he wanted to be judged for who he was, not what he had done — and even his wife didn't know until she met his mother, who spilled the beans. Today, he is 65 and lives in rural Glenfield, New York, where he works as a farm veterinarian, and says he has no regrets about giving up his acting career.

Question: Why does my 2-month-old bunny hate going in her big wire cage?
Answer: Because rabbits don't belong in cages. If I put you in a “big wire cage", would you be jazzed about it? A cage is a cage is a cage. A rabbit that doesn't want to be in its own living space is in the wrong living space, and/or is not being given enough free roaming time. A rabbit's home should be a safe haven, not a prison. My rabbit loves his free roam time, but his pen is his safe space, and he freely goes in and out whenever the door is open, which is every evening for a good four or five hours. I would suggest a puppy exercise pen instead of a cage. Four feet by four feet, at least 30 to 36 inches tall. You can buy these on Amazon or Chewy for around $50, much cheaper than any cage. I'll also reiterate that a rabbit needs free roaming time, at least a few hours a day, in a rabbit-proofed area. She should have free access to go in and out, meaning the entrance should be on the floor and you shouldn't have to pick her up to take her out or put her in. If you give a rabbit choices, they make them. If you give her an adequately sized enclosure with lots of toys and enrichment, as well as a litterbox and hidey house, she will come to see it as a home that makes her feel safe, not a cell she's always being locked in. It's not supposed to be a punishment, but she seems to see it that way, which is why she doesn't want to go in. So make it less of a punishment.

Question: What are the best tribute songs?
Answer: “Green Grass and High Tides", Outlaws. People tend to assume it's about weed, due to the title, but Hughie Thomasson actually wrote it as a tribute to some of his deceased rock idols, most notably Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, and Jim Morrison. The title was a reversal of High Tide and Green Grass — the subtitle of the Rolling Stones' first greatest hits album. I never got super into the Outlaws, but that particular song is a masterpiece. Also, “Song to Woody", by Bob Dylan. Bob's tribute to his idol Woody Guthrie, it was the first song he ever wrote, and he's said that prior to writing it, he didn't see himself as a songwriter — he had only covered old folk songs. Dylan had become friendly with Guthrie after seeking him out in the psychiatric hospital where Woody was dying of Huntington's disease. When Woody became too sick for Dylan to visit him anymore, Bob wrote “Song to Woody". The melody is that of Woody's song “1913 Massacre", and it's one of my favorite Dylan songs. Just beautiful.

Question: Is it possible to have a pet for depression even when pets are not allowed because I rent?
Answer: It depends on where you are, but in the U.S., if you have a legitimate mental illness (like depression), you can have a pet certified as an emotional support animal (ESA). The certification has to come from a therapist or other mental health professional, and there has to be a diagnosis. ESAs do not have the same privileges as service animals — you can't take them into public places that only allow service animals, for instance, and airlines are not required to allow them to fly in the cabin — but they do allow you to apply to have a “no pets” policy waived for rental housing. Federal law prohibits discrimination against people with mental illness, and not allowing a legitimate ESA is usually seen as discrimination. If you do not have an actual diagnosis of depression or another mental health condition, absolutely do not try to get around it. There are sketchy organizations out there that will write you a fraudulent ESA letter, but because a lot of people have gone this route, protections for ESAs have been lowered, so falsifying it only hurts others who have legitimate mental illness and ESAs. As a side note, in the U.S., just about any species of pet can be designated an ESA — not just dogs and cats, but also rabbits, rodents, ferrets, birds, mini horses, even reptiles. It just has to be demonstrated that the animal provides legitimate emotional comfort and support.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is the politics of New York basically NYC vs Upstate?
Answer: Not necessarily. Where I live now would probably be considered upstate, and it's considerably more liberal than Staten Island, which is in New York City, or Putnam County, in the NYC metro area, where I grew up. My cousins live in an equally rural town about half an hour from here, and they literally constitute the only majority-liberal branch of my family aside from me and my brothers — my family members from NYC are all much more conservative. The larger cities in New York state — Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse, Albany, etc. — tend to be more liberal, while a lot of more rural areas are more conservative, but that's not always the case, either. My farming town is very small and quite rural, but the county — which is equally rural, not a single actual city in it — has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 1992. (I was quite amused recently when some lady on here asserted that the people where I live aren't “real" rural people because they're not uber conservative.) There are also a lot of people in upstate New York who are transplants from elsewhere, including NYC. I know several people in my area who moved up here from the city or its suburbs. When people move, they often bring their personal politics with them. I guess the short answer is, it's not a cut and dried thing. If you look at a political map of New York state, you'll find an awful lot of red upstate, but also pockets of blue, while parts of downstate, the city, and Long Island are heavily red. So it's definitely not fair to say that all of upstate is conservative, or that all of NYC is liberal.

Question: How do I save my rabbit? He's refusing to eat and hasn't been for the past few days. My mom says she doesn't have any money so the vet isn't an option. What do I do?
Answer: Honestly? There's not much you can do, because you don't know why he's not eating. Rabbits don't just stop eating unless there is something wrong with them, and only a vet can tell you what the problem might be. He needs to see a vet. Call local vets and see if a payment plan is a possibility. If not, you can try syringe feeding him Critical Care, if you can get some, to at least keep his digestive tract moving, but if that's not a possibility, ultimately, if you really love him, you do the right thing and surrender him to a no-kill shelter or rescue where he might be able to be saved. Rabbits hide signs of illness or injury for as long as possible, so by the time it's evident that they're sick, the window of time to save them is often very small. Frankly, questions like this infuriate me, and I'd like to shake your mother. If you cannot afford to provide vet care for an animal, you don't get an animal. Animals get sick and injured. They're living beings, not objects, and not taking a sick animal to the vet is outright animal cruelty.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What was the most legendary thing your grandmother did?
Answer: My Gramma, Catherine “Kitty” Finnegan, was her parents' oldest surviving child — they had 8 kids, but four, including their firstborn, Annie, died in childhood. My great-grandmother, Mary, had her 8th child, my great-uncle Joe, in March of 1922. Gramma was 13, her brother John was 7, and her sister Elizabeth (Lee) was three and a half. Mary died of childbirth complications shortly after Joe's birth, leaving her husband John a single father of four, including a newborn. My great-grandfather was not a wealthy man. He also had no family in the United States; they were all back in Ireland, as he and Mary had immigrated in 1907. So he was faced with the very real possibility of having to put his children in an orphanage, because he could not afford a nanny and had to work. But the kids didn't end up in an orphanage. Because Gramma raised her three younger siblings herself. 13 years old, and she took on a 7-year-old, a toddler, and a newborn. She did the cooking and cleaning and washing, she got them fed and off to school. It must have been incredibly difficult, and in her later years, my Gramma wore her early life's hardship all over her face, which always looked older than its years. She was also an eternally patient woman, and I guess she'd have to have learned patience, basically being the mother to three kids when she was mostly still a kid herself. But she kept her family together. I remember myself at 13, and there is literally no way I could have raised three kids. I couldn't have raised one kid. I've always seen my Gramma — who also, as an adult, went on to raise four kids of her own, and to handle all the family's bills and finances, since my Grampa was illiterate — as possibly the most badass woman ever. That's my Gramma on the right, with my Great-Uncle Mike (Lee's husband), my Grampa Jack, my Uncle Jackie, and my mom. Taken at my grandparents' apartment in the Bronx in the mid-1950s.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What person destroyed their entire life by making one simple mistake?
Answer: Samantha Josephson. In March of 2019, New Jersey native Samantha was 21, about to graduate from the University of South Carolina, and then go on to law school at Drexel University, where she had a full scholarship. On the evening of March 29th, she went out for drinks in downtown Columbia with some friends, but grew tired, and told them she was going to take an Uber back to campus. But Samantha never made it home. Instead, her body was found by turkey hunters in a rural area 65 miles from Columbia the next day. She'd been stabbed 120 times. Surveillance footage from local businesses showed Samantha getting into her Uber — a black Chevy Impala. Except it wasn't her Uber — that was Samantha's mistake. The car was owned by 24-year-old Nathaniel Rowland, who had reportedly been driving around the neighborhood hoping someone would mistake it for an Uber. The car had childproof locks engaged, so once Samantha got in, she was trapped, and the terror she must have felt when Rowland began driving in the opposite direction from campus must have been nightmarish. We don't know exactly why Rowland — who had no history of violent crime — killed Samantha. He didn't know her, had never even met her. The day after the murder, he was posting casually on Facebook as if it was business as usual, even as he still had her phone and blood in his car, and her DNA under his fingernails. It's believed that he just wanted to kill someone, and Samantha was the person unlucky enough to get into his car. The judge called it a “crime of opportunity". Rowland, who was said to be remorseless and emotionless during his trial, was found guilty of first degree murder and sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. It's terrifying that such people exist (and also why I refuse to use services like Uber or Lyft) — this wasn't revenge, or jealousy, or greed, it was just murder for the sake of murder. Samantha Josephson made one simple mistake, and she paid for it with her life.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Do you think any of the Manson family members will ever get paroled?
Answer: Assuming you mean Manson murderers — Squeaky Fromme was paroled in 2009 after serving 34 years for her attempted assassination of President Gerald Ford, and several other Manson Family members have served time for various crimes — one has already been paroled. People seem to focus solely on the Tate-LaBianca murders, and to overlook the fact that Manson and his followers were convicted of two other slayings: those of music teacher Gary Hinman, and Spahn Ranch hand and movie stuntman Donald “Shorty" Shea. Bobby Beausoleil remains incarcerated for Hinman's murder, and Bruce Davis is also still incarcerated for his participation in both murders. However, also convicted of murdering Shea was 18-year-old Steve “Clem" Grogan. Grogan was a high school dropout whose parents sent him to live on Spahn Ranch to work, in hopes of correcting his budding criminal behavior, but instead he met Charles Manson, and soon fell under Charlie's spell. Steve Grogan after his arrest: Grogan, along with Tex Watson (allegedly) and Davis, beat, tortured, and stabbed the 35-year-old Shea to death on Manson's orders. He was initially sentenced to death for the crime, but his sentence was subsequently reduced to life in prison by Judge James Kolts, who called him “too stupid and too hopped up on drugs to decide anything on his own". Shorty Shea with his wife Magdalene, whose race was reportedly just one reason Manson, an unapologetic racist, disliked Shorty: Throughout his incarceration, Grogan was a model prisoner who worked with young inmates to deter them from a life of crime; he denounced and distanced himself from Manson very early on, and helped investigators locate Shea's remains not far from Spahn Ranch in 1977. He was paroled in 1985, at age 34, and to the best of my knowledge, has never been in trouble since. He reportedly married, had two children, and lives in the San Francisco Bay Area, where he is a musician. Should he have been paroled? If the prison system is supposed to be about rehabilitating people, I don't see why not. The fact that he's been a free man for almost 40 years and has never re-offended would indicate that he was, in fact, reformed and rehabilitated. (Perhaps Shorty Shea's family would disagree with me, and I probably couldn't blame them if they did.) So, again, one of the Manson murderers has, in fact, been paroled already. Will any of the others — Beausoleil, Davis, Tex Watson, Patricia Krenwinkel, Leslie Van Houten — ever be paroled? I doubt it. Perhaps people forgot about Shorty Shea — I mean, there have never been photos of his desecrated corpse made public, the details of his murder differ depending on who you ask, and his body wasn't found until 8 years after he was killed. But the Tate-LaBianca murders, at least, are still prominent in many minds, and the sheer savagery of Hinman's torture and murder also probably means that Beausoleil and Davis — who today are 75 and 80 years old, respectively — will never be released. Van Houten, whom it's often been said is the only one of the Tate-LaBianca killers with a legitimate shot at parole, has actually been recommended for parole four times, but each time, California's governor — first Jerry Brown, then Gavin Newsom — has overruled the parole board, and she remains in prison. It's just too easy for people to look at the photos of Rosemary LaBianca's savaged body, so I don't believe Van Houten will ever be released. And if Leslie, who only participated in Rosemary's murder (and may not even have stabbed her until she was already dead), won't be released, neither will any of the others. (EDIT: I forgot to add that Davis — once described as Charlie's right hand man, now a born-again Christian and pastor — has also been recommended for parole multiple times, and like Van Houten, the sitting governor has vetoed it each time.) Steve Grogan will likely go down in history as the only convicted Manson murderer to ever be paroled.
